options.B: Electrical impulses travel too fast through the damaged heart chambers.
options.C: Inflammation damages the heart muscle cells, reducing their ability to contract effectively.
options.D: Fluid builds up inside the pericardial sac and crushes the coronary arteries.

explanation: When the heart muscle (myocardium) is inflamed, it gets tired and weak, losing its strong pumping power. This causes blood to back up—leading to heart failure symptoms.

question: Why must blood cultures be drawn BEFORE starting antibiotics in a suspected heart infection?

options.A: To prevent antibiotics from killing the bacteria in the sample and masking the diagnosis
options.B: To make sure the patient's blood pressure remains stable during the blood draw
options.C: To allow the white blood cell count time to normalize naturally
options.D: To ensure the laboratory technician is available to process the blood immediately

explanation: If we give antibiotics first, they might kill the germs in our lab sample, leaving us guessing about what infection we are fighting!

question: A patient is admitted with suspected infective endocarditis. Which test is best for directly viewing the valve growths?

options.A: Standard 12-lead ECG
options.B: Chest X-ray
options.C: Echocardiogram
options.D: Complete blood count

explanation: An echocardiogram uses sound waves (like an ultrasound for the heart) to let doctors actually see those moving valve growths clearly.

question: How long do patients usually need antibiotic treatment for infective endocarditis?

options.A: Four to six weeks
options.B: Six months to a year
options.C: One to two weeks
options.D: Three to five days

explanation: Germs hiding inside heart valve growths are very hard for drugs to reach. That's why patients need a long course of IV antibiotics, usually 4 to 6 weeks.

question: Why is colchicine sometimes given along with NSAIDs to treat pericarditis?

options.A: To dissolve existing blood clots inside the heart chambers
options.B: To destroy resistant bacterial strains in the bloodstream
options.C: To permanently lower the patient's resting heart rate
options.D: To help prevent future episodes of the condition from returning

explanation: Colchicine is a helpful anti-inflammatory medicine added to treatment to stop pericarditis from coming back to trouble the patient again.

question: Which of these is a common reason a patient with infective endocarditis might need surgical valve replacement?

options.A: Temporary joint pain in the lower extremities
options.B: Heart failure caused by severe valve damage
options.C: A slight elevation in white blood cell count
options.D: Mild fatigue during routine daily activities

explanation: When an infection destroys the heart valves so badly that the heart starts failing or fluid overloads the body, surgery becomes necessary to fix or replace the valve.

question: What is a major nursing priority right after a patient has heart valve surgery for endocarditis?

options.A: Stopping all antibiotic medications once the patient leaves the operating room
options.B: Encouraging immediate heavy physical exercise to strengthen the heart muscle
options.C: Restricting fluid intake completely to prevent any swelling
options.D: Monitoring closely for signs of infection and evaluating neurological status for emboli

explanation: Great nursing care here means staying alert! We watch for any lingering infection and check the patient's brain function (neurological status) to catch any loose clots early.

question: What common complication happens when pieces of a heart valve growth break off and travel in the bloodstream?

options.A: Bone fracture
options.B: Kidney stones
options.C: Stroke
options.D: Asthma attack

explanation: When those infected clumps break free, they travel through blood vessels and can block blood flow to the brain, leading to a stroke. Spotting this early saves lives!

question: Why must high-risk heart patients take antibiotics before certain dental procedures?

options.A: Dental manipulation can introduce bacteria into the bloodstream, which may latch onto damaged heart valves.
options.B: Dental medications frequently interact negatively with cardiac drugs like digoxin.
options.C: Tooth decay directly causes inflammation of the outer pericardial sac.
options.D: Local anesthetics used by dentists weaken the heart muscle permanently.

explanation: Gum bleeding during dental work lets mouth bacteria sneak into the bloodstream. For a vulnerable heart, prophylactic antibiotics act like a shield!

question: What is the name of the thick muscular middle layer of the heart wall that pumps blood?

options.A: Myocardium
options.B: Epicardium
options.C: Pericardium
options.D: Endocardium

explanation: The myocardium is the muscular middle layer of the heart that does the hard work of contracting and pumping blood to the body! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why is inflammation affecting any layer of the heart considered a serious medical concern?

options.A: It exclusively affects the lungs and has no impact on circulation
options.B: It only causes temporary skin rashes on the chest wall
options.C: It can severely compromise the heart's ability to pump blood effectively
options.D: It instantly stops all electrical activity without warning

explanation: Swelling and damage to heart tissues disrupt the normal pumping action, which can lead to heart failure and poor circulation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which position usually helps make chest pain feel better when a patient has pericarditis?

options.A: Reclining deeply with legs elevated
options.B: Lying completely flat on the back
options.C: Sitting upright and leaning forward
options.D: Turning sharply onto the left side

explanation: Leaning forward pulls the heart away from surrounding tissues, reducing painful friction and giving the patient sweet relief. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h2)

question: What creates that scratchy 'pericardial friction rub' sound heard through a stethoscope?

options.A: Blood leaking backward through a faulty valve
options.B: Blood rushing too fast through narrowed coronary arteries
options.C: Rough, inflamed heart sac layers rubbing against each other
options.D: Air trapped inside the chest cavity

explanation: Think of it like sandpaper: when the pericardial layers get rough from inflammation, they scratch against each other with every heartbeat, creating that distinct sound. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h2)

question: What is the most common cause of myocarditis?

options.A: Viruses
options.B: Fungi
options.C: Parasites
options.D: Prions

explanation: Viruses are the top culprits behind myocarditis worldwide, often attacking the heart muscle after a normal viral infection. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h3)

question: How does myocarditis usually affect the function of the heart muscle?

options.A: It thickens the coronary arteries completely
options.B: It turns the heart muscle hard like bone
options.C: It weakens the muscle walls and lowers pumping efficiency
options.D: It permanently opens up all the valves

explanation: Because inflammation damages the muscle tissue, the heart struggles to squeeze hard, leading to reduced pumping power. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h3)

question: What do we call the infected clumps of platelets and germs that grow on heart valves in endocarditis?

options.A: Atheromas
options.B: Vegetations
options.C: Aneurysms
options.D: Thromboemboli

explanation: In infective endocarditis, clusters of bacteria, platelets, and fibrin build up on the valves like little growths called vegetations. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h4)

question: A patient with endocarditis has small, painful reddish bumps on their finger pads. What are these called?

options.A: Petechiae
options.B: Roth spots
options.C: Osler's nodes
options.D: Janeway lesions

explanation: Osler's nodes are tender, painful bumps that pop up on fingers and toes due to immune complexes settling there. Remember: O for 'Ouch' in Osler's! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h4)

question: Which medication is often given alongside NSAIDs to stop pericarditis from coming back?

options.A: Warfarin
options.B: Digoxin
options.C: Atropine
options.D: Colchicine

explanation: Colchicine works brilliantly alongside NSAIDs to calm down stubborn inflammation and prevent flare-ups. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why do patients with endocarditis need to take antibiotics for many weeks instead of just a few days?

options.A: Pills take a very long time to reach the stomach
options.B: Heart valves have no blood supply and drugs can't reach them easily
options.C: Bacteria hiding inside valve vegetations are hard for drugs to reach
options.D: Short courses always cause skin allergies

explanation: The clumps of bacteria and platelets (vegetations) don't have their own blood vessels, so it takes a long, steady course of antibiotics to fully wipe them out. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why is strict bed rest ordered during the early, active phase of myocarditis?

options.A: To lower the workload on the inflamed heart muscle
options.B: To stop blood clots from forming in the legs
options.C: To stop the kidneys from making too much urine
options.D: To keep the patient's blood pressure high

explanation: Resting lowers the heart rate and reduces the amount of work the heart has to do, giving the sore muscle time to heal. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h6)

question: Which nursing action is most important for tracking fluid buildup in a patient with heart inflammation?

options.A: Doing reflex checks on both arms
options.B: Checking the patient's vision every four hours
options.C: Testing grip strength twice a day
options.D: Checking daily weights and tracking intake and output

explanation: Tracking daily weights and fluid charts is your best early warning system for fluid retention and failing heart function. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h6)

question: What emergency procedure is used to drain extra fluid from around the heart during cardiac tamponade?

options.A: Thoracentesis
options.B: Cardioversion
options.C: Pericardiocentesis
options.D: Paracentesis

explanation: Pericardiocentesis involves gently passing a needle into the pericardial sac to draw out fluid and relieve dangerous pressure on the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h7)

question: What classic set of signs points to cardiac tamponade?

options.A: Slow pulse, flushed skin, and high temperature
options.B: High BP, strong pulses, and clear breath sounds
options.C: Fast breathing, pinpoint pupils, and quiet tummy
options.D: Low BP, muffled heart sounds, and swollen neck veins

explanation: Known as Beck's triad, these three signs (low blood pressure, muffled heart tones from fluid, and distended neck veins) are huge red flags for tamponade! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h7)

question: Why must nurses stress finishing the full course of antibiotics for heart infections?

options.A: Patients will need pills for the rest of their lives
options.B: Incomplete doses make you immune to everything
options.C: Antibiotics expire very quickly in hot weather
options.D: Stopping early can cause the infection to roar back

explanation: Stopping antibiotics early leaves the toughest germs alive, allowing the infection to bounce right back stronger than before. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h8)

question: What routine self-care practice is strongly emphasized to patients at risk for infective endocarditis to prevent bacteria from entering the bloodstream?

options.A: Refusing all routine vaccinations at local health clinics
options.B: Drinking large quantities of palm wine daily
options.C: Maintaining good oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups
options.D: Avoiding all physical exercise for the rest of their lives

explanation: Oral bacteria can easily enter the bloodstream during dental procedures or daily hygiene, making dental care a primary prevention target for endocarditis. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h8)

question: Why can even a small tumour inside the heart cause big trouble?

options.A: The heart muscle cannot heal after a tumour forms
options.B: Cardiac tumours always release toxic chemicals into the blood
options.C: The heart is a constantly moving organ that pumps blood
options.D: Cardiac tumours prevent the lungs from breathing oxygen

explanation: Think about it like a busy pump in a tight space! Because the heart beats continuously, any extra growth inside its chambers gets in the way of normal blood flow. You've got this!

question: Why do some heart tumours cause symptoms that look just like regular heart failure?

options.A: The tumour causes the coronary arteries to permanently spasm
options.B: The tumour takes up space in the heart chambers and reduces the amount of blood pumped out
options.C: Cardiac tumours completely stop the production of red blood cells
options.D: Cardiac tumours directly destroy the brain's ability to regulate heart rate

explanation: When an extra mass takes up room inside the heart, the chambers can't hold or push out enough blood. This causes fluid to back up, mimicking heart failure. Great job thinking it through!

question: What is the most common type of primary heart tumour found in adults?

options.A: Papillary fibroelastoma
options.B: Rhabdomyoma
options.C: Myxoma
options.D: Angiosarcoma

explanation: Myxomas take the crown here! They are the most common primary heart tumours in adults and usually like to set up shop in the left atrium. Keep up the great memorisation!

question: Why can a non-cancerous (benign) heart tumour still be dangerous?

options.A: Its location inside the heart can block blood flow and cause dangerous blockages
options.B: It destroys all the red blood cells passing through the heart
options.C: Benign heart tumours automatically spread to the lungs and liver
options.D: Benign tumours always turn into aggressive cancers over time

explanation: Even though benign tumours aren't cancer, location is everything! Being stuck inside a vital organ means they can physically block blood flow or cause clots. You're doing brilliantly.

question: Which type of heart tumour do nurses see more often in clinical practice?

options.A: Primary papillary fibroelastomas
options.B: Primary malignant sarcomas
options.C: Congenital rhabdomyomas
options.D: Secondary metastatic tumours

explanation: Cancers that travel to the heart from other parts of the body (metastatic tumours) actually happen much more often than tumours that start directly in the heart tissue. Everyday nursing knowledge!

question: How does metastatic cancer commonly affect the heart tissue?

options.A: It prevents the coronary arteries from ever getting blocked
options.B: It causes fluid to build up in the pericardial sac around the heart
options.C: It completely cures any underlying heart valve disease
options.D: It turns the heart muscle into bone tissue

explanation: Cancer cells traveling from elsewhere often invade the sac around the heart (pericardium), causing fluid to build up and squeeze the heart. You're learning clinical realities step by step!

question: Why might a patient with a left atrial myxoma suddenly faint when changing body position?

options.A: The tumour causes a sudden drop in the patient's body temperature
options.B: The heart muscle instantly grows twice its normal size
options.C: The mobile tumour temporarily plugs up the mitral valve, stopping blood flow
options.D: The patient's lungs stop taking in oxygen due to an allergic reaction

explanation: Some tumours hang on a little stalk. When the patient moves, the tumour can swing over and block the valve like a cork in a bottle, cutting off blood supply and causing fainting. Fascinating clinical detail!

question: Which of these is NOT a typical symptom category for patients with heart tumours?

options.A: Signs of heart failure like shortness of breath
options.B: Constitutional signs like fever and weight loss
options.C: Complete loss of the sense of taste
options.D: Embolisation symptoms such as a stroke

explanation: Loss of taste has nothing to do with heart tumours! On the flip side, heart failure signs, fevers, and stroke symptoms are classic warning signs. You've got this!

question: What is usually the first imaging test doctors use to find a heart tumour?

options.A: Routine chest X-ray
options.B: Electrocardiogram (ECG)
options.C: Complete blood count
options.D: Echocardiogram

explanation: An echo uses sound waves to let us safely peek inside the heart chambers. It's quick, painless, and the go-to tool for spotting masses. Brilliant nursing insight!

question: Why do doctors avoid doing a direct needle biopsy of a heart mass?

options.A: It destroys all the electrical conduction pathways in the heart
options.B: It carries a high risk of breaking off pieces of the tumour to cause an embolism
options.C: It is completely impossible to insert any catheter into the heart chambers
options.D: It causes the heart to permanently stop beating within seconds

explanation: Poke a fragile heart tumour with a needle, and pieces might break off and travel through the bloodstream to cause a stroke! Safety first in clinical practice.

question: What is the standard treatment to cure a benign primary heart tumour?

options.A: High-dose radiation therapy alone
options.B: Strict bed rest and fluid restriction
options.C: Surgical excision
options.D: Long-term oral antibiotic therapy

explanation: Since it's a physical mass, the best way to deal with a benign heart tumour is to surgically cut it out. Clean and effective!

question: What is the main goal when caring for a patient with a secondary metastatic tumour in the heart?

options.A: Palliative care and managing symptoms while treating the primary cancer source
options.B: Preventing the patient from ever moving their arms or legs
options.C: Permanent replacement of all four heart valves with artificial ones
options.D: Complete surgical cure of the heart muscle using a heart transplant

explanation: When cancer has spread from elsewhere, the focus shifts to keeping the patient comfortable, managing symptoms, and treating the original cancer source. Compassionate nursing at its best!

question: Why is watching a patient's brain function so important after heart tumour surgery?

options.A: The brain stops receiving oxygen if the patient lies flat
options.B: Tumour fragments or tiny clots could dislodge during surgery and cause a stroke
options.C: Patients with heart surgery always develop sudden memory loss
options.D: Anesthesia permanently damages the brain's visual cortex

explanation: Working inside the heart chambers can accidentally send tiny bits of debris or clots up to the brain. Neurological checks help nurses catch a stroke early!

question: A patient is in the ICU after having a heart myxoma removed. What is a top nursing priority?

options.A: Encouraging heavy weightlifting to rebuild chest muscle strength
options.B: Restricting all fluid intake to zero for the first week
options.C: Monitoring continuous cardiac telemetry and vital signs
options.D: Removing the chest tubes without provider orders

explanation: After heart surgery, keeping a close eye on the heart rhythm and vital signs lets you spot and tackle complications right away. You are thinking like a real ICU nurse!

question: What is the general long-term outlook for a patient who has a benign heart tumour completely removed?

options.A: Poor, with a life expectancy of only a few weeks
options.B: Hopeless without a full heart transplant
options.C: Guarded, because benign tumours always spread to the liver
options.D: Excellent, with most patients returning to normal activities

explanation: Once a benign tumour is successfully taken out, the cure rate is super high and patients usually get right back to their normal lives. Wonderful news for patients!

question: Why do patients who had a myxoma removed still need occasional follow-up scans?

options.A: To check if the lungs are growing new blood vessels
options.B: To measure how fast the patient's hair is growing
options.C: To confirm that the heart has doubled in size
options.D: To monitor for potential recurrence of the tumour over time

explanation: Even though they are benign, certain primary heart tumours can sometimes try to grow back. Routine follow-ups keep patients safe and healthy!

question: What is the primary danger when blood rapidly accumulates inside the pericardial sac?

options.A: It creates high blood pressure throughout the entire body.
options.B: It restricts the heart from filling with blood properly.
options.C: It causes an immediate thickening of the heart valves.
options.D: It stops the lungs from absorbing enough oxygen.

explanation: Blood filling the rigid pericardial space creates pressure that compresses the heart chambers, preventing normal filling during diastole and dropping cardiac output. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why does a heart wall rupture quickly lead to pulseless electrical activity (PEA)?

options.A: The coronary arteries experience massive spasms that stop electrical impulses.
options.B: The brain receives signals to shut down the heart completely.
options.C: The electrical system stops working because the heart muscle dies.
options.D: Blood escapes completely out of the heart chambers, leaving no volume to pump.

explanation: When the heart wall tears, blood pours out into the chest. The electrical sparks might keep firing for a bit, but with no blood left inside to pump, you get PEA. You've got this!

question: Which heart chamber is most frequently injured in penetrating chest trauma due to its front-facing position?

options.A: Left atrium
options.B: Left ventricle
options.C: Right atrium
options.D: Right ventricle

explanation: The right ventricle sits directly behind the sternum, making it the most exposed and frequently injured chamber when sharp or high-speed objects penetrate the chest. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h2)

question: Why is blunt heart injury often harder to spot right away compared to a stab wound?

options.A: X-ray machines cannot take pictures of blunt force trauma.
options.B: The chest wall often shows no open wounds or obvious external damage.
options.C: The heart stops beating completely right away.
options.D: Symptoms only appear several weeks after the accident.

explanation: Because the skin and ribs stay intact, there's no open wound to warn you. That's why nurses have to stay alert for hidden internal bruising!

question: What is a common cause of blunt cardiac injury during a motor vehicle accident?

options.A: Inbreathing toxic exhaust fumes from the damaged engine
options.B: The seatbelt cutting directly across the neck muscles
options.C: The driver hitting their chest against the steering wheel
options.D: Sudden exposure to cold air through broken windows

explanation: Direct impact against the steering wheel during rapid deceleration transmits massive blunt force straight through the sternum to the heart muscle. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h3)

question: A patient develops sudden chest pain and low blood pressure right after getting a central line placed in their neck. What likely happened?

options.A: An infection of the lungs starting in the bronchi
options.B: Iatrogenic cardiac perforation or tamponade
options.C: A severe allergic reaction to the skin cleanser
options.D: A spontaneous heart attack unrelated to the procedure

explanation: Medical procedures like central line placements carry a small risk of accidentally poking the heart or nearby vessels, leading to bleeding around the heart (tamponade). Don't worry, you'll master these procedural complications in no time!

question: What are the three classic signs that make up Beck's triad for cardiac tamponade?

options.A: Chest pain, sweating, and numbness in the left arm
options.B: Muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins, and low blood pressure
options.C: High fever, rapid breathing, and severe coughing fits
options.D: High blood pressure, slow heart rate, and clear lung sounds

explanation: Beck's triad groups together muffled heart sounds from fluid in the pericardium, elevated pressure in the neck veins, and hypotension due to poor cardiac output. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why might a nurse not see all three signs of Beck's triad in every patient with cardiac tamponade?

options.A: Intravenous fluids always hide these specific physical signs.
options.B: Beck's triad only occurs during blunt trauma, never penetrating trauma.
options.C: The triad only appears after the patient has fully recovered.
options.D: The classic signs do not show up in every single patient.

explanation: Textbook signs are great to learn, but real patients don't always read the textbook! Clinical signs vary depending on how fast the bleeding happens.

question: What is the main purpose of doing a FAST scan at the bedside of an emergency trauma patient?

options.A: To count the precise number of broken ribs in the chest wall
options.B: To quickly check for fluid around the heart or in the abdomen
options.C: To test the blood oxygen levels in the main arteries
options.D: To measure the exact electrical output of the heart muscle

explanation: A FAST exam is a rapid ultrasound tool used right at the bedside to spot free fluid or blood around the heart or belly in emergency situations.

question: Which tool is best for giving a detailed, live look at heart valve movement and internal wall damage?

options.A: Bedside pulse oximetry
options.B: Routine blood chemistry panel
options.C: Echocardiogram
options.D: Standard chest X-ray

explanation: An echocardiogram uses sound waves (ultrasound) to let us see the heart valves and walls moving in real time. It's a powerful tool in cardiac care!

question: Why must IV fluids be given carefully to a trauma patient with low blood pressure and suspected heart injury?

options.A: Fluids make the patient's blood too thick to pass through catheters.
options.B: Fluids will instantly cause severe kidney failure within minutes.
options.C: Intravenous solutions interfere with the action of heart medications.
options.D: Too much fluid can increase bleeding and worsen pressure on the heart.

explanation: While fluids help treat shock, pumping too much in too fast can blow away fresh clots, increase bleeding, and put even more dangerous pressure on the heart.

question: A patient with a chest stab wound suddenly loses their pulse and shows PEA (pulseless electrical activity) on the monitor. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Wait for a formal chest X-ray to confirm the cardiac arrest
options.B: Place the patient in a flat, prone position to rest the back
options.C: Administer oral blood pressure medications through a feeding tube
options.D: Prepare equipment for emergency thoracotomy and active resuscitation

explanation: Traumatic arrest with PEA is a critical emergency. It often needs immediate teamwork, resuscitation, and sometimes opening the chest in the trauma bay to save the patient's life.

question: What is the main goal of surgery when treating a patient with a torn heart muscle?

options.A: Replacing the damaged heart with an artificial mechanical pump
options.B: Directly suturing the tear and relieving pressure in the pericardium
options.C: Removing the entire outer layer of the pericardial sac permanently
options.D: Tying off the coronary arteries to prevent further blood loss

explanation: The surgeon's priority is to stitch up the heart muscle tear and open the sac to drain trapped blood so the heart can beat freely again.

question: How is the care for a stable patient with a bruised heart (contusion) different from someone with a bleeding heart wound?

options.A: The blunt injury patient requires immediate open-heart surgery every time.
options.B: The blunt injury patient often receives monitoring and supportive care instead of immediate surgery.
options.C: Medical management is never used for any form of chest trauma.
options.D: Penetrating injuries are always treated with rest and pain medication alone.

explanation: If a patient is stable with a bruised heart, we usually watch them closely in the ICU. But an active stab or gunshot wound? That needs immediate surgery!

question: Which nursing action is essential after chest surgery to prevent lung complications like pneumonia?

options.A: Keeping the patient completely immobile in bed for two weeks
options.B: Administering strong sleeping pills to eliminate night coughing
options.C: Restricting all oral fluid intake to keep the lungs completely dry
options.D: Encouraging deep breathing and the use of an incentive spirometer

explanation: Getting patients to take deep breaths and use an incentive spirometer expands their tiny air sacs (alveoli), keeping pneumonia and lung collapse away!

question: Why do patients recovering from severe heart trauma need continuous heart rhythm monitoring?

options.A: Rhythm strips are legally required to prove the surgery was successful.
options.B: Monitors are only used to calculate the exact daily calorie intake of the patient.
options.C: Damaged heart tissue can trigger dangerous irregular heart rhythms days after the injury.
options.D: The electrical system of the heart heals instantly and never causes issues later.

explanation: Bruised or repaired heart tissue is electrically irritable. Monitoring helps us catch dangerous rhythm changes early and keep our patient safe!

question: What is the main job of your nasal cavity when you breathe in air?

options.A: To store excess air during heavy exercise
options.B: To produce sound waves for vocalization
options.C: To exchange oxygen directly into the bloodstream
options.D: To warm, humidify, and filter incoming air

explanation: Spot on! Your nose acts like a natural air conditioner, warming, cleaning, and moistening the air before it travels down into your lungs.

question: Why is the epiglottis such an important little flap in your throat?

options.A: It separates the nasal cavity from the oral cavity
options.B: It regulates the speed of airflow into the lungs during exercise
options.C: It prevents food and liquid from entering the trachea during swallowing
options.D: It produces mucus to trap dust particles in the nasal passages

explanation: You got it! The epiglottis acts like a clever trapdoor, closing over your windpipe when you swallow so food goes safely down your food pipe instead.

question: What stops your windpipe (trachea) from squishing or collapsing when you breathe?

options.A: Surfactant produced by the lining
options.B: C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage
options.C: Positive pressure from the chest
options.D: Thick layers of skeletal muscle

explanation: Exactly! Those sturdy C-shaped cartilage rings keep your airway open wide and clear at all times.

question: If someone accidentally swallows or breathes in a small object, why is it more likely to go down the right bronchus?

options.A: The left bronchus is blocked by the heart's position
options.B: The right bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical
options.C: The right lung has three lobes instead of two
options.D: Air flows at a much faster speed on the right side

explanation: Correct! The right main tube makes a much straighter, wider path down from the windpipe, making it an easier slipway for anything unwanted.

question: What is the key job of the special fluid called surfactant in your lungs?

options.A: To reduce surface tension and prevent alveolar collapse
options.B: To bind oxygen molecules directly for transport
options.C: To moisten the trachea and primary bronchi
options.D: To trap dust and bacteria entering the deep lungs

explanation: Brilliant! Surfactant keeps the tiny air sacs from sticking together and collapsing on themselves when you breathe out.

question: Why is the membrane inside the lungs where gas exchange happens so incredibly thin?

options.A: To allow the lungs to stretch easily during inhalation
options.B: To reduce the overall weight of the thoracic organs
options.C: To prevent white blood cells from entering the alveoli
options.D: To allow fast and efficient diffusion of gases

explanation: Spot on! A super thin wall means oxygen and carbon dioxide can zip back and forth between your lungs and blood instantly.

question: What actually makes air rush into your lungs when you take an inhalation?

options.A: Intrapulmonary pressure drops below atmospheric pressure
options.B: Surfactant expands the alveolar volume rapidly
options.C: Atmospheric pressure drops below intrapulmonary pressure
options.D: The diaphragm relaxes and pushes the chest upward

explanation: You nailed it! When your chest gets bigger, the pressure inside drops lower than the outside air, sucking air naturally right in.

question: Which muscle does most of the heavy lifting when you take a normal, quiet breath in?

options.A: Internal intercostals
options.B: Sternocleidomastoid
options.C: Rectus abdominis
options.D: Diaphragm

explanation: Correct! The dome-shaped diaphragm is your main breathing muscle, moving down to pull air into your chest effortlessly.

question: How is the vast majority of oxygen carried around your body in the blood?

options.A: Converted into stable bicarbonate molecules
options.B: Dissolved directly in the blood plasma
options.C: Attached to white blood cell membranes
options.D: Bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells

explanation: You got it! Hemoglobin inside your red cells acts like a fleet of tiny delivery trucks carrying oxygen everywhere it's needed.

question: If a patient has severe anemia with very low hemoglobin, what is the most direct problem this causes?

options.A: Complete cessation of carbon dioxide production
options.B: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
options.C: Inability of the diaphragm to contract properly
options.D: Immediate collapse of alveolar air sacs

explanation: Spot on! Fewer delivery trucks (hemoglobin) mean the blood just can't pack and carry enough oxygen to the body tissues.

question: Where in the brain is the main control center that keeps your breathing rhythm on autopilot?

options.A: Hypothalamus and pituitary gland
options.B: Medulla oblongata and pons
options.C: Cerebrum and cerebral cortex
options.D: Cerebellum and spinal cord

explanation: Correct! The brainstem quietly manages your breathing rhythm in the background so you don't have to think about it.

question: What is the main chemical trigger in your blood that tells your brain it is time to breathe?

options.A: Nitrogen gas dissolved in plasma
options.B: High levels of blood glucose
options.C: Carbon dioxide levels in the blood
options.D: Oxygen levels in the arterial blood

explanation: You got it! A buildup of carbon dioxide is the strongest alarm bell your body uses to say 'time to take a breath.'

question: During a quick nursing assessment, which of these is an early warning sign that a patient is struggling to breathe?

options.A: Use of accessory muscles to breathe
options.B: Warm and dry skin on the extremities
options.C: A slow and irregular heart rate
options.D: Normal resting respiratory rate

explanation: Spot on! When breathing gets tough, patients start using their neck and shoulder muscles to help pull air in.

question: If you hear fine crackling sounds in a patient's lower lung fields using your stethoscope, what does that usually mean?

options.A: Complete obstruction of the trachea
options.B: Fluid accumulation in the alveoli
options.C: Enlargement of the primary bronchi
options.D: Severe spasm of the vocal cords

explanation: Brilliant! Those crackles happen when tiny, fluid-filled or sticky air sacs pop open as the patient breathes in.

question: What is the primary function of the respiratory system that gets disrupted during disorders?

options.A: Nutrient absorption
options.B: Blood filtration
options.C: Fluid balance control
options.D: Gas exchange

explanation: The main job of the respiratory system is moving oxygen into the blood and removing carbon dioxide. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why do patients experience shortness of breath when they have a respiratory problem?

options.A: The kidneys are retaining too much water
options.B: The heart is pumping too much blood to the muscles
options.C: The stomach is pushing upward against the diaphragm
options.D: The body is trying to fix low oxygen or high carbon dioxide levels

explanation: Think of shortness of breath as an alarm bell! It's your body's clever way of telling you it needs more oxygen or needs to blow off extra carbon dioxide. Great effort!

question: What term is used to describe shortness of breath that occurs specifically when a patient lies flat?

options.A: Tachypnea
options.B: Apnea
options.C: Bradypnea
options.D: Orthopnea

explanation: Orthopnea is breathing difficulty that worsens when lying down and improves when sitting upright. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h2)

question: A patient wakes up gasping for air two hours after falling asleep and has to sit by the window to breathe. What is this called?

options.A: Acute bronchial asthma
options.B: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
options.C: Simple sleep apnea
options.D: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

explanation: You're doing great! Waking up suddenly in the middle of the night feeling starved for air is known as paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND). It's a classic sign often seen in heart issues.

question: What does a rust-colored sputum sample often point toward?

options.A: Simple dehydration
options.B: Severe throat irritation
options.C: Pneumococcal pneumonia
options.D: Common viral cold

explanation: Rust-colored sputum contains blood mixed with inflammatory exudate, which is typical of pneumococcal pneumonia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h3)

question: Why is pink and frothy sputum an urgent sign that nurses must report immediately?

options.A: It is a normal byproduct of taking cough syrup
options.B: It means the patient is swallowing too much saliva
options.C: It indicates fluid backing up into the air sacs from the heart
options.D: It shows the patient has been smoking too many cigarettes

explanation: Well done! Pink and frothy sputum tells us fluid is leaking into the tiny air sacs in the lungs (pulmonary edema)—definitely something you want to catch and report fast!

question: What is the medical term for coughing up blood from the lungs?

options.A: Epistaxis
options.B: Hemothorax
options.C: Hematemesis
options.D: Hemoptysis

explanation: Hemoptysis refers specifically to blood that comes up from the respiratory system through coughing. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h4)

question: Why do many lung diseases cause sharp chest pain only when the patient takes a deep breath?

options.A: Air is getting trapped inside the stomach muscles
options.B: The main airway is swelling shut during inhalation
options.C: The heart muscle is stretching too hard against the ribcage
options.D: The inflamed lining of the lungs rubs against the chest wall during movement

explanation: Think of it like a skin scrape rubbing against clothing: when the pleural lining of the lungs gets inflamed, every deep breath causes those sore layers to rub together and hurt!

question: What physical sign involves a bluish color of the skin due to low oxygen in the blood?

options.A: Jaundice
options.B: Pallor
options.C: Cyanosis
options.D: Erythema

explanation: Cyanosis is the bluish tint seen on the skin and lips when deoxygenated hemoglobin levels rise. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h5)

question: Why might a severely anemic patient NOT show a blue skin color (cyanosis) even when their oxygen is dangerously low?

options.A: Their skin is naturally thicker and hides color changes better
options.B: Anemia causes the blood vessels to dilate and turn the skin red instead
options.C: They do not have enough red blood cells or hemoglobin to display the blue color
options.D: Their lungs absorb extra oxygen from the surrounding air

explanation: You're getting the hang of it! Cyanosis needs enough hemoglobin (the stuff in red blood cells that carries oxygen) to show that blue tint. If a patient is severely anemic, they simply don't have enough to show the color!

question: Which breath sound is described as a continuous musical whistle heard when airways are narrowed?

options.A: Crackles
options.B: Wheezes
options.C: Rhonchi
options.D: Stridor

explanation: Wheezes are high-pitched musical sounds created when air flows through constricted bronchial tubes. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h6)

question: A nurse listens with a stethoscope and hears moist, popping sounds at the lung bases of a patient with heart failure. What are these sounds called?

options.A: Friction rubs
options.B: Crackles
options.C: Wheezes
options.D: Rhonchi

explanation: Great job! Crackles sound just like Velcro pulling apart or bubbles popping, caused by fluid opening up those tiny air sacs.

question: What is finger clubbing typically associated with in chronic conditions?

options.A: Rapid dehydration from fever
options.B: Sudden bacterial throat infections
options.C: Long-term low oxygen levels in the blood
options.D: A temporary lack of dietary vitamins

explanation: Finger clubbing develops gradually as a result of chronic hypoxia and tissue changes in the extremities. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h7)

question: Why do many patients with severe, long-term lung disease experience noticeable weight loss and muscle wasting?

options.A: The physical effort of breathing uses up enormous amounts of energy
options.B: Their digestive tracts stop absorbing nutrients completely
options.C: They deliberately avoid eating to prevent shortness of breath
options.D: Liver damage prevents them from storing body fat

explanation: Think about how hard it is to run a race—now imagine working that hard just to breathe all day! That heavy effort burns massive amounts of energy and leads to weight loss.

question: What is the very FIRST thing a nurse should do when a patient suddenly gets severe shortness of breath?

options.A: Help the patient sit up and check their oxygen delivery
options.B: Leave the room immediately to find the attending doctor
options.C: Document the exact time the symptoms started
options.D: Have the patient lie flat on their back for rest

explanation: Patient comfort and breathing come first! Always help them sit upright and check their oxygen before you start writing notes or running off.

question: Which of the following is NOT helpful to include when charting about a patient's cough?

options.A: Factors that make the coughing worse
options.B: The color and amount of any sputum produced
options.C: The brand of soap used in the hospital room
options.D: Whether the cough is dry or productive

explanation: You got it! The soap brand won't change lung assessment findings, but details about sputum, triggers, and cough type are clinical gold!

question: What is the normal resting respiratory rate for a healthy adult?

options.A: 8 to 11 breaths per minute
options.B: 22 to 30 breaths per minute
options.C: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
options.D: 35 to 40 breaths per minute

explanation: A normal, healthy adult at rest breathes between 12 and 20 times every minute. Rates outside this range can indicate underlying respiratory or metabolic problems. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h1)

question: Why is cyanosis considered a poor early indicator of hypoxia?

options.A: It only appears after severe oxygen shortage has already developed
options.B: It is easily confused with normal pigmentation changes in the skin
options.C: It disappears completely when the patient stands up
options.D: It only occurs when the patient is holding their breath

explanation: Cyanosis is a late sign of low oxygen in the blood. Restlessness and confusion show up much earlier, so nurses must not wait for blue skin to give oxygen. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of the huff coughing technique?

options.A: To measure the total lung capacity of the patient
options.B: To force air deeply into closed alveoli sacs
options.C: To prevent the tongue from blocking the throat
options.D: To move mucus upward without collapsing the airways

explanation: Huff coughing keeps the vocal cords open while the patient exhales sharply, helping push mucus up from the lower airways safely. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h2)

question: A patient with thick lung secretions refuses to drink water because of nausea. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Force the patient to drink a full cup of water immediately
options.B: Report the fluid refusal and suggest IV hydration or anti-nausea medication
options.C: Document that the patient refuses care and leave the room
options.D: Stop all respiratory treatments until the nausea goes away on its own

explanation: Good hydration thins out thick mucus so it can be cleared easily. Addressing nausea and providing fluids through alternative routes helps maintain airway clearance. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h2)

question: Which oxygen delivery device provides the most precise and controlled oxygen concentration?

options.A: Non-rebreather mask
options.B: Standard nasal cannula
options.C: Simple face mask
options.D: Venturi mask

explanation: The Venturi mask uses interchangeable adapters to mix exact amounts of room air with oxygen, delivering a very specific percentage of gas. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h3)

question: Why must nurses enforce strict fire safety rules around patients receiving oxygen therapy?

options.A: Oxygen strongly supports combustion and makes fires spread much faster
options.B: Electrical equipment creates sparks that turn oxygen into a liquid
options.C: Patients on oxygen are more likely to fall asleep while smoking
options.D: Oxygen tanks will automatically explode if they touch plastic

explanation: While oxygen itself does not burn, it feeds fires vigorously, turning small sparks into dangerous blazes instantly. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h3)

question: When a patient needs both a bronchodilator and an inhaled corticosteroid, why should the bronchodilator be used first?

options.A: It stops the side effects of the steroid from harming the heart
options.B: It neutralizes stomach acid that might interfere with breathing
options.C: It opens the airways so the steroid can reach deeper into the lungs
options.D: It cleans the mouth so the patient does not develop a fungal infection

explanation: Using the bronchodilator first widens the bronchial tubes, allowing the corticosteroid to penetrate further down into the respiratory tree. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h4)

question: A patient is prescribed a metered-dose inhaler without a spacer and complains that the medicine just hits their throat. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Instruct the patient to hold their breath for five minutes after inhaling
options.B: Call the doctor to change the prescription to a skin patch
options.C: Advise the patient to obtain and use a spacer device to improve drug delivery
options.D: Tell the patient to swallow the medicine instead of breathing it in

explanation: Spacers act as a holding chamber that slows down the spray, preventing medication from depositing in the mouth and throat instead of the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h4)

question: What is the best initial position for a patient experiencing acute respiratory distress?

options.A: High Fowler's position
options.B: Flat on the back
options.C: Trendelenburg position
options.D: Left lateral recovery position

explanation: Sitting upright in high Fowler's position allows gravity to lower the diaphragm, giving the lungs maximum room to expand and making breathing easier. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h5)

question: How does pursed-lip breathing help a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?

options.A: It forces extra oxygen directly into the bloodstream through the mouth
options.B: It relaxes the stomach muscles to improve digestion
options.C: It stops the patient from coughing up thick mucus plugs
options.D: It slows down exhalation and keeps airways open longer

explanation: Pursed-lip breathing creates back-pressure in the airways, preventing them from collapsing too early and helping trap less air in the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h5)

question: What is the main job of our respiratory system?

options.A: Producing red blood cells
options.B: Bringing in oxygen and removing carbon dioxide
options.C: Regulating body temperature
options.D: Filtering bacteria out of the bloodstream

explanation: Spot on! The lungs trade gases with every breath we take—bringing in fresh oxygen our body loves and blowing out waste carbon dioxide.

question: Why do lung problems often affect the rest of the body?

options.A: Lung infections spread directly to the brain within hours
options.B: Every organ relies heavily on a steady supply of oxygen from the lungs
options.C: Poor breathing causes the stomach to stop digesting food completely
options.D: The heart stops pumping blood when the lungs become inflamed

explanation: You got it! If the lungs aren't working well, oxygen delivery drops, and every single tissue in the body starts to suffer. Oxygen is food for our cells!

question: What do we call a dangerously low level of oxygen in the blood?

options.A: Hemothorax
options.B: Atelectasis
options.C: Hypoxemia
options.D: Hypercapnia

explanation: Well done! 'Hypo-' means low, and 'oxemia' refers to oxygen in the blood. Put them together and you have hypoxemia.

question: Which type of breathing problem involves a dangerous buildup of carbon dioxide?

options.A: A buildup of carbon dioxide due to poor ventilation
options.B: A sudden drop in oxygen caused by fluid in the alveoli
options.C: High blood pressure inside the arteries of the lungs
options.D: A complete collapse of the lung tissue from air in the chest

explanation: Correct! When a patient isn't moving air in and out well enough (poor ventilation), carbon dioxide gets trapped inside.

question: What actually is 'cor pulmonale'?

options.A: Bleeding into the chest cavity following trauma
options.B: An infection of the lining surrounding the lungs
options.C: Right-sided heart failure caused by long-term lung disease
options.D: A sudden collapse of a lung lobe due to a blocked airway

explanation: You nailed it. Long-term lung trouble makes the heart work extra hard on the right side, eventually leading to right-sided heart failure.

question: A patient develops cor pulmonale from chronic lung disease. What sign might you spot as a nurse?

options.A: A sudden spike in blood glucose levels
options.B: Sudden sharp chest pain and absent breath sounds
options.C: Bright red blood coming up when coughing
options.D: Swollen lower legs and distended neck veins

explanation: Spot on! Since the right side of the heart is struggling to pump forward, fluid backs up into the body, causing swollen legs and puffy neck veins.

question: In simple terms, what is atelectasis?

options.A: An abnormal collection of air in the pleural cavity
options.B: A severe bacterial infection inside the lung tissue
options.C: The collapse or closure of a lung resulting in reduced gas exchange
options.D: High pressure inside the blood vessels of the lungs

explanation: Correct! Atelectasis happens when tiny air sacs (alveoli) deflate or collapse, making it harder to trade gases.

question: How does fluid in the chest cavity (pleural effusion) make it hard to breathe?

options.A: Fluid enters the alveoli and destroys the natural surfactant
options.B: It blocks the main windpipe and chugs off air supply
options.C: Fluid physically presses against the lung, stopping it from expanding fully
options.D: It forces the heart to beat too fast, causing sudden shock

explanation: You got it! The fluid takes up space in the chest and squeezes the lung from the outside, so it can't puff up nicely when breathing in.

question: What fills the chest space when a patient has a hemothorax?

options.A: Air
options.B: Serous fluid
options.C: Blood
options.D: Pus

explanation: Easy and clear! 'Hemo' means blood, and 'thorax' means chest. It's blood inside the chest cavity.

question: Why is a tension pneumothorax such a major emergency?

options.A: Trapped air builds up pressure and shifts the heart and major blood vessels
options.B: It stops the kidneys from producing urine within minutes
options.C: It floods both lungs with thick, yellow mucus
options.D: It causes an immediate massive infection in the bronchial tubes

explanation: Correct! Trapped air keeps stacking up like a balloon, pushing everything in the chest sideways and stopping blood from returning to the heart.

question: If a patient holds onto too much carbon dioxide because they aren't breathing deeply enough, what acid-base imbalance happens?

options.A: Respiratory alkalosis
options.B: Respiratory acidosis
options.C: Metabolic acidosis
options.D: Metabolic alkalosis

explanation: Well done! Carbon dioxide acts like an acid in the body. If it builds up in the lungs, the blood becomes too acidic—hence respiratory acidosis.

question: A patient is having a panic attack and breathing way too fast. What are they at risk for?

options.A: Metabolic acidosis
options.B: Metabolic alkalosis
options.C: Respiratory alkalosis
options.D: Respiratory acidosis

explanation: Spot on! Breathing too fast blows off too much carbon dioxide. Losing too much acid makes the blood basic (alkaline), causing respiratory alkalosis.

question: What is usually the very first clue that a patient's oxygen level is dropping?

options.A: A drop in body temperature
options.B: Swelling in the feet
options.C: Restlessness and confusion
options.D: Severe chest pain

explanation: You got it! The brain is super sensitive to oxygen. When it starts running low, the patient often gets fidgety, anxious, or confused before anything else happens.

question: Which sign tells you a patient is struggling and working extra hard to breathe?

options.A: Use of accessory muscles in the neck during inhalation
options.B: Warm and dry skin across the chest and arms
options.C: A slow and steady heart rate below 60 beats per minute
options.D: Quiet and effortless breathing sounds throughout both lung fields

explanation: Correct! When normal breathing isn't enough, the body recruits extra muscles in the neck and shoulders to help pull air in.

question: Why do we teach pursed-lip breathing to patients with chronic lung issues?

options.A: It lowers the patient's blood pressure immediately
options.B: It stops all coughing episodes within a few minutes
options.C: It replaces the need for using oxygen therapy
options.D: It keeps airways open longer and helps expel trapped air

explanation: Well done! Breathing out through pursed lips creates a gentle back-pressure, stopping tiny airways from collapsing too soon.

question: What is the best way to help prevent atelectasis in a patient after surgery?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to prevent fluid overload in the chest
options.B: Administering a strong sleeping pill to ensure total rest
options.C: Encouraging regular deep breathing and incentive spirometry
options.D: Keeping the patient completely flat in bed to rest the lungs

explanation: Spot on! Getting the patient to take deep breaths and use their incentive spirometer pops those little air sacs wide open and keeps the lungs clear.

question: What is the main job of the mucociliary escalator in our airways?

options.A: Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide in the tiny air sacs
options.B: Making surfactant to keep the lungs from collapsing
options.C: Filtering big dust bits right inside the nose
options.D: Sweeping trapped dirt and mucus upward toward the throat

explanation: Think of the mucociliary escalator like a tiny conveyor belt in your respiratory tract. It uses beating hair-like cilia and mucus to push dust and germs up to your throat so you can swallow or cough them out cleanly!

question: Which nursing action is a great example of secondary prevention for respiratory health?

options.A: Running a community talk on the dangers of smoking
options.B: Teaching an asthma patient how to use their inhaler properly
options.C: Giving the yearly flu shot to a healthy adult
options.D: Screening high-risk factory workers with routine breathing tests

explanation: Secondary prevention is all about early detection! Screening tests help catch signs of trouble early, before a patient even notices symptoms.

question: What is the single biggest preventable cause of chronic lung disease (COPD) worldwide?

options.A: Childhood asthma attacks
options.B: Inhaling coal dust at work
options.C: Smoke from indoor cooking fires
options.D: Tobacco smoke exposure

explanation: Tobacco smoke is tough on the airways and air sacs over time. Because people can choose to avoid or quit it, it stands out as the number one preventable cause of COPD globally.

question: A patient living in a rural home with poor kitchen ventilation uses wood for daily cooking and now has a lasting cough. What is the best primary prevention advice?

options.A: Give them a course of strong oral antibiotics right away
options.B: Recommend using a quick-relief rescue inhaler every day
options.C: Order a chest X-ray to check for tuberculosis
options.D: Advise the family to switch to cleaner cooking fuel and improve kitchen airflow

explanation: Primary prevention stops the problem before it starts or worsens. Fixing indoor smoke exposure removes the root environmental trigger keeping that cough going!

question: Why do people need to take the influenza vaccine every single year?

options.A: The government needs yearly numbers for health records
options.B: The vaccine turns toxic if stored for more than a year
options.C: The flu virus mutates and changes its shape from year to year
options.D: Immunity from last year's shot completely disappears in six months

explanation: Flu viruses are clever changelings! They undergo constant changes (antigenic drift), so scientists update the vaccine annually to match whatever strain is currently spreading.

question: Which group of people benefits the most from herd immunity against respiratory infections?

options.A: Young adults working in busy office buildings
options.B: Older adults who get their flu shots on time
options.C: People who are too young or have weak immune systems to get vaccines
options.D: Healthy athletes training outdoors

explanation: Herd immunity acts like a protective shield. When most of the community is vaccinated, it stops the germ from spreading to vulnerable people who cannot take vaccines themselves.

question: In occupational health, what is the FIRST and best line of defense against workplace air hazards?

options.A: Putting up exhaust fans in the work area
options.B: Giving workers certified face masks or respirators
options.C: Rotating shifts so workers spend less time near the hazard
options.D: Completely removing or replacing the dangerous material

explanation: Elimination and substitution are top priorities in safety. If you get rid of the hazard entirely, nobody has to rely on masks or fans to stay safe!

question: Which of these is a classic lung disease caused by breathing in mineral dust at work?

options.A: Cystic fibrosis
options.B: Silicosis
options.C: Acute bronchitis
options.D: Lobar pneumonia

explanation: Silicosis happens when workers breathe in tiny crystalline silica dust, often found in mining, construction, or masonry jobs.

question: What is the main reason for doing screening spirometry on healthy workers who are at high risk?

options.A: To measure how much oxygen is floating in the blood
options.B: To cure existing chronic lung disease
options.C: To catch early breathing trouble before any symptoms show up
options.D: To find out which exact bacteria is causing an infection

explanation: Spirometry is a breathing test that can spot small changes in lung function long before a worker starts feeling short of breath.

question: Which of the following is NOT a goal of secondary prevention in respiratory health?

options.A: Finding small pulmonary nodules on routine diagnostic imaging
options.B: Reversing the genetic mutations that cause inherited lung disorders
options.C: Identifying early airway obstruction using breathing tests
options.D: Catching latent infections before they become active and contagious

explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on early detection and treatment of existing disease, not genetic modification or primary prevention of DNA mutations. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the main goal of tertiary prevention for someone living with COPD?

options.A: Slowing down the disease and preventing troublesome complications
options.B: Preventing airway inflammation back when they were a child
options.C: Screening healthy family members for hidden lung issues
options.D: Completely curing the permanent damage in the air sacs

explanation: Tertiary prevention steps in after a chronic illness is already present. The aim is to help the patient manage symptoms, stay active, and avoid severe flare-ups.

question: What activities are normally included in a pulmonary rehabilitation program?

options.A: Supervised exercise training and breathing exercises
options.B: Continuous high-dose antibiotic therapy
options.C: Long-term isolation so the patient avoids all outside air
options.D: Surgical replacement of damaged lung tissue

explanation: Pulmonary rehab is wonderful for chronic lung patients! It combines guided physical activity and breathing techniques to help them breathe easier and build stamina.

question: How does a nurse best show public health advocacy regarding breathing disorders?

options.A: Doing deep lung biopsies in local health clinics
options.B: Isolating every single person with a seasonal flu
options.C: Supporting policies that cut down air pollution and tobacco use
options.D: Prescribing strong bronchodilators to people in the neighborhood

explanation: Advocacy goes beyond the hospital bedside. Nurses advocate by supporting healthier environments, clean air policies, and community tobacco control.

question: A nurse is teaching an asthma patient how to use an inhaler. What is the best way to make sure the teaching worked?

options.A: Explaining the complex chemistry of the aerosol drug
options.B: Giving the patient a textbook chapter to read at home
options.C: Telling a family member to always give the medicine for them
options.D: Demonstrating the technique and asking the patient to show it back

explanation: Return demonstration is the gold standard of patient education! It lets you watch the patient do it themselves so you know they truly understand the steps.

question: What is a tracheostomy?

options.A: A tube inserted through the nose into the stomach
options.B: A small incision made in the upper chest wall
options.C: A flexible scope passed down the throat
options.D: A surgical opening made into the trachea

explanation: A tracheostomy involves creating a surgical opening directly into the trachea through the neck. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h1)

question: How does a tracheostomy differ from an endotracheal tube?

options.A: An endotracheal tube is always permanent
options.B: A tracheostomy bypasses the upper airway via the neck
options.C: A tracheostomy goes through the mouth and nose
options.D: An endotracheal tube requires no mechanical support

explanation: Endotracheal tubes enter through the mouth or nose, whereas tracheostomy tubes enter directly through a surgical neck incision. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h1)

question: What is a common reason a patient needs a tracheostomy?

options.A: Long-term mechanical ventilation
options.B: Acute stomach ulcers
options.C: Severe lower leg fractures
options.D: Chronic kidney disease

explanation: Patients needing a ventilator for an extended period often receive a tracheostomy for safety and comfort. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h2)

question: Why would a patient with severe facial swelling get a tracheostomy instead of a normal breathing tube through the mouth?

options.A: It lets the patient speak normally right away
options.B: It bypasses the blocked upper airway completely
options.C: It stops all future lung infections completely
options.D: It needs zero nursing checks afterward

explanation: When facial trauma blocks the upper airway, a tracheostomy makes a fresh, clear pathway below the blockage. You're doing great!

question: What is the job of the obturator in a tracheostomy kit?

options.A: To collect thick mucus from the lungs
options.B: To secure the ties around the patient's neck
options.C: To inflate and deflate the tracheal cuff
options.D: To guide smooth insertion of the tube without injury

explanation: Think of the obturator as a smooth guide! Its rounded tip helps slide the tracheostomy tube right into place without scratching the tissue.

question: Why does a tracheostomy tube have a removable inner cannula?

options.A: It allows easy cleaning and removal of dried mucus
options.B: It acts as a backup if the patient stops breathing
options.C: It measures the exact pressure in the lungs
options.D: It allows the patient to talk without a valve

explanation: Mucus builds up fast! The inner cannula can be easily taken out and cleaned so the airway stays open and clear.

question: When is the right time to apply suction during tracheostomy suctioning?

options.A: While pushing the catheter down into the airway
options.B: Continuously throughout the entire procedure
options.C: Only while withdrawing and rotating the catheter
options.D: Before inserting any tubing into the stoma

explanation: Never apply suction on the way in! You only suction gently while twisting and pulling the catheter out to protect the delicate airway lining.

question: What is the most important safety rule when changing a patient's tracheostomy neck ties?

options.A: Have an assistant hold the tube in place
options.B: Do it quickly without washing hands
options.C: Inflate the cuff to maximum pressure
options.D: Remove the inner cannula permanently

explanation: Always have a partner hold the tube securely during tie changes. One good cough can pop the tube right out!

question: What spare equipment must always stay right at the bedside for a patient with a tracheostomy?

options.A: A set of surgical scalpels and sutures
options.B: A backup mechanical ventilator machine
options.C: A spare tracheostomy tube and obturator
options.D: An extra oxygen tank and nasal cannula

explanation: Safety first! A matching spare tube and obturator must always be ready at the bedside in case of an emergency replacement.

question: A patient accidentally pulls out their fresh tracheostomy tube and panics. What is your immediate nursing action?

options.A: Place a simple nasal cannula over the open stoma
options.B: Wait for the primary surgeon to arrive on the unit
options.C: Call for help and attempt to reinsert the tube or secure the airway
options.D: Administer oral pain medication immediately

explanation: An accidental decannulation is an emergency! Call for help right away and try to reinsert the tube to keep the airway open.

question: In tracheostomy care, what does the term 'decannulation' mean?

options.A: Permanent removal of the tracheostomy tube
options.B: Inserting a new mechanical ventilation machine
options.C: Inflating the cuff to maximum pressure
options.D: Cleaning the inner cannula with sterile water

explanation: Decannulation simply means the tube is finally and permanently removed because the patient no longer needs it. You're mastering the terminology!

question: What generally happens to the tracheostomy hole (stoma) after the tube is permanently removed?

options.A: It requires major plastic surgery to sew shut
options.B: It naturally heals closed with a simple dressing
options.C: It must be plugged with a permanent metal cap
options.D: It remains permanently open for air passage

explanation: Nature is amazing! Covered with a simple dressing, the stoma usually shrinks and closes up on its own within a few days.

question: What is the main purpose of an under-water seal drainage system?

options.A: To restore negative pressure in the pleural space
options.B: To measure the exact daily urine output of a patient
options.C: To pump sterile water directly into the lung tissue
options.D: To deliver high-flow oxygen straight into the chest cavity

explanation: The primary goal of chest tube drainage is to evacuate air or fluid, thereby re-establishing the normal negative pressure needed for lung expansion. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h1)

question: How does the water seal chamber stop air from rushing back into the patient's chest?

options.A: It uses electronic suction to block all backward movement of gases
options.B: It freezes the tubing shut whenever the patient tries to breathe in
options.C: It creates a chemical barrier that destroys outside bacteria instantly
options.D: It acts as a one-way valve that lets air out but not back in

explanation: Think of it like a one-way street! Air bubbles out when the patient breathes out, but the water blocks outside air from getting back in.

question: What is the medical term for blood collecting inside the pleural space?

options.A: Pleural effusion
options.B: Hemothorax
options.C: Chylothorax
options.D: Pneumothorax

explanation: You've got this! 'Hemo' means blood and 'thorax' means chest, so blood in the chest is a hemothorax.

question: A patient arrives at the ward after a knife wound to the chest, and you notice absent breath sounds on one side. What condition should you expect the doctor to treat with a chest tube?

options.A: Pulmonary edema
options.B: Pneumothorax
options.C: Bronchial asthma
options.D: Myocardial infarction

explanation: Chest trauma often lets air leak into the pleural space, causing a pneumothorax that needs a chest tube to let the lung expand again.

question: In a standard three-chamber chest tube setup, what is the job of the very first chamber?

options.A: To filter out all bacteria entering from the room air
options.B: To add sterile water directly into the patient's lung tissue
options.C: To control the exact wall suction pressure applied to the unit
options.D: To collect and measure fluid draining from the patient

explanation: Chamber one is simply the catch basin. It safely collects whatever fluid, blood, or pus drains out so you can measure it easily.

question: What is the main role of the water seal chamber in a chest drainage unit?

options.A: To humidify the oxygen being delivered to the patient's lungs
options.B: To provide a source of sterile irrigation fluid for the chest wall
options.C: To actively pump excess blood out of the pleural cavity
options.D: To prevent outside air from flowing backward into the patient

explanation: Great job! The water seal acts like a protective gate that lets trapped air escape while keeping room air out of the chest.

question: Which patient position is best for chest tube insertion to help expand the lung and make the area easy to reach?

options.A: Left lateral decubitus position only
options.B: Semi-Fowler's or high-Fowler's position
options.C: Trendelenburg position with feet elevated
options.D: Prone position flat on the abdomen

explanation: Sitting the patient up (semi or high-Fowler's) helps fluid flow downward and air rise upward, making the procedure safer and easier.

question: Why must a nurse tape all tubing connections securely right after a chest tube is put in?

options.A: To increase the speed of fluid drainage into the collection chamber
options.B: To stop the patient from bending the tubing during sleep
options.C: To prevent the water in the seal chamber from evaporating away
options.D: To prevent accidental disconnection and a collapsed lung

explanation: Loose connections can let room air slip into the chest, which can quickly turn into a dangerous emergency. Always double-check your joints!

question: What does 'tidaling' mean in the water seal chamber?

options.A: A sudden backflow of blood into the patient's subcutaneous tissue
options.B: The rise and fall of water levels with the patient's breathing
options.C: Rapid continuous bubbling caused by a major air leak in the system
options.D: The gradual evaporation of sterile water from the suction chamber

explanation: Tidaling is just like the ocean tide! The water level goes up and down smoothly as the patient breathes in and out, showing that the system is working.

question: You notice tidaling has suddenly stopped in the water seal chamber of a stable patient. What should you check first?

options.A: Check the tubing for kinks, blockages, or loops hanging too low
options.B: Call the surgeon to request immediate removal of the chest tube
options.C: Disconnect the drainage system from the wall suction source
options.D: Immediately clamp the chest tube with two heavy metal hemostats

explanation: Don't panic! When tidaling stops, it often just means something is blocking the tube, like a kink or a loop resting under the bed. Check the lines first.

question: Where should the chest drainage unit be placed at all times?

options.A: Below the level of the patient's chest
options.B: Above the patient's head on an IV pole
options.C: Directly level with the patient's mattress
options.D: Attached firmly to the foot of the bed

explanation: Gravity is your friend here! Keeping the unit below chest level ensures fluid drains away from the body instead of flowing back inside.

question: Why is routine clamping of a chest tube strongly discouraged when moving a patient?

options.A: It permanently ruins the plastic collection chambers of the unit
options.B: It increases the risk of severe infection at the insertion site
options.C: It can quickly cause a life-threatening tension pneumothorax
options.D: It causes the sterile water in the seal chamber to evaporate

explanation: Clamping traps air and fluid with nowhere to go. This can cause the lung to collapse rapidly, so avoid clamping unless ordered for specific tests!

question: What is your very first action if a patient's chest tube accidentally disconnects from the drainage unit?

options.A: Apply tight adhesive tape all around the open tubing end
options.B: Clamp the chest tube securely near the insertion site
options.C: Submerge the end of the tube in sterile water
options.D: Lower the patient flat onto their back in bed

explanation: Quick thinking! Putting the tube tip in sterile water instantly creates a temporary seal and keeps air from rushing into the chest.

question: A patient's chest tube accidentally falls completely out of their chest. What should you do immediately?

options.A: Leave the open chest wound completely uncovered and run to find a doctor
options.B: Put clean gloves on and push the exact same tube back into the chest wound
options.C: Clamp the remaining chest tubing tightly to preserve negative pressure
options.D: Cover the site with a sterile petroleum dressing taped on three sides

explanation: A three-sided petroleum dressing acts like a smart flap—it lets trapped air escape while stopping room air from sucking back in.

question: What is the most important thing to watch out for after a patient has their chest tube removed?

options.A: Mild redness around the edges of the healed skin suture line
options.B: Total daily urine output measured in a graduated container
options.C: Signs of breathing difficulty or the chest problem returning
options.D: Temporary soreness at the chest site when coughing

explanation: Always stay alert! The main worry after removal is that air or fluid might start building up again in the chest.

question: What is the primary purpose of inserting an endotracheal tube?

options.A: To secure and maintain a patent airway
options.B: To measure systemic blood pressure continuously
options.C: To prevent the stomach from producing acid
options.D: To treat underlying lung infections directly

explanation: The main goal of endotracheal intubation is to keep the airway open and secure so oxygen can reach the lungs safely. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h1)

question: A patient with a severe drug overdose has lost consciousness and normal gag reflexes. Why is intubation urgently required here?

options.A: To protect the lungs from choking on stomach contents
options.B: To reverse the chemical effects of the drug quickly
options.C: To increase blood flow to the brain tissue
options.D: To lower the patient's elevated body temperature

explanation: Unconscious patients lose protective airway reflexes, putting them at high risk of aspirating vomit into their lungs, which intubation prevents. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h1)

question: What is the name of the special alignment used to help visualize the vocal cords during intubation?

options.A: The sniffing position
options.B: The Trendelenburg position
options.C: The high Fowler position
options.D: The recovery position

explanation: Placing the patient's head in the sniffing position aligns the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes for a better view of the airway. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h2)

question: Why is checking the suction apparatus considered a critical step before beginning the intubation procedure?

options.A: To inflate the balloon cuff once the tube is in the trachea
options.B: To quickly clear vomit, blood, or secretions blocking the view
options.C: To measure the exact volume of air inside the patient's lungs
options.D: To deliver humidified oxygen straight down the breathing tube

explanation: Unforeseen fluids can instantly obscure the clinician's view of the vocal cords, making immediate suction essential for patient safety. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of pre-oxygenating a patient right before intubation?

options.A: To clean out bacteria from the upper respiratory tract
options.B: To relax the vocal cords so the tube slides in easily
options.C: To stimulate a strong cough reflex in the trachea
options.D: To build an oxygen reserve and prevent low blood oxygen

explanation: Pre-oxygenation fills the lungs with pure oxygen to give the healthcare team a safe window of time while securing the airway. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h3)

question: A patient receives a sedative medication right before intubation and suddenly becomes very dizzy with a dangerous drop in blood pressure. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: The bag-valve-mask was squeezed too hard during manual ventilation
options.B: The patient was not breathing enough oxygen before the procedure started
options.C: Many induction drugs cause blood vessels to relax and lower blood pressure
options.D: The endotracheal tube was inserted too deeply into the right mainstem bronchus

explanation: Sedatives and induction agents frequently cause vasodilation, which can drop blood pressure sharply, particularly in unstable patients. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h3)

question: What is the maximum recommended time limit for a single intubation attempt to protect the patient?
