question: What is the most critical dietary instruction for a patient newly diagnosed with celiac disease?

options.A: Maintain strict, lifelong elimination of all foods containing gluten
options.B: Avoid dairy products only during acute episodes of abdominal pain
options.C: Increase fiber intake temporarily until bowel villi fully regrow
options.D: Reduce fat intake to prevent steatorrhea during flare-ups

explanation: Celiac disease is a permanent condition requiring complete, lifelong removal of gluten to allow mucosal healing and prevent complications. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T8#GNS213_U3_T8_h8)

question: A nurse is discharging a patient who had a bowel obstruction from Crohn's disease. Which symptom should the nurse flag as an urgent emergency?

options.A: Feeling tired during normal daily physical activities
options.B: Mild gas and bloating after eating a small meal
options.C: Severe, unrelenting abdominal pain and persistent vomiting
options.D: A slight increase in daily bowel movement frequency

explanation: Never ignore severe, worsening pain and constant vomiting—they can signal a returning blockage or a serious bowel injury. You're becoming a great nurse!

question: What is the primary job of the large intestine in the human body?

options.A: Digesting complex fats and proteins
options.B: Filtering waste products out of the blood stream
options.C: Producing most of the body's digestive enzymes
options.D: Absorbing water and forming stool

explanation: The main function of the colon is to take liquid chyme from the small intestine, absorb the water and electrolytes, and turn it into solid feces. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T9#GNS213_U3_T9_h1)

question: Why are the normal bacteria living inside your large intestine so important?

options.A: They prevent all types of bacterial infections
options.B: They synthesize essential vitamins like vitamin K
options.C: They break down proteins into amino acids
options.D: They line the colon wall to protect against acid

explanation: You got it! Our friendly gut bacteria ferment leftover food and help produce important nutrients like vitamin K, which is essential for blood clotting.

question: What is the main purpose of doing a colonoscopy?

options.A: Viewing the entire colon lining and removing polyps
options.B: Flushing out impacted stool from the small intestine
options.C: Measuring the exact pressure inside the stomach
options.D: Checking liver enzymes through a small tissue sample

explanation: Well done! A colonoscopy allows the doctor to use a tiny camera scope to look directly at the large bowel lining, take tissue samples, or safely remove growths.

question: Why must a patient take a special bowel cleaning solution before having a colonoscopy?

options.A: To clear all stool so the doctor can see the lining clearly
options.B: To numb the inside of the rectum before the scope goes in
options.C: To relax the abdominal muscles and prevent cramping
options.D: To kill harmful bacteria living in the sigmoid colon

explanation: Exactly right! Any leftover stool blocks the camera view and can hide small polyps or early trouble spots, so a completely clean bowel is a must.

question: Which part of the digestive tract does Ulcerative Colitis affect?

options.A: Mainly the small intestine
options.B: From the mouth to the anus
options.C: Only the stomach and duodenum
options.D: Only the colon and rectum

explanation: Correct! Ulcerative Colitis keeps to the large intestine and rectum. Unlike Crohn's disease, it doesn't wander off into other parts of the gut.

question: How does Crohn's disease affect the bowel wall differently from Ulcerative Colitis?

options.A: Crohn's affects the full thickness of the wall, while colitis affects only the mucosa
options.B: Crohn's causes smooth continuous inflammation, while colitis causes patchy skip lesions
options.C: Crohn's affects only the rectum, while colitis affects the small intestine
options.D: Crohn's only causes mild irritation, while colitis always causes complete perforation

explanation: Great job! Crohn's disease goes deep, affecting all layers of the bowel wall (transmural), whereas Ulcerative Colitis stays on the inner lining surface.

question: What are diverticula?

options.A: Small pouches pushing outward through the colon wall
options.B: Benign growths attached to the inside of the rectum
options.C: Enlarged veins surrounding the outside of the anus
options.D: Scar tissue narrowing the middle of the transverse colon

explanation: Spot on! Diverticula are little pocket-like bulges that form where the muscle layer of the colon is weak, often due to pressure from hard stools.

question: A patient comes in with acute diverticulitis and severe lower left belly pain. Which diet order is best for this acute stage?

options.A: High-protein liquid supplement drinks
options.B: Clear liquids to let the bowel rest
options.C: High-fiber diet with extra raw vegetables
options.D: Regular solid food with high roughage

explanation: You got it! When diverticulitis flares up, the inflamed colon needs a break. Clear liquids help give the bowel time to rest and heal.

question: What do tests and scopes usually show in the colon of a patient with Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)?

options.A: There are deep ulcers throughout the sigmoid colon
options.B: Numerous inflamed pouches are present in the wall
options.C: A large mass is blocking the lower descending colon
options.D: The bowel structure and lining look completely normal

explanation: Correct! IBS is a functional disorder. That means even though the patient has real symptoms, tests and scopes show no physical damage, ulcers, or tumors.

question: Which symptom pattern is most typical for someone with Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)?

options.A: Severe sudden constipation that leads straight to a bowel blockage
options.B: Painless bleeding from the rectum every time they pass stool
options.C: Constant bloody stools accompanied by high fevers and weight loss
options.D: Recurrent abdominal pain tied to changes in stool frequency and form

explanation: Well done! IBS is diagnosed when belly pain keeps coming back and is linked with changes in how often and how hard or loose their stools are.

question: What do most cases of colorectal cancer start from?

options.A: Chronic twisting of the sigmoid colon
options.B: Enlarged external hemorrhoids near the anus
options.C: Severe bacterial infections in the appendix
options.D: Benign polyps on the inner lining of the colon

explanation: Spot on! Most colorectal cancers start out as harmless growths called adenomatous polyps that slowly change over many years.

question: Why are regular screening colonoscopies so good at preventing colorectal cancer?

options.A: They allow doctors to find and remove pre-cancerous polyps early
options.B: They prevent the body from absorbing dietary fats
options.C: They completely kill all harmful bacteria living inside the bowel
options.D: They strengthen the muscle wall of the descending colon

explanation: You nailed it! Finding and clipping out polyps during a routine check stops them from hanging around long enough to turn into cancer.

question: What is a very common cause of a large bowel obstruction?

options.A: Eating too much high-fiber food at one meal
options.B: A mild viral stomach flu causing diarrhea
options.C: An overgrowth of normal intestinal bacteria
options.D: Colorectal cancer or a twisted bowel loop

explanation: Correct! Tumors growing inside the colon or a loop of bowel twisting on itself (volvulus) are major physical reasons the large intestine gets blocked.

question: Why is a complete large bowel blockage considered a serious medical emergency?

options.A: High pressure can cause the bowel wall to rupture and spill contents
options.B: It immediately stops the kidneys from producing urine
options.C: It stops the liver from filtering toxins from the blood
options.D: It always causes permanent brain damage within two hours

explanation: Spot on! As gas and stool pile up behind the blockage, pressure builds, cutting off blood flow and risking a dangerous rupture (perforation).

question: What should a healthy, newly formed intestinal stoma look like when you check it?

options.A: Pink and moist
options.B: Pale and dry
options.C: Dark purple or black
options.D: Cold and hard

explanation: Great job! A healthy stoma has great blood flow, so it should look pink to red and feel moist. A dark purple or black stoma means trouble with blood supply and is an emergency!

question: A patient with severe ulcerative colitis is having 10 bloody stools a day. What nursing action should you prioritize first?

options.A: Preparing the patient for heavy weight-lifting exercises
options.B: Monitoring intake and output and checking for signs of fluid loss
options.C: Encouraging a high-fiber raw vegetable diet to bulk up stool
options.D: Teaching the patient how to care for a permanent colostomy

explanation: You got it! Losing so much fluid through frequent diarrhea puts the patient at high risk for dehydration, making fluid tracking our top priority.

question: What are the two main systems combined within the genito-urinary tract?

options.A: The nervous and skeletal systems
options.B: The digestive and endocrine systems
options.C: The respiratory and circulatory systems
options.D: The urinary and reproductive systems

explanation: The genito-urinary system is a combination of the urinary tract organs and the reproductive organs due to their close developmental and physical links. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T1#GNS213_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why are the urinary and reproductive systems studied together as one genito-urinary system?

options.A: They are both located exclusively within the upper abdominal cavity
options.B: They perform the exact same physiological functions in the body
options.C: They share closely linked embryonic origins and anatomical pathways
options.D: They are both controlled entirely by the same set of cranial nerves

explanation: Think about how we grow from an embryo! These two systems form from closely related tissues and even share pathways, like the urethra in males.

question: Where are the kidneys located in the human body?

options.A: Attached directly to the underside of the liver
options.B: Suspended freely within the lower pelvic cavity
options.C: Inside the peritoneal cavity near the stomach
options.D: Retroperitoneal against the back abdominal wall

explanation: Remember that 'retro' means behind! The kidneys sit safely tucked behind the main abdominal cavity, right against your back wall on either side of the spine.

question: How do the ureters move urine down from the kidneys into the bladder?

options.A: By creating high pressure using active ciliated cells
options.B: By relying solely on stretchy downward pull of gravity
options.C: By passive diffusion through tiny microscopic pores
options.D: By rhythmic muscular contractions known as peristalsis

explanation: Even if you are lying flat on your back, urine still moves to your bladder! The walls of the ureters squeeze in waves called peristalsis to push it along.

question: What is the name of the smooth, triangular area found on the inner floor of the bladder?

options.A: The renal pelvis
options.B: The meatus
options.C: The glomerulus
options.D: The trigone

explanation: It's called the trigone (think 'triangle'). It is marked out by the openings of your two ureters and your urethra, and germs love to hang out here during bladder infections.

question: Why are women more likely to get bladder infections than men?

options.A: The female bladder lacks any form of transitional epithelial lining
options.B: Women produce significantly less urine volume over a 24-hour period
options.C: The female urethra is much shorter and closer to the anal opening
options.D: The female trigone is larger and traps bacteria much more easily

explanation: Anatomy plays a big role here! The female urethra is only about four centimeters long, giving outside bacteria a short and easy path straight into the bladder.

question: What is the very first step of urine formation in the kidney?

options.A: Tubular secretion
options.B: Glomerular filtration
options.C: Peristaltic propulsion
options.D: Tubular reabsorption

explanation: Everything starts at the glomerulus! Blood pressure forces water and small particles out of the blood and into Bowman's capsule to kick off urine making.

question: What happens during tubular reabsorption in the nephron?

options.A: Urine is pushed down the ureters through muscular contractions
options.B: Extra metabolic wastes are pumped from the blood into the tubule
options.C: Useful substances are moved from the renal tubules back into the blood
options.D: Blood pressure forces large proteins through the glomerular membrane

explanation: Your kidneys filter a lot of good stuff by accident at first! Tubular reabsorption acts like a salvage yard, pulling water, sugar, and nutrients back into your bloodstream.

question: Which hormone helps your kidneys save water when your body is dehydrated?

options.A: Anti-diuretic hormone
options.B: Insulin
options.C: Thyroxine
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Think of Anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) as your body's 'anti-pee' signal. It tells your kidney collecting ducts to hold onto water so you don't get dehydrated.

question: What is it called when a patient with kidney failure has a dangerous buildup of potassium in their blood?

options.A: Hypercalcemia
options.B: Hyperkalemia
options.C: Hypoglycemia
options.D: Hyponatremia

explanation: Break the word down: 'hyper' means high, 'kalium' is the Latin root for potassium, and 'emia' means in the blood. When kidneys fail, they can't clear out potassium, leading to hyperkalemia.

question: In males, which organ sits right below the bladder and wraps around the urethra?

options.A: The epididymis
options.B: The prostate gland
options.C: The testicle
options.D: The seminal vesicle

explanation: The prostate gland wraps like a ring around the upper male urethra. This is why an enlarged prostate in older men can make it hard to pass urine!

question: Why do males use the same tube (the urethra) for both urine and semen?

options.A: Both fluids exit the body through the urethra
options.B: The ureters connect directly to the reproductive tract
options.C: The bladder stores semen before ejaculation occurs
options.D: Both fluids are produced together inside the prostate gland

explanation: The male urethra pulls double duty as the final exit path for both urinary and reproductive fluids (though clever internal valves make sure they never mix at the wrong time).

question: Where does the urinary bladder sit in relation to the uterus in females?

options.A: Lateral to the right and left ovaries
options.B: Directly posterior to the rectal wall
options.C: Posterior and superior to the uterus
options.D: Anterior and inferior to the uterus

explanation: In simple terms, your bladder sits right in front of (anterior) and lower down (inferior) than your uterus. That's why pregnancy puts so much direct squeeze on the bladder!

question: Why do pregnant women often feel the need to urinate frequently?

options.A: The bladder lining sheds its transitional epithelium completely
options.B: The ureters double in length to accommodate the growing fetus
options.C: Pregnancy hormones cause the kidneys to stop producing any ADH
options.D: The expanding uterus places direct physical pressure on the bladder

explanation: As the baby and uterus grow, they take up more space in the pelvis and press right down on the bladder, leaving less room to hold urine.

question: Which type of nerve signals tell the bladder muscle to squeeze when it's time to pass urine?

options.A: Parasympathetic fibers
options.B: Sympathetic fibers
options.C: Enteric nerve fibers
options.D: Somatic sensory fibers

explanation: When you are ready to use the restroom, parasympathetic nerves from your lower spinal cord kick in to contract your bladder wall (the detrusor muscle) and let urine out.

question: Which structure lets you consciously hold your urine until you reach a toilet?

options.A: The detrusor smooth muscle
options.B: The internal urethral sphincter
options.C: The ureteral peristaltic pump
options.D: The external urethral sphincter

explanation: Good news for your social life! Your external urethral sphincter is made of skeletal muscle, meaning you have voluntary control over it to hold your urine until you find a restroom.

question: What is the primary difference between blunt and penetrating genitourinary trauma?

options.A: Penetrating trauma is caused exclusively by sports-related accidents.
options.B: Blunt trauma always requires immediate emergency surgery.
options.C: Penetrating trauma involves objects breaking through the skin and organ walls.
options.D: Blunt trauma only affects the kidneys and never the external genitalia.

explanation: Penetrating trauma is defined by a foreign object like a knife or bullet entering the body, whereas blunt trauma results from compressive force without an open wound. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h1)

question: Why is the urinary bladder easily injured when someone has a pelvic fracture?

options.A: Pelvic fractures cause the bladder to instantly rupture from high pressure.
options.B: The bladder is located completely outside the bony pelvis.
options.C: Fractures stop blood flow to the bladder, causing tissue death.
options.D: Sharp broken edges of the pelvic bones can puncture the bladder wall.

explanation: Think of the bladder resting right behind the pubic bone. When that bone breaks, the sharp edges can easily poke or tear the bladder next to it. Simple and logical!

question: What is the most common and clear sign that a patient has a kidney injury?

options.A: Severe swelling of both legs
options.B: Yellow discoloration of the skin
options.C: Inability to pass any stool
options.D: Blood in the urine

explanation: Seeing blood in the urine (medical name: hematuria) is the classic red flag that tells us the kidneys have taken a hit. Always watch out for this in trauma cases!

question: Why might a patient with a badly damaged kidney have clear urine with no blood at all?

options.A: The blood supply or ureter to that kidney may be completely blocked or torn.
options.B: Blood from the injury goes directly into the stomach instead of the bladder.
options.C: The other healthy kidney absorbs all the blood before it reaches the urine.
options.D: The kidneys stop producing blood completely after a sudden physical impact.

explanation: If the tube carrying urine (the ureter) or the main blood vessel gets completely torn off, urine and blood from that injured kidney cannot flow down into the bladder. Makes sense, right?

question: Which of these is a classic sign of a torn urethra in a male patient?

options.A: Painless swelling of the scrotum
options.B: Sudden uncontrollable diarrhea
options.C: Blood at the urethral meatus
options.D: Yellowing of the eye sclera

explanation: Seeing a bit of blood right at the opening of the penis tells us immediately that the urethra might be torn. Great clinical clue to keep in mind!

question: A male patient with a pelvic fracture has blood at the tip of his penis and cannot urinate. What is the safest nursing action?

options.A: Hold off on placing a standard urinary catheter and report the finding immediately.
options.B: Massage the lower abdomen firmly to force the patient to void naturally.
options.C: Insert a rigid plastic catheter gently until resistance disappears.
options.D: Force a standard Foley catheter past the blockage to relieve the bladder pressure.

explanation: Never force a catheter if you suspect a torn urethra—it can make the injury much worse! Always pause, leave it alone, and inform the doctor right away.

question: What actually happens when a man has a 'penile fracture'?

options.A: A severe calcium deficiency inside the bone structure of the pelvis
options.B: A tear in the protective outer sheath surrounding the erectile tissue
options.C: The complete detachment of the penis from the pelvic floor muscles
options.D: A clean break of the pubic bone underlying the base of the penis

explanation: Don't let the name fool you—there are no bones in the penis! A penile fracture is actually a tear in the tough outer covering (tunica albuginea) around the erectile chambers.

question: Which finding strongly suggests a testicular rupture after a heavy blow to the scrotum?

options.A: Painless enlargement of both testicles over a period of several weeks
options.B: Clear watery drainage leaking from a small scratch on the scrotal skin
options.C: Loss of the normal outline of the testicle on ultrasound with severe local tenderness
options.D: Complete inability to control bowel movements after the impact

explanation: When the testicle bursts, it loses its smooth oval shape on an ultrasound scan, and the patient will have intense pain and swelling. You're mastering trauma assessments!

question: Which imaging test uses a special dye to check the urethra for tears before putting in a catheter?

options.A: Intravenous pyelogram scan
options.B: Retrograde urethrogram
options.C: Plain abdominal X-ray
options.D: Renal duplex ultrasound

explanation: A retrograde urethrogram involves gently putting contrast dye into the urethral opening to take a picture and ensure there are no tears before inserting any tubes.

question: Why is a CT scan with contrast usually preferred for a stable patient with suspected kidney trauma?

options.A: It uses zero radiation and requires no intravenous line placement.
options.B: It can be performed instantly at the bedside without moving an unstable patient.
options.C: It replaces the need to ever inspect the patient's urine for blood.
options.D: It clearly shows active bleeding, urine leaks, and the exact depth of organ damage.

explanation: A contrast CT scan gives doctors a crystal-clear, detailed map showing if blood vessels are bleeding or if urine is leaking into the body. Super helpful tool!

question: What is the main goal of conservative management (non-surgical care) for a mild kidney injury?

options.A: Permanently stopping all urine production from both kidneys
options.B: Repairing the kidney capsule immediately via emergency open surgery
options.C: Dissolving internal blood clots with high-dose oral anticoagulants
options.D: Allowing the organ to heal naturally through close monitoring and bed rest

explanation: For minor injuries, the body is amazing at healing itself! Conservative care just means resting and watching the patient closely without rushing into surgery.

question: During non-surgical care for a kidney injury, which nursing sign is most important to report immediately?

options.A: An increase in sleepiness after receiving a scheduled pain medication
options.B: Mild bruising fading to a yellow color around the flank area
options.C: A sudden drop in blood pressure paired with a fast heart rate
options.D: A slight yellow tinge in the normal daily urine output

explanation: A fast heart rate and dropping blood pressure are early warning signs of hidden internal bleeding. Catching this early can save a life!

question: Which of these situations calls for immediate surgery in genitourinary trauma?

options.A: Hemodynamic instability and active internal bleeding
options.B: A small bruise on the skin over the lower ribs
options.C: Mild hematuria that clears up within two hours
options.D: Anxiety about the hospital environment

explanation: If a patient's vital signs are crashing because of ongoing internal bleeding, surgery is needed right away to stop the leak. Safety first!

question: What is a key nursing priority when caring for a patient with a new suprapubic catheter after bladder surgery?

options.A: Clamp the drainage tubing tightly every two hours to train the bladder muscles.
options.B: Change the catheter insertion tract daily using dry gauze pads only.
options.C: Ensure the tubing stays unobstructed and check the insertion site for leaking urine or infection.
options.D: Flush the drainage system forcefully with sterile water if urine output slows down.

explanation: Keeping the tube clear and watching the site keeps urine flowing smoothly and stops germs from causing an infection. You've got this nursing routine down!

question: What does the term 'stricture' mean when talking about urinary tract injuries?

options.A: A complete widening of the bladder wall from excessive urine pressure
options.B: A narrowing of a tubular structure like the urethra caused by scar tissue
options.C: The sudden permanent cessation of urine production in both kidneys
options.D: An abnormal connection between the bowel and the urinary bladder

explanation: A stricture happens when scar tissue forms as an injury heals, pinching the tube (like the urethra) so it becomes too narrow for urine to flow easily.

question: Why do patients who recover from a severe kidney injury need long-term blood pressure checks?

options.A: Kidney damage can disrupt blood flow regulation and trigger chronic hypertension.
options.B: Blood pressure medication prevents the formation of scar tissue in the ureter.
options.C: High blood pressure is the primary cause of external genital trauma.
options.D: Kidney injuries always cause permanent low blood pressure due to fluid loss.

explanation: Our kidneys help control our blood pressure. If scarring messes up their hormone signals, it can lead to long-term high blood pressure down the road.

question: What is the primary reason for establishing trust during a genitourinary assessment?

options.A: To eliminate the requirement for formal medical documentation
options.B: To prevent the need for diagnostic laboratory tests
options.C: To speed up the physical examination process
options.D: To encourage the patient to share sensitive health details

explanation: Genitourinary symptoms involve private bodily functions, making trust essential for an honest and accurate patient history. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why must a nurse evaluate both the urinary and reproductive systems together?

options.A: Patients cannot distinguish between urinary and reproductive pain
options.B: Issues in one system often directly affect the other
options.C: The anatomical structures share the exact same nerve supply
options.D: Hospital policies mandate performing both exams simultaneously

explanation: Because the urinary and reproductive systems share close anatomical proximity and pathways, pathology in one frequently impacts the other. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h1)

question: What medical term is used to describe pain or a burning sensation when passing urine?

options.A: Nocturia
options.B: Dysuria
options.C: Proteinuria
options.D: Hematuria

explanation: Dysuria is the clinical term for painful or difficult urination, commonly reported during infections. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h2)

question: A patient reports waking up three times every night to pass urine. What term should the nurse document?

options.A: Enuresis
options.B: Nocturia
options.C: Polyuria
options.D: Oliguria

explanation: Nocturia specifically refers to interrupted sleep caused by the need to void during the night. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which physical assessment technique is used to check for kidney tenderness at the back?

options.A: Inspection
options.B: Percussion
options.C: Retraction
options.D: Auscultation

explanation: Great job! Gently tapping (percussing) the costovertebral angle at the back helps us check if the kidneys are inflamed or tender.

question: When gently pressing on the lower abdomen of a healthy adult, what should you normally expect?

options.A: The urethra should feel tender and slightly thickened
options.B: The urinary bladder is not palpable unless distended
options.C: The ureters should be clearly felt along the flank
options.D: Both kidneys should feel firm and easily movable

explanation: Spot on! When the bladder is empty, it hides safely deep in the pelvis. You only feel it when it is full and distended with urine.

question: Which blood tests are most commonly used to evaluate kidney filtration function?

options.A: Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen
options.B: White blood cell count and hemoglobin
options.C: Serum electrolytes and platelet count
options.D: Prothrombin time and international normalized ratio

explanation: Creatinine and blood urea nitrogen are waste products filtered by the kidneys, making them reliable indicators of renal function. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why is proper cleaning of the urethral meatus required before collecting a clean-catch urine sample?

options.A: To decrease burning sensations caused by dysuria during the collection
options.B: To stimulate the bladder muscles and encourage full voiding
options.C: To prevent bacteria from the skin from contaminating the urine culture
options.D: To ensure the specific gravity remains within normal limits

explanation: Skin flora can easily enter the urine stream during collection, leading to false-positive culture results. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary advantage of using an ultrasound for genitourinary assessment?

options.A: It requires general anesthesia for every patient
options.B: It provides a biopsy of the kidney tissue automatically
options.C: It does not expose the patient to radiation
options.D: It measures blood pressure inside the renal arteries

explanation: Ultrasound relies on sound waves rather than ionizing radiation, making it a safe diagnostic imaging option. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which finding is considered a normal, expected temporary side effect following a cystoscopy procedure?

options.A: Mild burning during urination and slight pink-tinged urine
options.B: Inability to feel the need to urinate for several weeks
options.C: Severe lower abdominal pain radiating to the shoulders
options.D: Complete absence of urine output for twenty-four hours

explanation: Passing the scope through the urethra causes minor irritation and mucosal trauma, leading to temporary burning and light bleeding. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h5)

question: What type of data includes measurable physical signs and laboratory test results?

options.A: Objective data
options.B: Anecdotal data
options.C: Historical data
options.D: Subjective data

explanation: Objective data consists of observable and measurable facts gathered through physical examination and diagnostic testing. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h6)

question: Why is accurate documentation of genitourinary assessment findings essential for patient care?

options.A: It establishes a reliable baseline to monitor treatment progress
options.B: It replaces the need for verbal communication between shift nurses
options.C: It guarantees that no further diagnostic tests will be needed
options.D: It eliminates the legal liability of the healthcare facility

explanation: Clear documentation provides a factual record that allows the healthcare team to track changes in a patient's condition over time. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h6)

question: What primary body system does an intravenous pyelogram examine?

options.A: The central nervous system
options.B: The urinary system
options.C: The respiratory system
options.D: The digestive tract

explanation: An IVP specifically targets the kidneys, ureters, and bladder to evaluate how well urine flows through the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h1)

question: How does the contrast dye help visualize the urinary structures during an IVP?

options.A: By speeding up the heart rate to increase blood flow to kidneys
options.B: By dissolving blockages inside the renal pelvis immediately
options.C: By staining the outer skin to track the dye path visually
options.D: By making the structures show up clearly on x-ray images

explanation: Radiopaque contrast dye blocks x-ray beams, creating a clear picture of the urinary tract's interior on the final images. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h1)

question: The main cause of hematuria investigated by an IVP is...

options.A: low white blood cell count in blood
options.B: blood present in the urine sample
options.C: elevated fasting blood sugar levels
options.D: excessive fluid intake during meals

explanation: Hematuria simply means blood in the urine, and an IVP helps find where that bleeding is originating along the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h2)

question: A patient arrives at the clinic with recurring kidney stones and severe flank pain. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate to visualize the exact location of the stones in the ureters?

options.A: Intravenous pyelogram
options.B: Electrocardiogram
options.C: Pulmonary function test
options.D: Echocardiogram

explanation: An IVP uses contrast dye to highlight the urinary tract, making it very effective for spotting kidney stones causing flank pain. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard contraindication for an intravenous pyelogram?

options.A: Severe kidney failure
options.B: Known allergy to iodine dye
options.C: Mild seasonal pollen allergy
options.D: Confirmed pregnancy

explanation: Allergies to pollen do not interfere with iodine contrast dye, whereas iodine allergies, kidney failure, and pregnancy are major contraindications. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why must metformin be withheld from patients receiving an iodine contrast agent?

options.A: To stop the contrast dye from crystallizing inside the stomach lining
options.B: To keep the patient's blood pressure from dropping too low during the test
options.C: To prevent the dangerous buildup of lactic acidosis if kidneys struggle
options.D: To ensure the x-ray machine captures a clear picture of the pancreas

explanation: If the contrast temporarily impairs kidney function, metformin can accumulate and trigger a severe metabolic complication called lactic acidosis. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the main reason a patient is given a laxative the evening before an IVP?

options.A: To lower the patient's blood pressure prior to injection
options.B: To clear gas and stool from the bowels for clear x-ray views
options.C: To prevent the contrast dye from causing severe diarrhea
options.D: To empty the urinary bladder completely before morning

explanation: Stool and gas in the intestines can hide the kidneys and ureters on the x-ray film, so bowel cleansing is necessary. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why does the nurse instruct the patient to empty their bladder right before the procedure begins?

options.A: To test the urine for hidden infection before the radiologist arrives
options.B: To make sure the patient does not need to use the restroom during the dye injection
options.C: To get an accurate baseline and prevent residual urine from blocking the view
options.D: To reduce the overall fluid volume inside the body before taking pictures

explanation: An empty bladder ensures that the initial images show the true anatomy without old urine diluting or obscuring the incoming contrast dye. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the purpose of taking a plain x-ray of the abdomen before injecting the contrast dye?

options.A: To test if the intravenous line is working properly
options.B: To measure the exact amount of urine currently in the bladder
options.C: To warm up the x-ray machine before the actual test begins
options.D: To check patient positioning and verify bowel preparation

explanation: The initial scout film confirms that the bowels are clean enough and that the x-ray machine is positioned correctly over the kidneys. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why are compression bands sometimes placed on the patient's abdomen during an IVP?

options.A: To push the contrast dye through the bloodstream much faster
options.B: To prevent the patient from moving around on the hard x-ray table
options.C: To keep the intravenous needle securely taped inside the vein
options.D: To slow urine flow and keep the upper renal system filled with dye

explanation: Abdominal compression temporarily traps the contrast in the kidneys and ureters, making those structures easier to see on the x-ray films. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h5)

question: Which symptom experienced immediately after the contrast injection is considered a normal, expected reaction?

options.A: Sudden swelling of the tongue and lips
options.B: Complete inability to speak or move
options.C: Severe shortness of breath and wheezing
options.D: A warm flushing sensation and a salty taste

explanation: Most patients feel a sudden wave of warmth and notice a metallic or salty taste when the dye enters their bloodstream. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary reason for encouraging high fluid intake after an intravenous pyelogram?

options.A: To prevent the patient from feeling hungry after fasting
options.B: To help flush the contrast dye out of the kidneys quickly
options.C: To stimulate normal bowel movements following the procedure
options.D: To replace the fluid lost during the mandatory bowel preparation

explanation: Drinking plenty of fluids dilutes any remaining dye and encourages prompt urination, protecting the kidneys from potential injury. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h6)

question: What medication is immediately required if a patient experiences a severe anaphylactic reaction to contrast dye?

options.A: Insulin
options.B: Metformin
options.C: Aspirin
options.D: Epinephrine

explanation: Epinephrine is the life-saving first-line drug used to treat severe allergic reactions, opening airways and supporting blood pressure. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h7)

question: Which sign indicates that a patient is developing contrast-induced nephropathy days after an IVP?

options.A: A temporary metallic taste in the mouth
options.B: A sudden rash appearing on the chest
options.C: A delayed rise in serum creatinine levels
options.D: A mild episode of dizziness right after standing

explanation: Kidney injury from contrast dye typically shows up as an abnormal elevation in blood creatinine levels within two days of the test. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h7)

question: What does hydronephrosis mean when seen on an IVP result?

options.A: An infection caused by bacteria inside the bladder wall
options.B: Shrinking of the kidney size due to chronic high blood pressure
options.C: Bleeding originating from the inner lining of the ureters
options.D: Swelling of the renal pelvis and calyces due to blockage

explanation: Hydronephrosis happens when urine backs up behind an obstruction like a stone, causing the collecting system of the kidney to swell. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h8)

question: A patient's IVP report notes a 'filling defect' in the right ureter. What condition is the radiologist most likely describing?

options.A: An abnormal mass or kidney stone taking up space
options.B: An area where the contrast dye failed to reach at all
options.C: A normal pocket of air trapped inside the bladder
options.D: A normal variation in the size of the right kidney

explanation: A filling defect is an area where something like a stone or tumor displaces the contrast dye, creating a dark spot on the x-ray film. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h8)

question: What primary part of the kidney is inflamed in Acute Glomerulonephritis?

options.A: The glomeruli
options.B: The renal pelvis
options.C: The loop of Henle
options.D: The ureteral walls

explanation: Acute Glomerulonephritis specifically targets and inflames the glomeruli, which are the primary filtering units of the kidneys. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why does fluid and waste build up in the body during an episode of Acute Glomerulonephritis?

options.A: The bladder becomes too weak to push urine out
options.B: Too much water is produced directly inside the liver
options.C: Inflamed filtering units fail to clean the blood properly
options.D: The ureters completely block the flow of urine

explanation: When glomeruli become swollen and inflamed, their normal filtering function drops, causing fluid and waste products to accumulate in the body. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h1)

question: What gets stuck in the tiny kidney filters to spark the inflammation in glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Bile pigment molecules
options.B: Red blood cells
options.C: Excess glucose droplets
options.D: Immune complexes

explanation: Think of immune complexes as sticky trouble-makers floating in the blood that accidentally get trapped in the kidney filters, starting the inflammation party we don't want!

question: Why do red blood cells end up leaking into the urine when someone has Acute Glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Severe infection inside the urinary meatus
options.B: Rapid breakdown of muscular tissue in the legs
options.C: Direct physical trauma to the external bladder lining
options.D: The damaged filtering membrane becomes too porous

explanation: When inflammation damages the filter, the tiny holes become too wide (porous)—letting red blood cells slip right through into the urine. Makes sense, right?

question: What is the single most common trigger for Acute Glomerulonephritis globally and in Nigeria?

options.A: Streptococcal infection
options.B: Direct kidney trauma
options.C: A severe snake bite
options.D: High dietary salt intake

explanation: Post-streptococcal infection is overwhelmingly the most frequent cause of this type of nephritis. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical source of infection linked to Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis?

options.A: A recent streptococcal throat infection
options.B: An infected skin sore or boil
options.C: An untreated impetigo skin lesion
options.D: An inherited defect in heart valves

explanation: Heart valve issues are structural and something a person is born with, whereas glomerulonephritis is triggered by bacterial infections like throat sores or impetigo.

question: What unusual color does urine often turn in a patient with Acute Glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Thick bright orange
options.B: Cola or smoky brown
options.C: Bright neon green
options.D: Milky white and cloudy

explanation: Because red blood cells break down as they pass through the inflamed kidneys, the urine ends up looking dark like Coca-Cola or smoky brown. A classic clinical sign!

question: A child is brought to the clinic with puffiness around the eyes every morning, dark urine, and high blood pressure. Which condition is most likely?

options.A: Acute Glomerulonephritis
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Acute appendicitis
options.D: Bacterial meningitis

explanation: Periorbital edema, dark urine, and hypertension are the classic triad of signs pointing directly to Acute Glomerulonephritis. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h4)

question: Which blood test helps prove that a patient recently had a strep infection?

options.A: Liver function panel
options.B: Anti-Streptolysin O (ASO) titer
options.C: Complete blood count (CBC)
options.D: Fast blood sugar level

explanation: An elevated ASO titer is the specific lab test doctors use to check if strep antibodies are floating around after a recent infection.

question: What happens to C3 complement protein levels in the blood during active Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis?

options.A: They rise to very high levels
options.B: They fluctuate every few hours
options.C: They drop below normal levels
options.D: They remain completely unchanged

explanation: Think of C3 proteins as defense workers that get completely used up and depleted by the ongoing immune battle in the kidneys, leaving low levels in the blood test.

question: What type of drug is given to clear away any lingering strep bacteria in these patients?

options.A: Anticoagulants
options.B: Bronchodilators
options.C: Antipyretics
options.D: Antibiotics

explanation: We use antibiotics like penicillin to wipe out any stubborn strep bacteria still hiding in the body. Spot on!

question: Why do doctors frequently prescribe diuretics (water pills) for patients with Acute Glomerulonephritis?

options.A: To permanently cure the underlying bacterial infection
options.B: To stimulate a massive increase in red blood cell production
options.C: To reduce fluid overload and swelling
options.D: To lower the patient's body temperature during fever

explanation: Diuretics help the kidneys push out extra water and salt, which quickly brings down swelling and lowers dangerous blood pressure. Excellent nursing pharmacology!

question: What is the most reliable daily indicator of fluid balance changes in a hospitalized child with nephritis?

options.A: Morning body temperature
options.B: Skin color assessment
options.C: Abdominal girth measurement
options.D: Daily body weight

explanation: Daily weighing is the single most sensitive and accurate way to track fluid retention or loss in patients with kidney problems. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h7)

question: A nurse is caring for a patient with acute glomerulonephritis. Which nursing action is most critical during the acute phase?

options.A: Providing a high-protein diet to rebuild lost muscle
options.B: Massaging swollen legs to improve local circulation
options.C: Accurately measuring every intake and output volume
options.D: Encouraging high fluid intake by offering extra water

explanation: Tracking every drop that goes in and comes out (I&O) is essential to monitor failing kidney function and catch dangerous fluid buildup early.

question: What serious brain complication can happen if a patient's blood pressure shoots up dangerously high from nephritis?

options.A: Hypertensive encephalopathy
options.B: Bacterial meningitis
options.C: Cerebellar atrophy
options.D: Peripheral neuropathy

explanation: When blood pressure goes through the roof, it overwhelms the blood vessels in the brain, causing swelling known as hypertensive encephalopathy. A true medical emergency!

question: What life-threatening emergency happens when fluid overload backs up all the way into the lungs?

options.A: Pleural mesothelioma
options.B: Chronic bronchial asthma
options.C: Spontaneous pneumothorax
options.D: Acute pulmonary edema

explanation: When the kidneys can't clear fluid, it backs up into the air sacs (alveoli) of the lungs, causing acute pulmonary edema and severe breathing distress. You're mastering critical care concepts!

question: What is the usual long-term outlook for children who get Acute Glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Poor, with guaranteed progression to failure
options.B: Moderate, leading to chronic heart disease
options.C: Excellent, with most making a full recovery
options.D: Unpredictable, with lifelong dialysis needed

explanation: Unlike adults, kids with AGN almost always bounce back completely with the right care and rest. Such a relief to know for young patients and their families!

question: Why must nurses stress to parents the importance of finishing a child's entire course of antibiotics?

options.A: To prevent the child from developing a skin rash
options.B: To permanently boost the child's daily appetite
options.C: To completely wipe out the bacteria and prevent relapse
options.D: To ensure the child gains healthy weight rapidly

explanation: Stopping antibiotics early just because the child 'looks better' can let hidden bacteria bounce back and cause more kidney damage. Patient education at its finest!

question: What main physical change happens inside the kidneys during chronic glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Sudden kidney enlargement
options.B: Rapid bacterial infection
options.C: Severe internal bleeding
options.D: Scarring of the glomeruli

explanation: You've got this! Chronic glomerulonephritis causes long-term damage that leads to glomerulosclerosis—which is just a fancy medical word for permanent scarring of the kidney's filtering units.

question: Why is chronic glomerulonephritis often discovered quite late?

options.A: It develops silently over many years before symptoms show
options.B: Lab tests cannot detect kidney problems early
options.C: Symptoms only appear after dialysis starts
options.D: Patients always ignore early severe pain

explanation: Spot on! The disease moves so slowly that the healthy parts of the kidneys work extra hard to cover for the damaged parts, hiding the problem for a long time.

question: What gets trapped inside the kidney's filtering membranes to kick off inflammation?

options.A: Red blood cells
options.B: Digestive enzymes
options.C: Excess platelets
options.D: Immune complexes

explanation: Great job! When immune complexes get stuck in the kidney tissues, they sound the alarm and trigger white blood cells to start an inflammatory attack.

question: What happens when surviving nephrons have to overwork because their neighbors broke down?

options.A: They regenerate completely to cure the disease
options.B: They stop working immediately to rest the kidney
options.C: They turn into normal liver cells
options.D: They undergo hyperfiltration and suffer further damage

explanation: Think of it like carrying extra load—when healthy nephrons take over for damaged ones, the heavy workload puts them under stress, wearing them out faster too.

question: Which systemic autoimmune condition is a common underlying cause of chronic glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Systemic lupus erythematosus
options.B: Chronic asthma
options.C: Iron deficiency anemia
options.D: Rheumatoid arthritis only

explanation: Lupus (SLE) is a well-known condition where the body's immune system attacks its own tissues, very frequently targeting the delicate filters in the kidneys.

question: How does high blood pressure cause damage to a patient's kidneys?

options.A: High pressure strains and hardens the delicate blood vessels in the glomeruli
options.B: Hypertension directly causes the bladder to shrink
options.C: High blood pressure washes away all the red blood cells in the body
options.D: High pressure stops the heart from pumping blood to the lungs

explanation: Think of high pressure like a rushing river beating against a weak fence. It puts harsh mechanical stress on tiny kidney capillaries, causing them to scar over time.

question: Why do patients with chronic glomerulonephritis sometimes notice foamy urine?

options.A: High amounts of sugar
options.B: Too many white blood cells
options.C: Presence of excess protein
options.D: Excessive water intake

explanation: You've got this! When damaged glomeruli let large protein molecules slip through into the urine, it creates bubbles, giving the urine a noticeable foamy look.

question: A patient with chronic glomerulonephritis feels exhausted all the time and looks pale. Why?

options.A: High blood sugar affecting the brain
options.B: Dehydration from drinking too little water
options.C: Anemia caused by reduced erythropoietin production
options.D: Muscle injury from exercising too hard

explanation: Kidneys do more than filter waste—they also make erythropoietin (EPO), the hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells. When kidneys fail, EPO drops and anemia sets in!

question: What is a classic ultrasound finding in someone with long-standing chronic glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Normal kidney size
options.B: Small, shrunken kidneys
options.C: A single missing kidney
options.D: Enlarged, fluid-filled cysts

explanation: Years of tissue scarring and nephron loss cause the kidneys to physically lose mass and shrink down, which doctors and sonographers easily spot on scans.

question: Which lab test is the most reliable way to track declining kidney function?

options.A: Platelet aggregation rate
options.B: White blood cell count
options.C: Serum sodium concentration
options.D: Glomerular filtration rate

explanation: The GFR (Glomerular Filtration Rate) tells us directly how well the kidneys are cleaning the blood, making it the gold standard for checking kidney health.

question: Why do doctors frequently prescribe ACE inhibitors or ARBs for chronic glomerulonephritis?

options.A: They replace the function of dialysis
options.B: They cure bacterial bladder infections instantly
options.C: They lower pressure inside the glomeruli and reduce protein loss
options.D: They stimulate the bone marrow to make red blood cells

explanation: These medications relax the tiny blood vessels leaving the kidney filters, which drops the pressure inside and protects the remaining nephrons from wearing out.

question: What is the main goal of medical treatment during the early and middle stages of this disease?

options.A: Completely curing the underlying genetic defect
options.B: Slowing disease progression and managing blood pressure
options.C: Regenerating completely healthy new kidney tissue
options.D: Stopping all urine production to rest the body

explanation: Since kidney scarring cannot be undone, the primary goal of treatment is to protect the nephrons we have left and keep the patient stable for as long as possible.

question: What is the easiest and most sensitive way for a nurse to check for early fluid buildup at home?

options.A: Weighing the patient daily at the same time
options.B: Measuring the circumference of the arm
options.C: Asking the patient if they feel thirsty
options.D: Checking shoe size once a week

explanation: Water weighs a lot! A sudden climb on the bathroom scale is almost always the earliest sign that fluid is starting to build up in the body.

question: Which common group of over-the-counter painkillers must patients with kidney disease strictly avoid?

options.A: Plain acetaminophen tablets
options.B: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
options.C: Multivitamins with vitamin C
options.D: Antacids containing calcium

explanation: NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or diclofenac) can severely cut off blood flow to struggling kidneys and cause even more damage. Always watch out for them in kidney patients!

question: Which dangerous electrolyte imbalance is most life-threatening in advanced kidney failure?

options.A: Hyponatremia
options.B: Hypocalcemia
options.C: Hypermagnesemia
options.D: Hyperkalemia

explanation: High potassium (hyperkalemia) is a major emergency because it messes with the heart's electrical rhythm and can lead to sudden cardiac arrest if not treated quickly.

question: What is the final long-term outcome if chronic glomerulonephritis keeps progressing without control?

options.A: End-stage renal disease requiring dialysis or transplant
options.B: Permanent stabilization without medical treatment
options.C: Transition of the disease into chronic liver failure
options.D: Complete recovery of normal kidney structure

explanation: When nephrons are gradually destroyed over time, the kidneys eventually stop working entirely, meaning the patient will need dialysis or a kidney transplant to survive.

question: What is the primary characteristic of acute renal failure?

options.A: A gradual increase in the body's red blood cell count
options.B: Permanent structural damage that develops over years
options.C: A sudden and rapid decline in kidney function
options.D: Slow scarring of the kidney tissue over months

explanation: Acute renal failure happens very quickly over hours or days, unlike chronic kidney disease which takes a long time to develop. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h1)

question: What is azotemia in a patient with acute kidney injury?

options.A: An excessive loss of protein through the urine
options.B: An abnormal increase in the production of red blood cells
options.C: A buildup of nitrogenous waste products in the blood
options.D: A severe drop in the total volume of circulating blood

explanation: When the kidneys fail suddenly, they cannot filter properly, causing waste like urea and creatinine to build up in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which of the following is a classic example of a prerenal cause of acute kidney injury?

options.A: Direct toxicity to the kidney tubules from certain drugs
options.B: Severe inflammation of the glomeruli inside the kidney
options.C: A large kidney stone blocking the ureter completely
options.D: Severe dehydration from heavy vomiting and diarrhea

explanation: Prerenal causes involve a lack of adequate blood flow to the kidneys, often due to fluid loss like severe dehydration or shock. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h2)

question: An enlarged prostate gland that blocks urine flow from the bladder falls under which category of acute renal failure?

options.A: Prerenal
options.B: Postrenal
options.C: Systemic
options.D: Intrarenal

explanation: Postrenal causes involve any blockage that prevents urine from leaving the body after it is formed by the kidneys. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h2)

question: What defines the oliguric stage of acute renal failure?

options.A: The complete absence of blood in the circulatory system
options.B: A sudden return of normal kidney filtering rates
options.C: A massive increase in daily urine production
options.D: A significant drop in daily urine output

explanation: During the oliguric stage, urine output decreases sharply, often dropping below 400 milliliters per day. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h3)

question: A patient entering the diuretic stage of acute renal failure is most at risk for which complication?

options.A: Dehydration and electrolyte loss
options.B: Sudden blockage of the ureters by stones
options.C: Severe fluid overload and high blood pressure
options.D: Permanent cessation of all kidney function

explanation: In the diuretic stage, damaged nephrons start recovering and pass large amounts of fluid, which can quickly lead to dehydration if fluid isn't replaced. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h3)

question: Which blood test is most commonly used alongside BUN to evaluate kidney filtration ability?

options.A: Serum creatinine
options.B: Hemoglobin levels
options.C: Serum calcium
options.D: White blood cell count

explanation: Serum creatinine is a reliable indicator of kidney function because it rises when the kidneys fail to filter waste effectively. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h4)

question: Why is a renal ultrasound often ordered when evaluating a patient with sudden kidney failure?

options.A: To test how well the liver is metabolizing circulating medications
options.B: To measure the exact amount of protein lost in a 24-hour period
options.C: To check for physical blockages or structural causes of urine backup
options.D: To determine the precise percentage of red blood cells in circulation

explanation: An ultrasound provides a clear image of the kidneys and urinary tract, helping doctors quickly identify postrenal obstructions like stones or an enlarged prostate. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of administering furosemide to a patient with acute renal failure and fluid overload?

options.A: To permanently repair damaged glomeruli in the nephrons
options.B: To dissolve large kidney stones blocking the ureters
options.C: To lower dangerous levels of blood glucose in the body
options.D: To stimulate urine output and reduce excess body fluid

explanation: Loop diuretics like furosemide help the kidneys excrete excess water and sodium when the patient is fluid overloaded. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why is high blood potassium treated urgently in a patient with acute renal failure?

options.A: To encourage the kidneys to immediately start producing concentrated urine
options.B: To prevent severe infection in the upper urinary tract
options.C: To prevent dangerous and life-threatening heart rhythm changes
options.D: To stop the sudden breakdown of muscle tissue throughout the body

explanation: Elevated potassium levels severely affect the electrical system of the heart, leading to fatal cardiac arrhythmias if left untreated. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h5)

question: What is the most sensitive daily indicator of fluid balance in a patient with acute renal failure?

options.A: Total daily fluid intake calculations
options.B: Skin turgor and mucous membrane check
options.C: Daily body weight measurement
options.D: Blood pressure readings every four hours

explanation: Weighing the patient daily is the most accurate way to detect rapid fluid gains or losses, where one kilogram equals one liter of fluid. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h6)

question: Why does a nurse monitor strict fluid intake and output on a patient with acute renal failure?

options.A: To detect early signs of fluid retention or worsening kidney output
options.B: To calculate the exact amount of dietary protein the patient needs
options.C: To prevent the development of a secondary urinary tract infection
options.D: To determine when the patient is ready to be discharged home

explanation: Tracking fluid balance helps nurses spot dangerous fluid accumulation or declining urine production before it causes severe complications. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h6)

question: Which of the following is a clear indication for starting dialysis in acute renal failure?

options.A: Normal laboratory values for serum creatinine and blood urea
options.B: A mild and stable increase in the patient's daily appetite
options.C: A temporary decrease in blood pressure caused by mild dehydration
options.D: Severe and persistent hyperkalemia that resists medical treatment

explanation: Dangerous electrolyte imbalances like unmanageable high potassium are a primary reason to start urgent dialysis. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h7)

question: Why is continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) often chosen over standard hemodialysis for critically ill patients?

options.A: It can be performed easily without any specialized equipment
options.B: It does not require any form of vascular access in the body
options.C: It completely cures chronic kidney disease within a few days
options.D: It removes fluids and toxins much more slowly and gently

explanation: CRRT filters blood continuously over 24 hours, making it much safer for hemodynamically unstable patients in the ICU. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h7)

question: What is the main difference between an acute kidney injury and chronic renal failure?

options.A: Chronic renal failure always resolves completely with proper hydration therapy.
options.B: Acute injury develops slowly over several years without causing any symptoms.
options.C: Acute injury only affects the bladder, while chronic failure affects the entire ureter.
options.D: Chronic renal failure involves permanent and irreversible loss of nephron function.

explanation: You've got this! Chronic renal failure causes permanent scarring and loss of nephrons over time. Acute injury, on the other hand, can often be reversed if caught early.

question: Why do the remaining healthy nephrons get larger (hypertrophy) during the early stages of chronic kidney disease?

options.A: To produce extra urine that completely flushes out all uremic toxins from the body
options.B: To increase blood pressure so that the heart pumps faster to the extremities
options.C: To compensate for the workload of the nephrons that have already been destroyed
options.D: To store extra electrolytes and vitamins for future metabolic needs

explanation: Think of it like a team picking up extra shifts when coworkers drop out. Healthy nephrons try to take over the filtering work, but this extra strain eventually causes them to burn out too.

question: What is the single most common cause of chronic renal failure here in Nigeria?

options.A: Congenital bladder defects
options.B: Polycystic kidney disease
options.C: Acute bacterial pneumonia
options.D: Chronic hypertension

explanation: Great clinical insight to carry into practice! High blood pressure puts constant, hard pressure on the tiny blood vessels in the kidneys, making it the leading cause of renal failure in our region.

question: How do unregulated herbal remedies often contribute to chronic kidney disease in clinical practice?

options.A: By lowering systemic blood pressure so drastically that blood stops flowing
options.B: By stimulating the overproduction of red blood cells in the bone marrow
options.C: By causing sudden dehydration that increases daily urine output permanently
options.D: By introducing heavy metals and toxic substances that damage the kidney tubules

explanation: As nurses, we see this often. Many traditional concoctions contain hidden toxins that gradually injure the delicate filtering structures of the kidneys over long periods of use.

question: Why do patients with chronic renal failure frequently look very pale and complain of severe tiredness?

options.A: The liver stops producing enough protein to carry vitamins.
options.B: Decreased erythropoietin production leads to anemia.
options.C: Excess sodium in the blood blocks oxygen from entering the lungs.
options.D: High potassium levels destroy red blood cells in the bloodstream.

explanation: Remember, damaged kidneys forget to make enough erythropoietin—the hormone that tells your bone marrow to build red blood cells. Without it, anemia sets in!

question: A patient with end-stage kidney disease complains of severe itching all over their body. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: An allergic reaction to the standard hospital soap used during morning care
options.B: Mineral imbalances causing calcium-phosphate crystals to deposit in the skin tissues
options.C: Excessive production of red blood cells causing severe pressure under the skin
options.D: A sudden viral skin infection caused by a weakened immune system

explanation: Poor kidneys struggle to balance calcium and phosphorus. When phosphorus builds up, tiny mineral crystals form under the skin, causing that intense, frustrating itch.

question: What is considered the best overall laboratory test to check how well the kidneys are working?

options.A: Random blood glucose level
options.B: Serum electrolyte balance
options.C: Total white blood cell count
options.D: Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR)

explanation: You'll see eGFR results on patient charts every day. It estimates how fast your glomeruli are filtering blood using creatinine levels, making it the gold standard for kidney function.

question: Why is finding protein persistently in a patient's urine an important warning sign?

options.A: It confirms that the liver is failing to process dietary nutrients properly.
options.B: It shows that the bladder is contracting too frequently during the day.
options.C: It indicates that the filtering barriers of the glomeruli have been damaged.
options.D: It proves that the patient is eating too much protein in their daily diet.

explanation: Healthy glomeruli act like a strict bouncer, keeping big protein molecules safely inside the blood. If protein leaks into the urine, it tells us those filters are injured.

question: Why are ACE inhibitor medications often given to kidney disease patients even if their blood pressure is completely normal?

options.A: They stimulate the bone marrow to produce extra white blood cells.
options.B: They absorb extra phosphorus directly from the gastrointestinal tract.
options.C: They reduce pressure inside the glomeruli and decrease protein leakage.
options.D: They dissolve calcium deposits that form inside the renal tubules.

explanation: Think of ACE inhibitors as pressure-relieving valves for the nephrons. By easing the internal filtering pressure, they protect the kidneys from wearing out faster.

question: What is the main goal of giving 'phosphate binders' to a patient with kidney failure?

options.A: To lower systemic blood pressure by relaxing blood vessel walls
options.B: To prevent dietary phosphorus from being absorbed in the gut
options.C: To increase daily urine output and reduce swelling in the legs
options.D: To stimulate red blood cell production in the bone marrow

explanation: Patients take these binders right with their meals. The medicine grabs onto phosphorus in the food and carries it out safely through the stool so it doesn't flood the blood.

question: During peritoneal dialysis, what part of the patient's body acts as the natural filtering membrane?

options.A: The peritoneal membrane inside the abdominal cavity
options.B: The inner lining of the urinary bladder walls
options.C: The basement membrane of the remaining renal tubules
options.D: The semipermeable filter inside the hemodialysis machine

explanation: Peritoneal dialysis is clever! It uses the patient's own rich network of blood vessels inside the abdominal lining (the peritoneum) to filter out waste and extra water.

question: What is a major, non-negotiable requirement for a patient who has received a successful kidney transplant?

options.A: Avoiding all forms of physical activity to protect the new incision site
options.B: Undergoing hemodialysis twice a week to clean the transplanted organ
options.C: Following a strict low-protein diet for the rest of their natural life
options.D: Taking lifelong immunosuppressive medications to prevent organ rejection

explanation: The body's immune system naturally views a new organ as a stranger and tries to fight it. Transplant patients must take anti-rejection drugs every single day to protect their new kidney.

question: You are assessing a patient with a newly created AV fistula in their arm. What finding tells you it is open and working well?

options.A: A palpable thrill and audible bruit over the fistula site
options.B: Absence of any sound or vibration when listening with a stethoscope
options.C: A cool hand with weak pulses past the surgical site
options.D: A strong pulse with severe pain and redness in the fingers

explanation: You'll love listening for this in the ward! When arterial and venous blood rush together, it creates a gentle vibration (thrill) and a swishing sound (bruit) that confirms good blood flow.

question: Why is stepping on the scale to check daily body weight so crucial in the care plan for kidney failure?

options.A: It measures how well the bone marrow is producing red blood cells.
options.B: It helps calculate the exact amount of protein the patient needs to eat.
options.C: It is the most sensitive daily indicator of fluid retention or loss.
options.D: It indicates whether the patient is taking their iron supplements on time.

explanation: Numbers don't lie! A sudden weight gain over a day or two almost always means the kidneys are struggling and the body is holding onto dangerous amounts of fluid.

question: What is the primary protein lost in the urine during nephrotic conditions?

options.A: Globulin
options.B: Fibrinogen
options.C: Albumin
options.D: Hemoglobin

explanation: Albumin is the most abundant protein in the blood and the main one that leaks through the damaged glomerular barrier into the urine. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h1)

question: Why does severe facial and body swelling occur in nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: Low blood protein reduces pressure that keeps fluid inside blood vessels
options.B: Infections block the lymphatic system in the neck and face
options.C: The heart pumps too much blood for the kidneys to handle
options.D: Excess salt intake causes the body to sweat less

explanation: When albumin levels drop in the blood, the pulling pressure that keeps water inside the blood vessels is lost, causing fluid to leak into tissues. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h1)

question: What is the most frequent cause of nephrotic syndrome in young children?

options.A: Membranous nephropathy
options.B: Systemic lupus erythematosus
options.C: Minimal change disease
options.D: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

explanation: Minimal change disease accounts for the vast majority of nephrotic syndrome cases in children and usually responds very well to steroid therapy. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h2)

question: How do secondary causes differ from primary causes of nephrotic conditions?

options.A: Secondary causes always resolve completely without medication
options.B: Secondary causes only affect adults over the age of sixty
options.C: Primary causes involve infections outside the urinary tract
options.D: Secondary causes are systemic diseases that damage the kidneys as a complication

explanation: You're doing great! Think of primary causes as starting right in the kidney, while secondary causes happen when a whole-body condition like diabetes or lupus ends up hurting the kidneys along the way.

question: What visual characteristic does urine often have in a patient with nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: Dark red and bloody
options.B: Frothy or foamy appearance
options.C: Thick and milky white
options.D: Bright neon green color

explanation: The large amount of protein spilling into the urine changes its surface tension, creating a noticeable frothy or foamy look when the patient voids. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h3)

question: A patient with severe nephrotic syndrome is most likely to report which initial pattern of swelling?

options.A: Severe swelling limited to the toes
options.B: Sudden swelling of only the right hand
options.C: Puffiness around the eyes upon waking up
options.D: Throbbing pain and swelling in the jaw

explanation: Periorbital edema is a classic early sign of fluid shifting into loose facial tissues overnight while the patient is lying flat. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h3)

question: What is the primary medication class used as first-line treatment for minimal change disease?

options.A: Antivirals
options.B: Antibiotics
options.C: Corticosteroids
options.D: Beta blockers

explanation: Corticosteroids reduce inflammation and immune activity that damage the glomerular filter, making them the standard starting treatment. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h4)

question: Why are ACE inhibitors or ARBs frequently prescribed for nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: They prevent bacterial infections in the urinary tract
options.B: They completely cure the underlying autoimmune disease
options.C: They replace lost albumin directly in the bloodstream
options.D: They decrease pressure inside the glomerulus to reduce protein leakage

explanation: These medications relax the tiny blood vessels leaving the glomerulus, lowering the pressure that forces protein out into the urine. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h4)

question: Why is a severely low-protein diet generally discouraged for patients with nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: It makes the urine completely stop flowing
options.B: It increases the risk of developing diabetes mellitus
options.C: It causes blood pressure to rise to dangerous levels
options.D: It does not stop protein loss and can lead to muscle breakdown

explanation: Don't worry if this tripped you up! Restricting protein doesn't stop the kidneys from leaking it; instead, it starves the patient's body and leads to muscle wasting.

question: Which nursing action provides the most accurate daily measurement of fluid retention in a hospitalized patient?

options.A: Asking the patient how tight their shoes feel each morning
options.B: Weighing the patient at the exact same time every day on the same scale
options.C: Measuring the abdominal girth with a soft tape measure once per shift
options.D: Counting how many times the patient asks to use the restroom

explanation: Daily weights using the same scale and clothing weight offer the most reliable data on whether fluid is accumulating or being successfully removed. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h5)

question: Why are patients with nephrotic syndrome at a much higher risk for blood clots?

options.A: They lie in bed all day without moving their legs
options.B: Their red blood cell count increases drastically
options.C: They lose clotting-regulatory proteins through their urine
options.D: Their blood pressure is always extremely high

explanation: The kidneys filter out proteins that normally prevent blood from clotting too easily, leaving the blood in a hypercoagulable state. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a major complication commonly associated with nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: Increased risk of blood clots
options.B: Severe bacterial infections
options.C: Permanent loss of hearing
options.D: High blood cholesterol levels

explanation: Hearing loss is not a standard complication of nephrotic syndrome, whereas clotting risks, infections, and high cholesterol are well-known dangers. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h6)

question: What crucial instruction should a nurse give a patient taking prescribed corticosteroid therapy?

options.A: Stop the medication immediately if you start to feel better
options.B: Never stop taking the medication suddenly without medical guidance
options.C: Increase your daily salt intake to balance the steroid effects
options.D: Take the pills on an empty stomach right before bedtime

explanation: Abruptly stopping steroids can trigger a dangerous adrenal crisis because the body stops producing its own natural stress hormones during treatment. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h7)

question: A patient discharged after treatment for nephrotic syndrome calls the clinic reporting a new, warm, swollen, and painful calf. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Normal muscle recovery after being on bed rest
options.B: An allergic reaction to the prescribed diuretic
options.C: Rapid healing of the kidney filtration barrier
options.D: A deep vein thrombosis due to protein loss

explanation: Unilateral calf pain and swelling in a patient with nephrotic syndrome is a classic red flag for a deep vein thrombosis caused by altered clotting factors. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h7)

question: What does a genitourinary neoplasm involve?

options.A: Inflammation of the prostate gland caused by pathogens
options.B: Chronic bacterial infections of the lower urinary tract
options.C: Abnormal tissue growths in the urinary and male reproductive systems
options.D: Sudden loss of kidney filtration due to dehydration

explanation: Think of a neoplasm simply as an abnormal growth or tumor. When we say genitourinary, we mean the organs of the urinary system and the male reproductive tract. You've got this!

question: Why is early recognition of genitourinary growths so important?

options.A: It directly improves survival rates and quality of life
options.B: It guarantees that the tumor will remain completely benign
options.C: It completely prevents the need for any future blood tests
options.D: It ensures the patient will never require surgical intervention

explanation: Catching these growths early gives our patients the best fighting chance. Prompt care stops things from getting worse and helps keep them comfortable and healthy.

question: What is the main trigger for cancer starting in the body?

options.A: Genetic mutations that cause uncontrolled cell division
options.B: Overgrowth of normal flora inside the renal pelvis
options.C: A sudden decrease in daily fluid intake and hydration
