explanation: Keeping the patient NPO reduces pancreatic stimulation by halting the secretion of digestive enzymes during acute inflammation. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h5)

question: A patient with chronic pancreatitis is prescribed pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy. When should the nurse instruct the patient to take these enzymes?

options.A: Once a day in the morning
options.B: Only at bedtime on an empty stomach
options.C: When abdominal pain peaks
options.D: With all meals and snacks

explanation: Pancreatic enzymes must be ingested with food to mix properly with nutrients and assist digestion; taking them without food is ineffective. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which lifestyle factor is recognized as the most significant environmental risk factor for pancreatic cancer?

options.A: Cigarette smoking
options.B: Low dietary fiber
options.C: Excessive sodium intake
options.D: Regular coffee consumption

explanation: Tobacco smoke contains potent carcinogens that significantly increase the lifetime risk of developing pancreatic cancer. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why do tumors located in the head of the pancreas typically present with jaundice early in the disease course?

options.A: They directly destroy red blood cells in the bloodstream
options.B: They impair liver cell synthesis of clotting factors
options.C: They obstruct the common bile duct, preventing bilirubin excretion
options.D: They cause immediate renal failure and uremia

explanation: The anatomical position of the pancreatic head surrounds the bile duct, meaning even small tumors can block bile flow and cause jaundice. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h6)

question: What is the name of the extensive surgical procedure performed for resectable cancer of the pancreatic head?

options.A: Billroth II resection
options.B: Cholecystectomy
options.C: Nissen fundoplication
options.D: Whipple procedure

explanation: The Whipple procedure involves the surgical removal of the pancreatic head, duodenum, and surrounding structures for localized pancreatic tumors. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of treatment when a patient is diagnosed with widespread, metastatic pancreatic cancer?

options.A: Permanent restoration of full exocrine enzyme production
options.B: Complete surgical cure via radical pancreatectomy
options.C: Palliative care to relieve symptoms and maximize quality of life
options.D: Immediate reversal of type 2 diabetes mellitus

explanation: Because metastatic pancreatic cancer is rarely curable, medical interventions focus on palliation, pain control, and comfort. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h7)

question: What is a major, life-threatening postoperative complication following a Whipple procedure involving anastomotic leakage?

options.A: Chronic constipation
options.B: Renal artery stenosis
options.C: Pancreatic fistula
options.D: Essential hypertension

explanation: A pancreatic fistula occurs when fluid leaks from the surgical connection sites, leading to potential infection and tissue breakdown. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h8)

question: Which nursing action is essential when caring for a patient with surgical drains after pancreatic surgery?

options.A: Monitoring and recording the volume, color, and character of drainage
options.B: Flushing the active drains routinely with sterile water every hour
options.C: Removing the surgical drains on the first postoperative morning
options.D: Clamping the drainage tubing permanently to encourage internal healing

explanation: Tracking drain output helps nurses detect early complications like hemorrhage or fistulas before clinical deterioration occurs. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is the primary physiological defect in Type 1 diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Temporary glucose intolerance during pregnancy
options.B: Target cell resistance to normal insulin levels
options.C: Excessive glucagon production by the liver
options.D: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells

explanation: Type 1 diabetes happens because the body's immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h1)

question: How does Type 2 diabetes differ fundamentally from Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Type 2 produces absolute insulin deficiency from birth
options.B: Type 2 is caused entirely by an acute viral pancreatic infection
options.C: Type 2 involves insulin resistance alongside relative insulin deficiency
options.D: Type 2 only affects elderly patients and requires immediate surgery

explanation: In Type 2 diabetes, the body still makes insulin, but the cells do not respond to it properly, and the pancreas cannot keep up with the extra demand. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which process causes the liver to release stored sugar into the blood when the body is low on insulin?

options.A: Glycolysis
options.B: Lipogenesis
options.C: Glycogenolysis
options.D: Erythropoiesis

explanation: Glycogenolysis is just a fancy medical word for breaking down stored sugar (glycogen) into glucose so the body can use it when energy is running low. You've got this!

question: Why do ketone bodies form when a patient lacks adequate insulin?

options.A: Excess dietary protein ferments rapidly in the gastrointestinal tract
options.B: The pancreas begins producing acids instead of digestive enzymes
options.C: The body breaks down fats for energy because glucose cannot enter cells
options.D: The liver stores extra water instead of filtering metabolic waste

explanation: When cells are starved of glucose due to missing or ineffective insulin, the body burns fat for fuel, producing acidic ketones as a byproduct. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h2)

question: Which of the following is a major modifiable risk factor for Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: Inherited HLA genetic markers
options.B: Advanced chronological age
options.C: Biological family history
options.D: Physical inactivity and obesity

explanation: Lifestyle factors like being overweight and inactive can be changed, unlike age, genetics, or family background. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h3)

question: A 40-year-old client with a desk job and a high body weight asks about their risk for diabetes. What is the best nursing explanation?

options.A: Physical inactivity and excess weight increase cellular resistance to insulin
options.B: High body weight prevents the kidneys from filtering normal blood sugar
options.C: Desk jobs cause the liver to stop producing necessary digestive enzymes
options.D: Sedentary habits directly destroy the beta cells inside the pancreas

explanation: Carrying extra body fat and lacking exercise make body tissues less responsive to the insulin your pancreas makes, leading to high blood sugar over time. Makes total sense when you break it down!

question: What is the medical term for excessive thirst experienced by a client with high blood sugar?

options.A: Proteinuria
options.B: Polyuria
options.C: Polyphagia
options.D: Polydipsia

explanation: Polydipsia is the medical word for extreme thirst, which happens because the body loses a lot of water through frequent urination. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why does a client with untreated diabetes experience frequent urination?

options.A: The kidneys enlarge to remove excess protein from the bloodstream
options.B: Excess glucose pulls water into the urine through osmotic diuresis
options.C: Infections destroy the sphincter muscles that control urine release
options.D: High blood sugar directly irritates the lining of the urinary bladder

explanation: When sugar spills into the urine, it acts like a sponge, drawing extra water along with it and causing high urine output. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h4)

question: What does the glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) test measure in a client?

options.A: The total amount of circulating insulin produced by the pancreas
options.B: Average blood glucose control over the past two to three months
options.C: Immediate blood sugar levels taken immediately after a heavy meal
options.D: Kidney filtration efficiency and the presence of protein in urine

explanation: HbA1c shows how well blood sugar has been controlled over the lifespan of a red blood cell, which is roughly 90 days. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h5)

question: Which fasting plasma glucose level is considered diagnostic for diabetes mellitus?

options.A: 100 to 125 mg/dL
options.B: 70 to 99 mg/dL
options.C: Below 60 mg/dL
options.D: 126 mg/dL or higher

explanation: A fasting blood sugar reading of 126 mg/dL or higher measured on two separate occasions is one of the standard diagnostic cutoffs for diabetes. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h5)

question: How does metformin mainly work to help manage Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: Triggering direct beta cell regeneration within the exocrine pancreas
options.B: Decreasing liver glucose production and improving insulin sensitivity
options.C: Stimulating immediate renal excretion of all circulating blood proteins
options.D: Blocking carbohydrate digestion enzymes inside the small intestine

explanation: Metformin is a classic drug you'll see everywhere in wards! It works mainly by stopping the liver from releasing too much extra sugar and helping your body's cells respond better to natural insulin.

question: Why is exogenous insulin therapy required for clients diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Their kidneys rapidly destroy all oral medications before they reach cells
options.B: Their stomach acid inactivates any dietary carbohydrates they consume
options.C: Their liver stores too much glycogen that oral pills cannot break down
options.D: Their pancreas has undergone autoimmune destruction and produces no insulin

explanation: Because Type 1 diabetes involves a total lack of internal insulin production, patients must receive insulin from an outside source to survive. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h6)

question: Which of the following is considered a microvascular complication of chronic diabetes?

options.A: Peripheral vascular claudication pain
options.B: Severe hypertension from aortic stenosis
options.C: Coronary artery disease and stroke
options.D: Diabetic retinopathy and nephropathy

explanation: Microvascular complications involve damage to small blood vessels, specifically harming the eyes (retinopathy) and the kidneys (nephropathy). [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is the main difference between Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS) and Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)?

options.A: The presence of severe hypoglycemia in HHS
options.B: The absence of significant ketoacidosis in HHS
options.C: The rapid onset of kidney failure in DKA
options.D: The lack of dehydration in DKA

explanation: HHS usually happens in Type 2 diabetes where there is still just enough insulin around to stop major fat breakdown, so ketones don't build up like they do in DKA. Great clinical distinction to master!

question: What is a common early symptom of hypoglycemia that a nurse should teach a client to recognize?

options.A: Extreme sweet-smelling breath
options.B: Severe peripheral edema
options.C: Shakiness and sweating
options.D: Kussmaul breathing patterns

explanation: When blood sugar drops too low, the nervous system reacts quickly, causing tremors, sweating, anxiety, and heart palpitations. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h8)

question: A client with diabetes calls the clinic feeling nauseous and vomiting with a mild fever. What is the best advice to give them?

options.A: Stop taking all diabetes medications immediately until your stomach settles down
options.B: Continue taking your insulin, drink plenty of fluids, and check your blood sugar often
options.C: Restrict all fluid intake for the next twelve hours to prevent vomiting episodes
options.D: Double your oral diabetes pills to clear out the excess toxins causing the fever

explanation: When patients are sick, stress hormones naturally push blood sugar up. Remind them: never stop insulin during illness, and keep pushing those fluids!

question: What does the back part of the pituitary gland (posterior pituitary) actually do?

options.A: It stores and releases hormones made by the hypothalamus.
options.B: It makes growth hormone and prolactin every single day.
options.C: It controls blood sugar levels using special insulin cells.
options.D: It filters harmful toxins out of the brain's blood supply.

explanation: Think of the posterior pituitary as a warehouse! It doesn't manufacture its own hormones; instead, it holds onto oxytocin and ADH made by the hypothalamus until it's time to release them.

question: Why do we call the pituitary gland the 'master gland' of the body?

options.A: It directly controls the activity of several other hormone glands.
options.B: It makes every single hormone needed to keep you alive without help.
options.C: It controls your conscious thought and memory along with the brain.
options.D: It is simply the largest endocrine organ located inside the skull.

explanation: You got this! It earns the title 'master gland' because its hormones act like boss signals telling other glands—like your thyroid and adrenals—when to release their own hormones.

question: What is the most common cause of trouble in the pituitary gland?

options.A: The body's immune system attacking the back part of the gland
options.B: Severe, long-term bacterial infections spreading through the brain
options.C: Cancerous tumors that have spread to the brain from the lungs
options.D: Benign (non-cancerous) tumors known as pituitary adenomas

explanation: Don't panic when you hear 'tumor'—most pituitary problems come from benign growths called adenomas. They can either pump out too many hormones or squish normal gland tissue.

question: Why do growing pituitary tumors often cause vision changes like trouble seeing out of the sides of your eyes?

options.A: Not having enough thyroid hormone causes the retina to wear out quickly.
options.B: Too much growth hormone makes the muscles around the eyeballs swell.
options.C: High pressure inside the skull damages the back part of the brain directly.
options.D: The growing mass presses upward directly against the optic chiasm.

explanation: Location is everything! The optic chiasm (where your eye nerves cross) sits right above the pituitary gland. When the gland swells up, it bumps right into those nerves.

question: What is the main physical sign you will see in an adult with acromegaly?

options.A: Enlargement of the hands, feet, and facial bones
options.B: Sudden and severe hair loss all over the scalp
options.C: Extreme weight loss with rapid muscle wasting
options.D: Sudden, very rapid growth in height during childhood

explanation: In adults, bone growth plates are already closed, so excess growth hormone can't make them taller. Instead, bones and soft tissues grow outward and thicken—giving broader hands, feet, and facial features.

question: A patient comes in with a 'buffalo hump' of fat, a round belly, and purple stretch marks on their skin. Which condition matches these signs?

options.A: Hypothyroidism
options.B: Cushing's disease
options.C: Acromegaly
options.D: Diabetes insipidus

explanation: These classic changes happen when the body is flooded with too much cortisol. In Cushing's disease, this is often kicked off by a tiny pituitary tumor pushing out extra ACTH.

question: What exactly is Sheehan's syndrome?

options.A: Immune system attack on the adrenal glands brought on by stress
options.B: Death of pituitary tissue due to severe blood loss right after childbirth
options.C: A benign tumor causing sudden vision loss in older men
options.D: A genetic inability to make antidiuretic hormone after bumping your head

explanation: During delivery, a massive hemorrhage can drop blood pressure so low that the hardworking pituitary gland is starved of blood and oxygen, leading to tissue death (necrosis).

question: Why is secondary adrenal insufficiency caused by pituitary problems so dangerous for a patient?

options.A: Blood sugar shoots up dangerously high because of a lack of balance.
options.B: The kidneys suddenly stop filtering waste products out of the blood.
options.C: Lacking ACTH makes the adrenal glands stop producing vital cortisol.
options.D: The heart rate goes completely out of control without nerve signals.

explanation: Without ACTH telling them what to do, the adrenal glands shrink and stop making cortisol. That leaves the body completely unable to handle stress, which can quickly lead to shock.

question: What is the biggest difference between Diabetes Insipidus (DI) and SIADH?

options.A: DI starts in the front pituitary, while SIADH only happens from kidney failure.
options.B: DI is caused by too much growth hormone, while SIADH is total thyroid failure.
options.C: DI causes fluid overload and high BP, while SIADH causes dehydration.
options.D: DI involves a shortage of ADH causing water loss, while SIADH involves too much ADH causing water retention.

explanation: Think of them as total opposites! DI stands for 'Dry Inside' (you pee out all your water), while SIADH 'Soaks It All In' (your body holds onto too much water and dilutes your blood).

question: A patient just had pituitary surgery and is now peeing out 500 mL of very clear, watery urine every single hour, and their blood sodium is climbing. What is happening?

options.A: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH)
options.B: Diabetes insipidus
options.C: Acute adrenal crisis
options.D: Cushing's syndrome

explanation: That massive output of dilute urine right after pituitary surgery is the classic hallmark of diabetes insipidus. The gland is stunned and temporarily (or permanently) stops making enough ADH.

question: What imaging test is considered the absolute gold standard for spotting a pituitary tumor?

options.A: An ultrasound scan of the blood vessels in the neck
options.B: A plain X-ray picture of the skull from the side
options.C: A standard CT scan of the head without any contrast dye
options.D: An MRI of the brain using contrast dye

explanation: MRI is the best choice because it gives super clear pictures of soft tissues. This lets doctors spot tiny adenomas and see if they are crowding nearby structures like the optic nerves.

question: Why must nurses regularly check the vision of a patient who has a pituitary tumor?

options.A: Swelling from fluid retention causes temporary double vision.
options.B: High prolactin levels directly burn out the retina and nerve endings.
options.C: Lacking growth hormone makes the eyes unable to focus on close things.
options.D: Growing tumors can press against the optic nerves and cause gradual blindness.

explanation: Because the pituitary lives right below the optic chiasm, any tumor that starts expanding upward will threaten the patient's eyesight first. Regular checks catch this early!

question: Through which pathway do surgeons typically reach the pituitary gland during a transsphenoidal hypophysectomy?

options.A: Through a large incision made just above the right ear
options.B: Through a small opening cut directly in the upper jawbone
options.C: Through the nasal cavity and the sphenoid sinus
options.D: Through the back of the neck right near the brainstem

explanation: The 'transsphenoidal' approach means going right through the nose and sphenoid sinus! This lets surgeons reach the pituitary safely without having to cut open the skull or go through brain tissue.

question: If a patient has their entire pituitary gland surgically removed, which of these medications do they NOT need to take for the rest of their life?

options.A: Thyroid hormone replacement
options.B: Sex hormone replacement
options.C: Cortisol replacement (glucocorticoids)
options.D: Insulin injections

explanation: Insulin is made by your pancreas, not your pituitary gland! Without a pituitary, the patient will need lifelong thyroid, adrenal, and sex hormone replacements, but their pancreas keeps making insulin just fine.

question: Why must you strictly tell a patient who just had transsphenoidal surgery NOT to blow their nose?

options.A: It triggers terrible allergic reactions to the nasal packing materials.
options.B: It pushes air into the ear tubes and causes permanent deafness.
options.C: It increases pressure inside the head and can ruin the surgical seal.
options.D: It causes too much mucus to form and blocks the sinus completely.

explanation: Blowing your nose spikes intracranial pressure. That sudden pressure can pop the tissue patch the surgeon placed over the surgical site, causing cerebrospinal fluid to leak out.

question: You notice clear fluid draining from the nose of a patient who just had pituitary surgery. What is a quick bedside test to see if it is cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)?

options.A: Smell the fluid to check for a sharp ammonia or vinegar odor.
options.B: Check the exact temperature of the fluid with a digital probe.
options.C: Shine an ultraviolet light directly onto the wet dressing.
options.D: Test the fluid for glucose using a standard urine dipstick.

explanation: CSF is rich in glucose, whereas normal nasal mucus is not! Touching a glucose test strip to the drainage is a fast, clever way at the bedside to check for a CSF leak.

question: What are the three core overlapping functions of the nervous system?

options.A: Filtration, concentration, and secretion
options.B: Digestion, absorption, and excretion
options.C: Sensory input, integration, and motor output
options.D: Circulation, oxygenation, and elimination

explanation: The nervous system constantly gathers sensory data, processes that information centrally, and directs an appropriate motor response to effector organs. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h1)

question: A patient touches a hot iron plate and immediately withdraws their hand. Which nervous system component directly initiates the muscle contraction to pull the hand away?

options.A: Motor output
options.B: Sensory input
options.C: Central integration
options.D: Endocrine regulation

explanation: Motor output represents the final command sent to effector organs like skeletal muscles to execute a physical action. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which brain structure is primarily responsible for coordinating smooth voluntary movements and maintaining balance?

options.A: Thalamus
options.B: Hypothalamus
options.C: Medulla oblongata
options.D: Cerebellum

explanation: The cerebellum monitors and fine-tunes motor activity, ensuring precise posture, balance, and coordination. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h2)

question: An injury to the brainstem is life-threatening primarily because this region regulates which vital process?

options.A: Visual and auditory interpretation
options.B: Basic cardiorespiratory functions
options.C: Abstract thought and memory
options.D: Voluntary hand and foot movements

explanation: The brainstem, particularly the medulla oblongata, houses critical autonomic centers that drive heart rate, blood pressure, and breathing. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the primary directional role of ascending tracts in the white matter of the spinal cord?

options.A: Synthesizing neurotransmitters for reflex arcs
options.B: Producing cerebrospinal fluid within the central canal
options.C: Carrying sensory signals toward the brain
options.D: Carrying motor instructions away from the brain

explanation: Ascending tracts are sensory pathways that relay environmental and internal bodily information up toward the cerebral cortex and other brain regions. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h3)

question: What structural characteristic distinguishes white matter from gray matter within the central nervous system?

options.A: Gray matter consists entirely of supportive neuroglial cells.
options.B: White matter houses all the primary sensory receptor endings.
options.C: Gray matter is found exclusively on the outer surface of the spinal cord.
options.D: White matter contains high concentrations of myelinated axons.

explanation: Myelin has a whitish appearance, which gives nerve fiber tracts their distinct color compared to the unmyelinated cell bodies of gray matter. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which branch of the peripheral nervous system controls voluntary movements of skeletal muscles?

options.A: Sympathetic nervous system
options.B: Autonomic nervous system
options.C: Parasympathetic nervous system
options.D: Somatic nervous system

explanation: The somatic division handles conscious, voluntary motor pathways connecting the central nervous system to skeletal muscle tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h4)

question: Which physiological response is most characteristic of parasympathetic nervous system activation?

options.A: Dilation of airways and accelerated heart rate
options.B: Decreased heart rate and enhanced digestive activity
options.C: Constriction of digestive sphincters and pupil dilation
options.D: Release of massive amounts of adrenaline into the blood

explanation: The parasympathetic system promotes housekeeping tasks like digestion and reduced cardiac output under calm conditions. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary function of dendrites on a neuron?

options.A: Receiving signals from other neurons and transmitting them toward the cell body
options.B: Generating and propagating action potentials away from the soma
options.C: Releasing chemical neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft
options.D: Producing myelin insulation to speed up electrical conduction

explanation: Dendrites act as the main receptive regions of the neuron, picking up electrochemical messages from neighboring cells. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h5)

question: Which glial cell type is responsible for forming myelin sheaths around axons in the peripheral nervous system?

options.A: Microglial cells
options.B: Schwann cells
options.C: Astrocytes
options.D: Oligodendrocytes

explanation: Schwann cells wrap around peripheral nerve fibers to create the myelin sheath, whereas oligodendrocytes perform this function in the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h5)

question: What ionic movement primarily causes depolarization during the rising phase of an action potential?

options.A: Calcium ions entering the synaptic vesicles
options.B: Chloride ions moving into the cytoplasm
options.C: Potassium ions rushing out of the cell
options.D: Sodium ions rushing into the cell

explanation: Opening voltage-gated sodium channels allows a rapid influx of positively charged sodium ions, making the inside of the membrane positive. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of neurotransmitters at a chemical synapse?

options.A: Providing metabolic energy directly to resting axons
options.B: Bridging the physical gap between neurons to transmit chemical signals
options.C: Maintaining the baseline resting membrane potential
options.D: Creating physical scars in damaged nervous tissue

explanation: Because neurons do not physically touch at synapses, chemical neurotransmitters carry the signal across the synaptic cleft to the next cell. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the correct order of the meningeal layers from the outermost layer to the innermost layer closest to the brain?

options.A: Dura mater, pia mater, arachnoid mater
options.B: Pia mater, arachnoid mater, dura mater
options.C: Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater
options.D: Arachnoid mater, dura mater, pia mater

explanation: The tough outer dura mater sits against the skull, the web-like arachnoid mater is in the middle, and the delicate pia mater clings tightly to the brain surface. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is a major physiological function of cerebrospinal fluid?

options.A: Delivering oxygen directly to hemoglobin in deep brain tissue
options.B: Synthesizing new neurons to replace damaged brain tissue
options.C: Providing mechanical cushion and buoyancy for the brain
options.D: Regulating core body temperature via the spinal cord

explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid suspends the brain in a fluid cushion, drastically reducing its effective weight and shielding it from physical trauma. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h7)

question: Which clinical assessment tool is widely used to monitor changes in a patient's level of consciousness?

options.A: Pain numeric rating scale
options.B: Apgar scoring system
options.C: Braden scale for pressure ulcers
options.D: Glasgow Coma Scale

explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale evaluates eye opening, verbal response, and motor performance to quantify neurological responsiveness. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h8)

question: Why is it clinically critical to monitor pupillary reflexes during a neurological assessment?

options.A: Unequal pupils always confirm damage specifically to the peripheral somatic motor nerves.
options.B: Changes in pupil size and reactivity can indicate rising intracranial pressure or brainstem compression.
options.C: Pupillary responses measure the exact concentration of neurotransmitters in the bloodstream.
options.D: Pupils directly synthesize the cerebrospinal fluid needed to protect the cerebrum.

explanation: Cranial nerve III runs near structures vulnerable to brain herniation, making pupillary changes an early warning sign of elevated intracranial pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of an electrophysiologic study?

options.A: To evaluate the electrical system and map cardiac arrhythmias
options.B: To assess structural valve stenosis and regurgitation severity
options.C: To remove atherosclerotic plaque from the coronary arteries
options.D: To measure the ejection fraction and stroke volume of the ventricles

explanation: An EPS is specifically designed to assess the heart's conduction system and pinpoint the electrical pathways responsible for abnormal heart rhythms. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h1)

question: Which vascular access route is most commonly utilized during catheter insertion for an EPS?

options.A: Carotid artery
options.B: Femoral vein
options.C: Jugular vein
options.D: Brachial artery

explanation: Specialized electrode catheters are typically introduced through the peripheral vasculature, with the femoral vein serving as the most frequent insertion site to reach the right side of the heart. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h1)

question: Which clinical presentation is a classic indication for scheduling an electrophysiologic study?

options.A: Recurrent unexplained syncope
options.B: Severe iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
options.D: Acute uncomplicated appendicitis

explanation: Unexplained fainting episodes often stem from transient, lethal arrhythmias that require invasive electrophysiologic testing for definitive diagnosis. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h2)

question: A patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is scheduled for an EPS primarily to achieve what objective?

options.A: Evaluate left ventricular muscle mass
options.B: Measure total systemic vascular resistance
options.C: Localize abnormal accessory conduction pathways
options.D: Assess the severity of coronary artery narrowing

explanation: Pre-excitation syndromes involve extra electrical connections between the atria and ventricles, which an EPS maps precisely to guide subsequent ablation. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h2)

question: Which laboratory value is most critical to check prior to an electrophysiologic study due to its direct effect on cardiac rhythm?

options.A: Blood urea nitrogen
options.B: Direct bilirubin count
options.C: Serum amylase level
options.D: Serum potassium

explanation: Potassium imbalances drastically alter the resting membrane potential of cardiac cells, increasing the risk of dangerous, unintended arrhythmias during testing. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h3)

question: A patient scheduled for an elective EPS tomorrow morning is currently taking a prescribed antiarrhythmic medication. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Ignore the medication order since it has no impact on EPS results.
options.B: Discontinue the drug permanently without consulting the medical team.
options.C: Verify with the cardiologist whether the drug should be withheld.
options.D: Administer an extra dose immediately to protect the heart overnight.

explanation: Antiarrhythmic drugs can suppress the very rhythm abnormalities the study aims to induce, so doctors frequently order them held, requiring explicit verification by the nurse. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h3)

question: What is an essential piece of emergency equipment that must be immediately available in the room during an electrophysiologic study?

options.A: Mechanical ventilator
options.B: Dialysis machine
options.C: Defibrillator
options.D: Gastric suction pump

explanation: Because the procedure intentionally provokes abnormal and potentially lethal heart rhythms, a functional defibrillator must be immediately accessible at all times. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h4)

question: Why is moderate sedation during an EPS typically maintained at a level where the patient remains responsive?

options.A: To eliminate the need for continuous blood pressure monitoring
options.B: To ensure the patient can operate the fluoroscopy machine independently
options.C: To prevent the patient from moving their arms during sterile catheter insertion
options.D: To allow the patient to report symptoms like chest discomfort or neurological changes

explanation: Keeping the patient responsive ensures they can verbally communicate adverse sensations, such as chest pain or dizziness, which signal hemodynamic compromise. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h4)

question: What is the primary rationale for enforcing strict limb immobilization and bedrest following femoral sheath removal?

options.A: To improve overall lung expansion and prevent postoperative pneumonia
options.B: To prevent bleeding and hematoma formation at the vascular access site
options.C: To accelerate the excretion of intravenous contrast dye through the kidneys
options.D: To lower the patient's systemic blood pressure and heart rate

explanation: Minimizing movement of the affected leg prevents disruption of the newly forming blood clot at the femoral puncture site, reducing hemorrhage risk. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h5)

question: Which clinical finding in a patient who underwent a femoral EPS two hours ago requires immediate nursing intervention?

options.A: A normal heart rate of 72 beats per minute on telemetry
options.B: Expressed mild boredom regarding the period of restricted bedrest
options.C: A rapidly expanding, firm swelling at the groin puncture site
options.D: Mild bruising and skin tenderness directly around the bandage

explanation: An expanding groin swelling indicates active bleeding or hematoma formation, which can compromise circulation or lead to severe blood loss. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h5)

question: Which interval measured during an electrophysiologic study specifically evaluates conduction through the His-Purkinje system?

options.A: HV interval
options.B: QT interval
options.C: PR interval
options.D: AH interval

explanation: The HV interval measures the time it takes for an electrical impulse to travel from the His bundle to the ventricular myocardium. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h6)

question: A patient is being discharged the morning after an uncomplicated EPS and catheter ablation. Which instruction is most appropriate for the nurse to provide?

options.A: Scrub the groin insertion site vigorously with soap twice daily
options.B: Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous physical activity for several days
options.C: Stop taking all prescribed cardiac medications starting today
options.D: Immobilize the affected leg completely for the next week

explanation: Patients should refrain from heavy lifting and strenuous exercise to protect the healing vascular access site from undue pressure and secondary bleeding. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h6)

question: What is the primary anatomical space entered during a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Bone marrow cavity
options.B: Subarachnoid space
options.C: Epidural space
options.D: Subdural space

explanation: The lumbar puncture needle passes through the layers of the back to enter the subarachnoid space where cerebrospinal fluid circulates. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h1)

question: Why might a clinician perform a therapeutic lumbar puncture?

options.A: To permanently seal a dural tear
options.B: To remove excess cerebrospinal fluid and lower pressure
options.C: To inject air into the ventricles for imaging
options.D: To extract bone marrow for cell counts

explanation: Therapeutically, the procedure can reduce elevated intracranial pressure by draining excess cerebrospinal fluid or deliver medications directly into the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h1)

question: At approximately which vertebral level does the adult spinal cord typically terminate?

options.B: L4-L5
options.C: S1-S2
options.D: L1-L2

explanation: The adult spinal cord ends around the L1-L2 level, which is why lumbar punctures are performed lower down to prevent cord injury. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h2)

question: What surface anatomical landmark helps identify the L4 spinous process?

options.A: The highest point of the iliac crest
options.B: The twelfth rib tip
options.C: The posterior superior iliac spine
options.D: The inferior angle of the scapula

explanation: Connecting the highest points of the iliac crests forms a transverse line that crosses the spine directly at the L4 spinous process or the L4-L5 interspace. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h2)

question: Which condition is a major contraindication for performing a lumbar puncture due to the risk of brain herniation?

options.A: Mild tension headache
options.B: History of controlled epilepsy
options.C: Peripheral neuropathy
options.D: Elevated intracranial pressure from a mass lesion

explanation: Removing cerebrospinal fluid when intracranial pressure is elevated due to a mass can create a pressure gradient, causing brain tissue to herniate through the foramen magnum. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h3)

question: Which of the following conditions represents a clear reason NOT to perform a lumbar puncture at the intended site?

options.A: A mild low-grade fever of unknown origin
options.B: Controlled essential hypertension
options.C: A localized skin infection over the lower lumbar spine
options.D: A history of migraine headaches

explanation: Inserting a needle through infected skin tracks bacteria directly into the spinal canal, potentially causing severe bacterial meningitis or epidural abscess. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h3)

question: What is an essential nursing responsibility immediately before a lumbar puncture begins?

options.A: Having the patient empty their bladder
options.B: Administering general anesthesia
options.C: Placing an indwelling urinary catheter
options.D: Starting total parenteral nutrition

explanation: An empty bladder increases patient comfort and prevents involuntary voiding when positioning or muscle tension occurs during the tap. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h4)

question: Why must the nurse check coagulation profiles before a spinal tap takes place?

options.A: To prevent the development of a spinal epidural hematoma
options.B: To calculate the correct volume of anesthetic needed
options.C: To check for hidden systemic bacterial infections
options.D: To determine the precise opening pressure of the CSF

explanation: Impaired blood clotting combined with needle trauma in the spinal canal can result in a hematoma that compresses the spinal cord and causes paralysis. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h4)

question: Which position is most commonly used for a lumbar puncture to widen the intervertebral spaces?

options.A: Trendelenburg position
options.B: Prone with a pillow under the abdomen
options.C: Lateral recumbent fetal position
options.D: Supine with legs elevated on pillows

explanation: Curling the body into a fetal position or leaning forward arches the back, maximizing the gaps between adjacent vertebrae for easier needle placement. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h5)

question: What is a key nursing duty while assisting with a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Reading the manometer pressure measurements aloud
options.B: Helping the patient maintain a steady, curved posture
options.C: Advancing the spinal needle into the subarachnoid space
options.D: Suturing the puncture site after needle removal

explanation: Patient movement can dislodge the needle or cause tissue trauma, making gentle, reassuring physical support by the nurse critical for safety. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h5)

question: Why is oral fluid intake often encouraged after a lumbar puncture?

options.A: To prevent sudden drops in systemic blood pressure
options.B: To stimulate normal bowel motility after bedrest
options.C: To flush out residual local anesthetic agents
options.D: To rapidly replace lost cerebrospinal fluid and prevent dehydration

explanation: Drinking plenty of fluids helps the body quickly regenerate the small amount of cerebrospinal fluid lost during the procedure. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h6)

question: What is the standard post-procedure positioning instruction for many patients after a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Prone position with extended legs
options.B: High-Fowler's position at ninety degrees
options.C: Trendelenburg position with tilted pelvis
options.D: Flat or low-Fowler's position

explanation: Keeping the patient flat reduces hydrostatic pressure at the dural puncture site, minimizing CSF leakage that causes post-lumbar puncture headaches. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h6)

question: A cerebrospinal fluid sample returns with a markedly reduced glucose level and elevated protein. Which condition is most strongly suspected?

options.A: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
options.B: Benign intracranial hypertension
options.C: Bacterial meningitis
options.D: Viral encephalitis

explanation: Bacterial pathogens consume glucose rapidly while releasing proteins and inflammatory cells into the CSF, producing low glucose and high protein levels. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h7)

question: What term describes the yellowish discoloration of cerebrospinal fluid caused by the breakdown of red blood cells?

options.A: Bilirubinemia
options.B: Hematuria
options.C: Xanthochromia
options.D: Proteinosis

explanation: Xanthochromia refers to the pink, orange, or yellow tint seen in CSF supernatant when red blood cells have been present in the subarachnoid space for several hours. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h7)

question: What is the most common adverse effect experienced by patients following a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Post-dural puncture headache
options.B: Permanent paraplegia
options.C: Spontaneous cerebral hemorrhage
options.D: Severe bacterial endocarditis

explanation: Leakage of cerebrospinal fluid through the dural puncture site can lower intracranial pressure, triggering a characteristic positional headache. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h8)

question: Which characteristic best describes a post-dural puncture headache?

options.A: It is constant regardless of body position and resists analgesics
options.B: It occurs exclusively at night and resolves upon waking
options.C: It presents as sharp unilateral facial pain triggered by chewing
options.D: It worsens when the patient sits upright and improves when lying flat

explanation: The upright posture increases traction on pain-sensitive cranial structures due to low CSF volume, whereas lying down relieves this traction and eases the pain. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h8)

question: What percentage of the resting cardiac output does the brain typically receive?

options.A: 15 to 20 percent
options.B: 5 to 10 percent
options.C: 45 to 50 percent
options.D: 30 to 35 percent

explanation: The brain has high metabolic demands and utilizes approximately 15 to 20 percent of the body's resting cardiac output despite its small relative weight. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h1)

question: What is the primary anatomical function of the Circle of Willis?

options.A: Producing neurotransmitters essential for motor coordination
options.B: Providing collateral circulation to protect against ischemia
options.C: Regulating systemic blood pressure via baroreceptor feedback
options.D: Filtering metabolic waste products from cerebrospinal fluid

explanation: The Circle of Willis creates an anastomotic connection between major cerebral arteries, allowing collateral blood flow if one pathway is blocked. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h1)

question: What defines the ischemic penumbra in a cerebrovascular event?

options.A: An area of localized bleeding directly into the subarachnoid space
options.B: A zone of irreversibly necrotic tissue at the center of the infarct
options.C: A metabolically sluggish zone of viable tissue that is potentially salvageable
options.D: The fluid-filled ventricular space where cerebrospinal fluid accumulates

explanation: The ischemic penumbra surrounds the necrotic core and contains tissue with reduced perfusion that can recover if blood flow is restored quickly. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h2)

question: How do hemorrhagic strokes primarily cause secondary damage to neural structures?

options.A: By increasing intracranial pressure and causing mechanical compression
options.B: By depleting systemic glucose stores rapidly
options.C: By stimulating excessive collateral vessel sprouting
options.D: By clearing atherosclerotic plaques too quickly

explanation: Extravasated blood pools within or around the brain, elevating intracranial pressure and physically compressing adjacent cerebral tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h2)

question: What is recognized as the single most prevalent and powerful risk factor for stroke in Nigeria?

options.A: Sickle cell anemia
options.B: Type 1 diabetes
options.C: Rheumatic fever
options.D: Hypertension

explanation: Chronic, poorly controlled high blood pressure places sustained stress on cerebral vessel walls, making hypertension the leading modifiable risk factor. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h3)

question: Why do strokes in Nigeria often present a unique clinical challenge regarding age demographics?

options.A: They bypass middle-aged populations entirely due to genetic immunity.
options.B: They present only in neonates with congenital heart defects.
options.C: They exclusively affect elderly citizens over the age of ninety.
options.D: They frequently manifest in younger, economically active adults.

explanation: Epidemiological data in Nigeria highlights a notable burden of stroke affecting younger working-age individuals due to poorly managed cardiovascular risk factors. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h3)

question: Which set of symptoms is most characteristic of a posterior circulation stroke?

options.A: Expressive aphasia and right-sided hemiplegia
options.B: Vertigo, ataxia, and cranial nerve palsies
options.C: Pure sensory loss in the left upper extremity
options.D: Contralateral leg numbness and urinary incontinence

explanation: The vertebrobasilar system supplies the brainstem and cerebellum, leading to balance issues, dizziness, and cranial nerve involvement when disrupted. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h4)

question: What is the primary clinical utility of the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS)?

options.A: To measure systemic blood pressure fluctuations over time
options.B: To screen for infectious etiologies of meningitis
options.C: To determine the exact histological type of atherosclerotic plaque
options.D: To quantify stroke severity and track neurological changes

explanation: The NIHSS provides a standardized scoring system that allows clinicians to objectively measure the severity of a patient's neurological deficits. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h4)

question: What is the primary diagnostic reason for performing an immediate non-contrast CT scan on a suspected stroke patient?

options.A: To differentiate ischemic stroke from cerebral hemorrhage
options.B: To visualize microscopic atherosclerotic plaque formations
options.C: To calculate the patient's exact cardiac output
options.D: To measure exact intracranial pressure levels

explanation: A non-contrast CT scan quickly rules out intracranial bleeding, which is critical because giving clot-busting drugs during a hemorrhage is fatal. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h5)

question: Why is random blood glucose assessed during the initial diagnostic evaluation of a patient presenting with stroke-like symptoms?

options.A: To prepare the patient for immediate insulin therapy
options.B: To rule out hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
options.C: To calculate the metabolic rate of the ischemic core
options.D: To diagnose underlying type 1 diabetes mellitus

explanation: Low blood sugar can cause focal neurological deficits that perfectly mimic an acute stroke, making rapid glucose testing an essential triage step. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h5)

question: What is the standard time window for initiating intravenous thrombolytic therapy in eligible ischemic stroke patients?

options.A: Within 48 hours of initial imaging
options.B: Within 4.5 hours of symptom onset
options.C: Within 7 days of stabilization
options.D: Within 12 to 24 hours of admission

explanation: Intravenous alteplase carries a strict time window of 4.5 hours from the moment symptoms start to maximize benefit and minimize bleeding risks. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h6)

question: A patient arrives at the emergency department 2 hours after experiencing sudden right-sided weakness and aphasia. A non-contrast CT scan shows no hemorrhage. Which management strategy is most appropriate?

options.A: Discharge home with outpatient physical therapy
options.B: Immediate administration of oral anticoagulants
options.C: Immediate administration of intravenous thrombolysis
options.D: Strict blood pressure reduction to normal baseline levels

explanation: With an ischemic presentation inside the 4.5-hour window and no hemorrhage on CT, the patient is an ideal candidate for intravenous thrombolytic therapy. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h6)

question: What is a mandatory nursing assessment that must be performed before offering food or fluids to an acute stroke patient?

options.A: A complete lipid profile blood draw
options.B: A 12-lead electrocardiogram
options.C: A formal swallowing screening
options.D: A comprehensive cognitive memory test

explanation: Dysphagia is common after a stroke, making a swallowing screen essential before oral intake to prevent aspiration pneumonia. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h7)

question: Why is frequent repositioning every two hours emphasized in the nursing care plan for immobile stroke survivors?

options.A: To clear secretions from the upper respiratory tract
options.B: To stimulate rapid recovery of paralyzed motor pathways
options.C: To increase systemic blood pressure to normal levels
options.D: To prevent the development of pressure injuries and contractures

explanation: Regular turning relieves prolonged pressure on bony prominences, protecting skin integrity and preventing joint contractures in weakened limbs. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h7)

question: Which medication class is primarily indicated for secondary prevention in a patient with an ischemic stroke caused by atrial fibrillation?

options.A: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.B: Direct vasoconstrictors
options.C: Inhaled bronchodilators
options.D: Oral anticoagulants

explanation: Atrial fibrillation promotes clot formation in the heart chambers, requiring oral anticoagulation to prevent cardioembolic stroke recurrences. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h8)

question: What is the primary objective of secondary prevention programs following a cerebrovascular event?

options.A: To completely reverse existing permanent brain tissue necrosis
options.B: To prevent the occurrence of recurrent strokes and vascular events
options.C: To eliminate the need for long-term blood pressure monitoring
options.D: To accelerate the natural aging process of cerebral blood vessels

explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on controlling risk factors and utilizing medical therapy to stop subsequent strokes from happening. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h8)

question: What is the leading cause of traumatic nervous system injuries in emergency departments across Nigeria?

options.A: Congenital degenerative disorders
options.B: Water-sport related drowning
options.C: Occupational factory accidents
options.D: Road traffic collisions

question: Why do injuries to the central nervous system typically result in permanent functional deficits?

options.A: Peripheral nerves migrate to replace lost brain cells
options.B: The blood-brain barrier prevents any surgical access
options.C: Cerebrospinal fluid rapidly dissolves damaged neurons
options.D: Neural tissue lacks significant regenerative capacity

explanation: Unlike other bodily tissues, mature central nervous system neurons do not readily divide or regrow after structural damage occurs. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h1)

question: Which mechanism defines a primary nervous system injury?

options.A: Secondary tissue necrosis resulting from intracranial swelling
options.B: Mechanical damage occurring at the exact moment of impact

options.D: Delayed cellular destruction driven by localized inflammation

explanation: Primary injury is the direct physical consequence of the traumatic force, such as a skull fracture or axonal shearing during the event. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h2)

question: What is the primary danger associated with secondary injury processes like cerebral edema?

options.A: Immediate regeneration of incorrect neural pathways
options.B: Elevated intracranial pressure reducing cerebral perfusion
options.C: Complete absorption of all cerebrospinal fluid cavities
options.D: Sudden conversion of gray matter into peripheral nerves

question: What term describes a spinal cord injury where some motor or sensory function remains intact below the level of the lesion?

options.A: Incomplete spinal injury
options.B: Secondary axonal disruption
options.C: Primary contusion syndrome
options.D: Complete transection injury

explanation: An incomplete injury preserves partial neural pathways across the lesion site, allowing for varying degrees of sensory or motor preservation. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h3)

question: Which clinical manifestations comprise Cushing's triad?

options.A: Tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, hyperventilation

options.C: Bradycardia, widening pulse pressure, irregular respirations
options.D: Fever, hypertension, rapid shallow breathing patterns

question: What are the three assessment categories evaluated using the Glasgow Coma Scale?

options.A: Blood pressure response, heart rate, oxygen saturation
options.B: Pupil reactivity, reflex arc speed, limb tone
options.C: Sensory perception, cranial nerve check, gait analysis
options.D: Eye opening, verbal response, motor performance

question: Why is a computed tomography scan typically preferred over a magnetic resonance imaging scan in the initial emergency evaluation of severe head trauma?

options.A: It provides superior resolution of fine spinal cord white matter tracts
options.B: It eliminates the need for any intravenous access lines
options.C: It is faster and more accessible for detecting acute hemorrhage
options.D: It uses non-ionizing radiation that poses zero physiological risk

explanation: CT scans are fast, widely available in emergency settings, and excel at showing fresh blood and bone fractures. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h4)

question: What is the primary physiological priority during the resuscitation of a client with severe head trauma?

options.A: Initiating active physical therapy within the first hour
options.B: Performing prompt lumbar punctures to drain blood
options.C: Administering high-dose oral sedatives immediately
options.D: Preventing hypoxia and systemic hypotension

explanation: Low blood oxygen and low blood pressure deprive the damaged brain of perfusion, rapidly accelerating secondary ischemic injury. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h5)

question: What is the main therapeutic goal of performing a surgical craniectomy in a client with severe brain trauma?

options.A: To completely eliminate the need for postoperative mechanical ventilation
options.B: To allow direct visual inspection of spinal nerve root pathways
options.C: To provide room for swollen brain tissue and reduce intracranial pressure
options.D: To permanently replace damaged grey matter with synthetic polymers

explanation: Removing a section of the skull relieves the dangerous pressure buildup caused by cerebral edema. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h5)

question: Why is the head of the bed typically elevated to thirty degrees in a client with a traumatic brain injury?

options.A: To prevent the spontaneous aspiration of gastric contents into the lungs
options.B: To allow easier access for oral hygiene and cranial nerve testing
options.C: To reduce the baseline metabolic rate of peripheral skeletal muscles
options.D: To promote venous drainage from the head and lower intracranial pressure

explanation: Head elevation facilitates gravity-assisted venous return from the cerebral vault, reducing intracranial pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h6)

question: Which nursing intervention is critical when managing a client with elevated intracranial pressure?

options.A: Placing the client in a flat, trendelenburg position
options.B: Aggressively preventing hyperthermia and fever
options.C: Encouraging active coughing exercises every two hours
options.D: Massaging dependent bony prominences every hour

explanation: Fever dramatically increases cerebral metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, which exacerbates secondary injury in compromised neural tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h6)

question: What triggers an episode of autonomic dysreflexia in a client with a high spinal cord injury?

options.A: Accidental discontinuation of prophylactic antibiotic therapy
options.B: Sudden drops in environmental temperature causing vasoconstriction
options.C: Noxious stimuli such as a distended bladder or bowel impaction
options.D: Excessive physical exercise of the upper extremities

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical complication of severe traumatic brain injury? (Select ONE)

options.A: Post-traumatic epilepsy
options.B: Obstructive hydrocephalus
options.C: Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus
options.D: Chronic muscle spasticity

explanation: Diabetes mellitus is an endocrine and metabolic disorder, whereas epilepsy, hydrocephalus, and spasticity are direct neurological complications of brain trauma. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h7)

question: What do we call a tumor that has traveled to the brain from another part of the body, like the lungs?

options.B: Primary tumor
options.C: Metastatic tumor
options.D: Congenital tumor

explanation: You've got this! When cancer cells break away from a spot like the breast or lungs and travel to the brain, we call it a metastatic (or secondary) tumor. Think of it as a traveler from another part of the body.

question: Even if a brain tumor is benign (non-cancerous), why can it still turn into a medical emergency?

options.A: The immune system attacks the tumor and causes severe swelling.
options.B: The rigid skull prevents expansion and causes dangerous pressure.
options.C: Benign tumors always turn into fast-growing cancers over time.
options.D: Benign brain tumors immediately destroy all local nerve cells.

explanation: Great thinking! The human skull is like a hard box that cannot stretch. Even a benign growth takes up precious space inside, crowding the brain and causing dangerous pressure. Location matters just as much as cell type!

question: Most primary brain tumors start growing from which type of supportive cells in the nervous system?

options.A: Neurons
options.B: Glial cells
options.C: Bone cells
options.D: Blood vessels

explanation: Spot on! While neurons get all the fame for sending nerve signals, most primary brain tumors actually arise from glial cells—the supportive glue and caretaker cells of the brain.

question: A patient is diagnosed with a slow-growing, usually benign tumor that develops from the protective membranes covering the brain. What is it called?

options.A: Pituitary adenoma
options.B: Glioblastoma
options.C: Astrocytoma
options.D: Meningioma

explanation: You got it! Meningiomas grow from the meninges—the protective layers surrounding your brain and spinal cord. They are usually slow-growing and benign, which is great news for the patient.

question: During an eye exam, what classic sign tells a doctor there is increased pressure inside the skull?

options.A: Papilledema
options.B: Cataracts
options.C: Retinal detachment
options.D: Conjunctivitis

explanation: Brilliant! Papilledema is simply the swelling of the optic nerve head. Because the optic nerve connects directly to the brain, high intracranial pressure pushes on it and shows up clearly during an eye check.

question: Which set of vital signs makes up the famous 'Cushing triad', warning us of severe brainstem compression?

options.A: Normal blood pressure, irregular pulse, and clear breath sounds
options.B: High fever, fast heart rate, and deep rapid respirations
options.C: Widening pulse pressure, slow heart rate, and irregular breathing
options.D: Low blood pressure, rapid pulse, and shallow breathing

explanation: You're doing great! The Cushing triad is a critical late warning sign. Watch out for a wide gap between top and bottom blood pressure numbers, a slow heart rate (bradycardia), and irregular breathing. It means the brainstem is in trouble!

question: Which imaging test is the absolute go-to choice for getting a clear picture of brain and spinal tumors?

options.A: Magnetic Resonance Imaging
options.B: Bone densitometry scan
options.C: Standard chest X-ray
options.D: Abdominal ultrasound

explanation: Spot on! MRI gives doctors the sharpest, most detailed look at soft tissues like the brain and spinal cord, making it the favorite tool for spotting nervous system growths.

question: A patient asks how doctors will know for sure if a brain tumor is cancerous. What procedure gives the definitive diagnosis?

options.A: Routine eye examination
options.B: Tissue biopsy
options.C: Neurological reflex test
options.D: Blood cell count

explanation: You nailed it! A biopsy is the gold standard. By looking at actual tumor cells under a microscope, pathologists can tell for sure if it's cancerous and figure out its grade.

question: Why do doctors frequently prescribe corticosteroid medications to patients with brain tumors?

options.A: To reduce brain swelling and intracranial pressure
options.B: To cure the underlying cancer cells completely
options.C: To lower the patient's blood pressure levels
options.D: To prevent the patient from developing an infection

explanation: Well done! Steroids like dexamethasone are lifesavers here. They don't kill the cancer, but they quickly shrink the puffy swelling (edema) around the tumor, bringing relief fast.

question: What is the biggest hurdle when trying to treat brain tumors using regular systemic chemotherapy drugs?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs only work on bones and muscles.
options.B: Chemotherapy causes permanent blindness in every patient.
options.C: Brain tissue absorbs too much medication and dissolves instantly.
options.D: The blood-brain barrier blocks many drugs from entering the brain tissue.

explanation: You got it! The blood-brain barrier is like a strict security guard—it protects the brain from toxins, but unfortunately, it also blocks many helpful chemotherapy drugs from getting inside.

question: How should you position a patient right after a craniotomy surgery to help keep intracranial pressure down?

options.A: Sitting upright at a 90-degree angle
options.B: Flat on the back with feet raised high
options.C: Head elevated 30 to 45 degrees
options.D: Lying flat on the operative side

explanation: Excellent clinical thinking! Elevating the head of the bed helps blood flow smoothly out of the head (venous return), preventing fluid backup and keeping pressure low.

question: You notice clear fluid leaking from a head dressing after a patient's craniotomy. What is this fluid likely to be?

options.A: Venous blood plasma only
options.B: Cerebrospinal fluid
options.C: Topical wound ointment
options.D: Gastric acid secretions

question: Which member of the healthcare team is best at helping a patient relearn everyday tasks like bathing, dressing, and cooking?

options.A: Occupational therapist
options.B: Speech pathologist
options.C: Respiratory therapist
options.D: Physical therapist

explanation: You're doing fantastic! Occupational therapists focus on daily 'occupations'—helping patients gain independence with self-care tasks so they can get back to living their lives.

question: What is a major safety worry for a patient dealing with dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) after brain surgery?

options.A: Loss of arm movement
options.B: Permanent hearing loss
options.C: Aspiration pneumonia
options.D: Sudden high blood pressure

explanation: You nailed it! When swallowing is weak, food or saliva can slip down the windpipe into the lungs. This puts the patient at high risk for a dangerous lung infection called aspiration pneumonia.

question: What is the primary characteristic of degenerative neurological disorders?

options.A: Progressive and irreversible loss of neuronal function
options.B: Complete recovery after prolonged physical therapy
options.C: Sudden onset following vascular occlusion
options.D: Transient inflammation of peripheral nerve roots

explanation: These conditions are marked by a gradual, ongoing decline in neuronal structure and function rather than a sudden event or temporary inflammation. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h1)

question: How do degenerative neurological disorders differ fundamentally from acute strokes?

options.A: Strokes involve an acute, sudden neurological insult
options.B: Degenerative disorders result from sudden vascular blockage
options.C: Strokes develop insidiously over many years
options.D: Degenerative disorders exclusively affect peripheral nerves

explanation: Acute strokes happen abruptly due to interrupted blood supply, whereas degenerative conditions feature a slow, progressive decline in neuronal integrity. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h1)

question: What is a primary cellular trigger in many neurodegenerative diseases?

options.A: Rapid regeneration of myelin sheaths
options.B: Excessive production of acetylcholine in synapses
options.C: Misfolding and aggregation of specific proteins
options.D: Hyperperfusion of the cerebral cortex

question: How does excitotoxicity contribute to neuronal cell death?

options.A: Through excessive calcium influx caused by high glutamate
options.B: By blocking the reuptake of dopamine in the basal ganglia
options.C: Via the massive release of cerebrospinal fluid
options.D: By depleting extracellular glucose stores

question: Which brain region is primarily affected in Parkinson's disease?

options.A: Hippocampus and temporal lobes
options.B: Substantia nigra and basal ganglia
options.C: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
options.D: Cerebellar vermis and hemispheres

question: A patient presenting with prominent chorea and cognitive changes is most likely suffering degeneration in which area?

options.A: Neuromuscular junction receptors
options.B: Primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe
options.C: Dorsal root ganglia of the spinal nerves
options.D: Caudate nucleus of the basal ganglia

explanation: Chorea, erratic involuntary movements characteristic of Huntington's disease, stems from degeneration in the basal ganglia, particularly the caudate nucleus. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h3)

question: How do clinical symptoms typically manifest in degenerative neurological conditions?

options.A: They fluctuate wildly from hour to hour without a trend
options.B: They appear overnight with maximum severity
options.C: They develop insidiously and progress over time
options.D: They remain static once the initial diagnosis is made

explanation: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by a slow onset and a continuous, progressive worsening of symptoms. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h4)

question: What is a common clinical feature in the advanced stages of almost all major neurodegenerative disorders?

options.A: Hyperactivity and accelerated metabolism
options.B: Spontaneous regeneration of lost neuronal pathways
options.C: Complete normalization of cognitive function
options.D: Development of profound immobility and dependence

explanation: As these disorders reach their advanced stages, widespread neuronal loss invariably leads to severe physical and cognitive disability requiring total care. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h4)

question: What is the primary role of neuroimaging like MRI in evaluating suspected neurodegenerative disorders?

options.A: To rule out other structural pathologies like tumors or hydrocephalus
options.B: To completely halt the ongoing process of neuronal degeneration

question: Why is the clinical history and neurological examination so critical in diagnosing these conditions?

question: Which assessment is crucial for a nurse caring for a patient with a progressive neurological disorder?

question: What is a frequent terminal complication in advanced neurodegenerative disorders?

question: Why is early discussion of advance directives particularly important in neurodegenerative conditions?

question: What is the primary characteristic of paroxysmal disorders?

question: How do non-epileptic paroxysmal events differ fundamentally from epileptic seizures?

question: Which neurotransmitter is primarily responsible for inhibitory control in the central nervous system?

question: What cellular event drives the excessive metabolic demand during a seizure discharge?

question: A patient suddenly stares blankly into space for ten seconds, stops talking mid-sentence, and immediately resumes normal activity with no post-ictal confusion. Which seizure type is most likely occurring?

question: Which of the following is a common environmental or behavioral trigger for acute seizures?

question: Why are central nervous system infections such as cerebral malaria or meningitis strongly linked to paroxysmal disorders?

question: What is the primary diagnostic tool used to record abnormal electrical activity in the brain?

question: Why is an eyewitness account particularly critical when assessing a patient with a suspected paroxysmal disorder?

question: What is the primary goal of pharmacological management in epilepsy?

question: What critical danger is associated with the abrupt cessation of antiepileptic medications?

question: How is status epilepticus defined regarding the duration of continuous seizure activity?

question: A patient is experiencing a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the hospital ward. Which nursing action is NOT appropriate during the active phase of the seizure?

question: What safety precaution should be emphasized to a patient with newly diagnosed, uncontrolled epilepsy?

question: Why is addressing the social stigma of epilepsy an important component of nursing care?

question: What is the primary anatomical difference between meningitis and encephalitis?

question: Why do central nervous system infections rapidly lead to life-threatening complications?

question: What is the most frequent route by which pathogens enter the central nervous system?

question: Which scenario represents contiguous extension as a route of nervous system infection?

question: Which form of meningitis is typically considered the most rapidly progressive and life-threatening?

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a lumbar puncture in suspected meningitis?

question: What is the clinical justification for starting antibiotics immediately without waiting for definitive cerebrospinal fluid culture results in suspected bacterial meningitis?

question: Why is it important to maintain a quiet, dimly lit environment for a patient hospitalized with meningitis?

question: Which seasonal and environmental factor heavily influences meningitis outbreaks in northern Nigeria?

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended public health measure for controlling meningococcal disease outbreaks?

question: What primary component is included in the peripheral nervous system?

question: What is the primary physiological function of the myelin sheath along an axon?

question: Why is spontaneous recovery rapid and complete in cases of mild neurapraxia?

question: A patient with chronic peripheral nerve damage presents with dry, shiny skin and non-healing foot ulcers. What underlying mechanism explains these physical findings?

question: How does needle electromyography (EMG) differ functionally from nerve conduction studies?

question: Which class of medication is commonly prescribed as a first-line treatment for chronic neuropathic pain?

question: A patient diagnosed with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy asks why standard pain relievers like paracetamol or ibuprofen provide little relief. What is the best clinical explanation?

question: What is an essential self-care practice a nurse should teach a patient with severe peripheral neuropathy affecting the lower extremities?

question: Why is testing bathwater temperature with a thermometer specifically recommended for individuals with peripheral sensory loss?

options.D: The personal opinions of the nurse regarding the family
