options.C: It completely eliminates all medicolegal liability for the surgical team
options.D: It guarantees that the wound will heal without any visible scarring

explanation: Informed consent respects patient autonomy by ensuring they are fully aware of what the procedure entails, including potential complications. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h4)

question: Which surgical instrument is typically used for blunt dissection inside an abscess cavity to break down loculations?

options.A: Suture holder
options.B: Thumb forceps
options.C: Mosquito forceps
options.D: Tissue scissors

explanation: Mosquito forceps are inserted closed into the abscess cavity and gently opened to break up internal walls or loculations without cutting major blood vessels. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of applying an antiseptic skin preparation like chlorhexidine around the abscess site before cutting?

options.A: To permanently bleach the surrounding skin for better visibility
options.B: To numb the superficial pain receptors instantly prior to local injection
options.C: To reduce resident skin flora and prevent introduction into the deep incision
options.D: To instantly dissolve the necrotic pus beneath the thick dermis layer

explanation: Skin preparation minimizes surface bacteria so that when the scalpel cuts the skin, those surface organisms are not pushed into the sterile subcutaneous tissues. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h5)

question: Why should local anesthetic infiltration ideally be placed around the perimeter of an abscess rather than directly into the center?

options.A: Direct injection causes the abscess wall to rupture prematurely before cutting
options.B: Peripheral injection is completely painless compared to central infiltration
options.C: Central injection forces bacteria directly into the underlying muscle layer
options.D: Inflamed acidic tissue neutralizes the local anesthetic, reducing its effectiveness

explanation: The acidic pH of infected tissue impairs the ionization and effectiveness of local anesthetics, making peripheral field blocks much more successful. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the clinical rationale for placing a loose gauze pack inside a large drained abscess cavity?

options.A: To absorb all the patient's arterial blood and stop minor capillary oozing instantly
options.B: To supply a continuous local dose of systemic antibiotics directly to the base
options.C: To prevent the superficial skin edges from sealing prematurely and trapping remaining pus
options.D: To stretch the skin permanently and eliminate the need for future bandaging

explanation: Packing acts as a wick and prevents the outer skin from closing too fast, ensuring the cavity heals from the inside out and does not reform. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h6)

question: When is a wound packing placed during an incision and drainage procedure typically scheduled for its first formal check or removal?

options.A: 7 to 10 days
options.B: Immediately after 2 hours
options.C: 24 to 48 hours
options.D: After 3 weeks

explanation: The initial post-procedure check usually occurs within 24 to 48 hours to assess drainage, remove packing if appropriate, and check for complications. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary benefit of encouraging a patient to perform warm saline soaks on a healing drainage site?

options.A: It replaces the need for any subsequent clinical dressing changes
options.B: It turns the open wound into a closed surgical incision overnight
options.C: It promotes local vasodilation and cleans away minor crusting
options.D: It permanently freezes the local nerve endings to stop all discomfort

explanation: Warm soaks increase blood flow to the healing area, bringing immune cells and nutrients while softening crusts to keep the wound clean. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h7)

question: Why are systemic antibiotics often unnecessary for a simple, small, well-drained superficial skin abscess?

options.A: Surgical drainage removes the infected purulent core, allowing the body to heal naturally
options.B: Bacteria inside skin abscesses are completely immune to all known pharmacological agents
options.C: Oral antibiotics are completely blocked from entering any soft tissue in the human body
options.D: The immune system shuts down entirely once a scalpel touches the epidermis layer

explanation: Once the pus and bacteria are physically evacuated from the closed space, the infection resolves without drugs unless surrounding cellulitis or systemic symptoms are present. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h8)

question: Which of the following clinical scenarios most strongly justifies prescribing systemic antibiotics following an incision and drainage procedure?

options.A: Complete absence of pain and swelling twenty-four hours post-op
options.B: Successful removal of all packing material on the first clinic visit
options.C: A small isolated lesion on the forearm of a healthy young adult
options.D: Presence of significant surrounding cellulitis and systemic fever

explanation: Systemic symptoms and spreading cellulitis indicate that the infection extends beyond the localized drained cavity and requires systemic antimicrobial coverage. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h8)

question: Which warning sign should patients be explicitly taught to report immediately following an abscess drainage procedure?

options.A: Dry skin flakes forming near the outer edges of the dressing
options.B: A slight pink tinge on the gauze during the first daily change
options.C: A mild decrease in local itching around the adhesive bandage
options.D: Spreading redness and red streaks extending from the wound

explanation: Spreading erythema and red streaks indicate worsening local infection or lymphangitis, requiring prompt medical re-evaluation. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h9)

question: What is an important household prevention measure to communicate to a patient treated for a recurrent skin abscess?

options.A: Apply heavy industrial grease to all exposed skin surfaces daily
options.B: Wash all household furniture with concentrated industrial bleach weekly
options.C: Permanently eliminate all physical exercise and outdoor movement
options.D: Avoid sharing personal items like towels and clothing with family members

explanation: Staphylococcal bacteria can easily spread among household contacts via shared towels, razors, and clothing, leading to recurrent infections. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h9)

question: What anatomical structure is removed during male circumcision?

options.A: The prepuce
options.B: The scrotal sac
options.C: The glans penis
options.D: The frenulum

explanation: Circumcision specifically involves excising the prepuce, which is the fold of skin covering the head of the penis. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why do global health bodies promote male circumcision in specific regions?

options.A: To reduce the transmission of certain viral infections
options.B: To replace standard barrier contraceptive methods entirely
options.C: To permanently eliminate all common dermatological conditions
options.D: To accelerate normal pubertal growth and development

explanation: Clinical trials confirm that removing the foreskin lowers the acquisition risk of specific viral pathogens, notably human immunodeficiency virus. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h1)

question: What is the name of the sensitive ventral fold of skin connecting the glans to the prepuce?

options.A: The corpus cavernosum
options.B: The frenulum
options.C: The corona
options.D: The pubic symphysis

explanation: The frenulum is a delicate ventral tissue bridge that contains a significant arterial branch requiring careful handling during surgery. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which penile structure directly encloses the male urethra?

options.A: The corpus spongiosum
options.B: The prepuce
options.C: The corona
options.D: The corpora cavernosa

explanation: The corpus spongiosum is the single ventral column of erectile tissue through which the urethra runs along its length. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which congenital anomaly makes routine circumcision an immediate contraindication?

options.A: Hydrocele
options.B: Cryptorchidism
options.C: Hypospadias
options.D: Phimosis

explanation: Surgeons must preserve the foreskin in hypospadias because plastic surgeons utilize this excess tissue for urethral reconstruction. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h3)

question: What defines the clinical state known as paraphimosis?

options.A: The retracted foreskin becomes trapped behind the corona and swells
options.B: The urethral opening develops on the ventral surface of the shaft
options.C: The foreskin remains permanently tight and cannot be pulled back
options.D: The scrotal contents become inflamed due to a bacterial infection

explanation: Paraphimosis acts as a tourniquet, cutting off circulation to the glans and requiring prompt manual reduction or emergency surgical intervention. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h3)

question: What is a primary nursing responsibility immediately prior to a neonatal circumcision?

options.A: Verifying valid informed consent from the parents
options.B: Performing a comprehensive neurological reflex assessment
options.C: Administering a full course of prophylactic oral antibiotics
options.D: Inserting a permanent indwelling urinary catheter

explanation: Legal and ethical protocols dictate that parents or legal guardians must sign an informed consent document before non-emergent surgical interventions on minors. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why might a scheduled routine circumcision be postponed during the preoperative nursing assessment?

options.A: The infant exhibits signs of active local skin infection or diaper rash
options.B: The mother expresses mild anxiety regarding surgical pain control
options.C: The patient consumed clear fluids four hours prior to the procedure
options.D: The parents request a traditional naming ceremony after recovery

explanation: Infection or severe skin breakdown increases the risk of wound contamination and poor healing, necessitating postponement until the skin is intact. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which circumcision device relies on ischemic necrosis to cause the foreskin to fall off naturally?

options.A: Plastibell
options.B: Scalpel blade
options.C: Mogen clamp
options.D: Gomco clamp

explanation: The Plastibell device cuts off blood supply to the distal foreskin using a tied string, allowing the dead tissue to drop off after several days. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h5)

question: How does the Gomco clamp achieve hemostasis during the procedure?

options.A: By applying a chemical cautery paste directly to the wound edges
options.B: By freezing the base of the foreskin with liquid nitrogen
options.C: By using an automated stapling device with absorbable clips
options.D: By crushing the tissue vessels before surgical excision

explanation: The Gomco clamp uses a metal bell and baseplate mechanism to crush the blood vessels in the foreskin, minimizing intraoperative bleeding. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why must epinephrine be avoided when preparing local anesthetics for penile blocks?

options.A: It stains the surgical field and obscures anatomical landmarks
options.B: It neutralizes the anesthetic agent and renders it completely ineffective
options.C: It triggers immediate generalized seizures in pediatric patients
options.D: It can cause severe vasoconstriction leading to ischemic tissue necrosis

explanation: The end-arterial blood supply of the penis makes it extremely vulnerable to intense vasoconstriction, which can cause gangrene if epinephrine is used. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is a primary intraoperative priority when preparing an infant for a surgical procedure?

options.A: Preventing hypothermia using radiant warmers and temperature monitoring
options.B: Administering broad-spectrum intravenous antiviral medications
options.C: Initiating central venous access for routine fluid replacement
options.D: Placing a nasogastric tube to decompress the stomach

explanation: Infants possess high body surface area to mass ratios and limited fat stores, making them highly susceptible to rapid heat loss in clinical settings. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is a key physiological indicator that must be monitored following a circumcision?

options.A: Passage of meconium or stool
options.B: Normal bowel sound return
options.C: Successful spontaneous urination
options.D: Stable central venous pressure

explanation: Checking that the patient voids ensures there is no acute urinary retention caused by post-procedural edema or tight bandaging. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h7)

question: Which nursing action best supports comfort management for a neonatal circumcision in the immediate recovery phase?

options.A: Encouraging immediate ambulation around the recovery ward
options.B: Administering prescribed analgesics and utilizing oral sucrose solutions
options.C: Applying cold ice packs directly to the exposed glans continuously
options.D: Placing tight compressive dressings to numb nerve endings

explanation: Combining pharmacological pain relief with non-pharmacological soothing techniques like sweet-tasting sucrose pacifiers effectively minimizes procedural distress in infants. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is the most frequent acute complication immediately following male circumcision?

options.A: Urethral stricture
options.B: Hemorrhage
options.C: Erectile dysfunction
options.D: Penile amputation

explanation: Bleeding from the rich vascular network of the prepuce or the frenular artery is the most common immediate post-procedural complication. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h8)

question: What emergency action is required if a Plastibell ring slips proximally onto the penile shaft?

options.A: Administration of high-dose intravenous systemic anticoagulants
options.B: Immediate application of warm saline soaks to dissolve the plastic
options.C: Prompt removal or cutting of the displaced ring by trained personnel
options.D: Insertion of a suprapubic catheter to bypass the obstruction

explanation: A slipped plastic ring acts as a tourniquet, requiring urgent mechanical removal using specialized wire cutters to restore vascular perfusion. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h8)

question: What home-care practice is commonly recommended to prevent the circumcision wound from sticking to a diaper?

options.A: Applying petroleum jelly to the site
options.B: Soaking the infant in cold water baths
options.C: Washing the area with harsh antiseptic soap
options.D: Covering the wound with tight gauze bandages

explanation: Petroleum jelly acts as a non-adherent barrier, preventing the raw healing edges from adhering to diaper material and causing trauma upon removal. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h9)

question: Which instruction should a nurse give parents whose child underwent a Plastibell circumcision?

options.A: Gently twist and pull the ring off after twenty-four hours
options.B: Scrub the ring daily with a stiff brush to remove crusts
options.C: Apply medicated adhesive tape over the ring to secure it
options.D: Allow the plastic ring to fall off naturally within several days

explanation: Premature manual removal of the Plastibell ring can cause severe hemorrhage and tissue damage; it must detach on its own as necrosis completes. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h9)

question: What is the primary advantage of intravenous drug administration over oral delivery?

options.A: It entirely eliminates the risk of systemic side effects.
options.B: It requires minimal technical skill and can be performed by patients.
options.C: It achieves immediate systemic circulation and rapid onset of action.
options.D: It prevents the liver from metabolizing any administered substances.

explanation: Bypassing the digestive tract allows therapeutic agents to enter the bloodstream directly for immediate systemic effects. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h1)

question: A patient arrives at the emergency ward severely dehydrated from acute gastroenteritis and unable to retain oral fluids. Why is an intravenous infusion selected over oral rehydration therapy?

options.A: To bypass the gastrointestinal tract and provide rapid fluid replacement
options.B: To slowly absorb nutrients through the mucosal lining of the stomach
options.C: To maintain a constant high blood pressure without affecting fluid volume
options.D: To stimulate peristalsis and improve overall digestive enzyme production

explanation: When oral intake fails or is clinically unsafe, the IV route ensures rapid and reliable restoration of circulating blood volume and hydration status. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which vein located in the antecubital fossa is commonly chosen for emergency access and blood draws due to its large size?

options.A: Internal jugular vein
options.B: Median cubital vein
options.C: Great saphenous vein
options.D: Radial artery

explanation: The median cubital vein is prominent, stable, and easily accessed in the antecubital fossa, making it ideal for urgent situations. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h2)

question: A nurse is preparing to insert an IV cannula into an adult patient. Which anatomical site should be avoided if possible due to the high risk of mechanical dislodgement from normal joint movement?

options.A: Antecubital fossa using the median cubital vein
options.B: Upper arm segment of the basilic vein
options.C: Dorsal metacarpal veins of the hand
options.D: Forearm veins along the cephalic pathway

explanation: Hand veins move frequently with wrist flexion and daily tasks, increasing the likelihood of infiltration and catheter displacement. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h2)

question: Which intravenous solution is classified as isotonic and commonly used for initial extracellular fluid resuscitation?

options.A: 0.9% Normal Saline
options.B: 3% Sodium Chloride
options.C: 0.45% Sodium Chloride
options.D: 10% Dextrose in Water

explanation: 0.9% Normal Saline has a tonicity similar to extracellular fluid, expanding blood volume without causing net fluid shifts into cells. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h3)

question: What is the primary physiological effect of infusing a hypertonic intravenous solution into a patient's bloodstream?

options.A: It neutralizes metabolic acidosis without altering fluid distribution.
options.B: It forces fluid from the blood vessels directly into the intracellular space.
options.C: It causes an immediate, equal expansion of all body fluid compartments.
options.D: It draws water out of the cells and into the intravascular space.

explanation: Hypertonic solutions have a higher solute concentration than serum, creating an osmotic gradient that pulls water out of cells and tissues. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h3)

question: Which piece of equipment is essential for securing the insertion site while allowing continuous visual inspection of the vein?

options.A: Standard cotton gauze pad
options.B: Elastic compression bandage
options.C: Non-porous adhesive tape
options.D: Transparent sterile dressing

explanation: Transparent dressings protect the insertion site from external contaminants while letting nurses inspect for redness, swelling, or infiltration. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h4)

question: Why is it important to select a larger gauge cannula, such as an 18-gauge, when preparing for rapid blood transfusion?

options.A: It allows the thick viscous blood components to pass through without clotting.
options.B: It completely eliminates the risk of developing superficial phlebitis.
options.C: It prevents the hemolysis of fragile blood cells during rapid flow.
options.D: It reduces the total volume of fluid required during resuscitation.

explanation: Smaller bores create high resistance and shear stress that can rupture red blood cells, making larger gauges necessary for blood products. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h4)

question: At what approximate angle should an intravenous cannula be inserted through the skin during peripheral access?

options.A: 45 to 60 degrees
options.B: 75 to 90 degrees
options.C: 5 to 10 degrees
options.D: 15 to 30 degrees

explanation: An insertion angle of 15 to 30 degrees allows safe penetration through the skin and subcutaneous tissue directly into the superficial vein lumen. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h5)

question: What is the clinical purpose of allowing the skin antiseptic to dry completely before inserting the IV cannula?

options.A: To ensure the tourniquet maintains adequate pressure on the limb
options.B: To reduce the burning sensation when the needle punctures the epidermis
options.C: To allow the chemical agents sufficient time to destroy microorganisms
options.D: To prevent the adhesive dressing from slipping off moist skin

explanation: Antiseptics like chlorhexidine require a specific contact drying time to achieve maximum antimicrobial effectiveness on the skin. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h5)

question: What drop factor is standard for micro-drip administration sets used in pediatric nursing care?

options.A: 15 drops per milliliter
options.B: 60 drops per milliliter
options.C: 20 drops per milliliter
options.D: 10 drops per milliliter

explanation: Micro-drip sets deliver 60 drops per milliliter, allowing for precise fluid volume regulation in patients requiring small amounts. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h6)

question: A patient is prescribed 1000 mL of normal saline to run over 8 hours using a manual infusion set with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What is the approximate flow rate in drops per minute?

options.A: 21 gtt/min
options.B: 42 gtt/min
options.C: 125 gtt/min
options.D: 31 gtt/min

explanation: Multiply 1000 mL by 15 gtt/mL to get 15000, then divide by 480 minutes (8 hours x 60 minutes), resulting in approximately 31.25 drops per minute. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h6)

question: How often should a routine peripheral intravenous site be visually inspected by the nurse during an ongoing infusion?

options.A: Only when the patient complains
options.B: At least every hour
options.C: Every 24 hours
options.D: Once every shift

explanation: Frequent hourly checks ensure early detection of complications such as infiltration, dislodgement, or phlebitis. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary rationale for routinely replacing peripheral IV cannulas and dressings according to hospital protocols?

options.A: To minimize the risk of localized infection and phlebitis
options.B: To prevent the plastic catheter from dissolving in the bloodstream
options.C: To test the patient's skin elasticity and healing capacity
options.D: To ensure the fluid bag remains at a consistent room temperature

explanation: Leaving a peripheral catheter in place too long significantly increases the risk of bacterial colonization and vessel inflammation. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h7)

question: Which clinical manifestation is most characteristic of fluid infiltration into the subcutaneous tissue around an IV site?

options.A: A hard, red cord running along the vein pathway
options.B: Sudden severe chest pain and severe cyanosis
options.C: Coolness and swelling around the insertion site
options.D: Spontaneous bleeding from the catheter hub

explanation: When IV fluid infuses into subcutaneous tissue instead of the vein, the local area becomes cool to the touch, pale, and edematous. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: A patient receiving an intravenous infusion suddenly develops respiratory distress, weak rapid pulse, and decreased blood pressure, and a suspected air embolism is noted. What immediate emergency position should the nurse place the patient in?

options.A: Supine flat position with legs elevated
options.B: Left lateral Trendelenburg position
options.C: Prone position flat on the abdomen
options.D: High Fowler position sitting upright

explanation: Placing the patient on their left side in Trendelenburg traps air in the apex of the right ventricle, preventing it from entering the pulmonary artery. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: Why is it important to inspect the catheter tip immediately after removing a peripheral intravenous cannula?

options.A: To determine if the cannula can be safely sterilized and reused later
options.B: To calculate the total volume of fluid that passed through the device
options.C: To check for blood clots that might indicate an underlying clotting disorder
options.D: To confirm that the catheter tip is intact and no fragment broke off inside the vein

explanation: Inspecting the removed catheter ensures that no broken portion of the plastic tip was left behind as an embolus in the patient's bloodstream. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h9)

question: What is the primary action a nurse should take immediately after withdrawing a peripheral IV cannula from a patient's arm?

options.A: Wash the puncture site thoroughly with soap and warm tap water.
options.B: Encourage the patient to immediately bend the elbow joint tightly.
options.C: Apply immediate direct pressure with sterile gauze to achieve hemostasis.
options.D: Massage the puncture wound vigorously to distribute residual antiseptic.

explanation: Applying direct pressure prevents hematoma formation and stops bleeding from the punctured vein. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h9)

question: What is the primary focus of cancer epidemiology?

options.A: Synthesizing novel chemotherapeutic agents in a laboratory setting
options.B: Performing surgical resections on localized malignant tumors
options.C: Mapping the intracellular signaling pathways of oncogenes
options.D: Investigating the distribution and determinants of cancer in populations

explanation: Cancer epidemiology studies disease frequency and patterns across different populations rather than focusing on individual clinical treatment or cellular biology. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why is population-level cancer data essential for healthcare planning?

options.A: It guarantees immediate cures for all newly diagnosed cancer patients
options.B: It standardizes hospital room pricing across different geopolitical zones
options.C: It helps allocate resources and target high-risk communities effectively
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for individual patient diagnostic testing

explanation: Understanding disease distribution allows health planners to direct preventive interventions and infrastructure where the burden is greatest. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which malignancy is most frequently diagnosed among women in Nigeria?

options.A: Endometrial cancer
options.B: Cervical cancer
options.C: Ovarian cancer
options.D: Breast cancer

explanation: Breast cancer remains the leading malignancy diagnosed among Nigerian women, frequently appearing at younger age brackets than seen globally. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What accounts for the high mortality-to-incidence ratio of cancer in sub-Saharan Africa?

options.A: Mandatory annual screening programs that overdiagnose benign lesions
options.B: The complete absence of traditional risk factors in the region
options.C: Late-stage presentation and limited access to specialized treatment
options.D: Genetically superior cancer cells unique to the African continent

explanation: Due to diagnostic delays, financial barriers, and healthcare shortages, patients often present when the disease is already advanced and harder to treat successfully. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What does cancer incidence specifically measure within a population?

options.A: The total percentage of people currently living with a tumor
options.B: The number of new cases diagnosed during a specific time period
options.C: The average lifespan of a patient following a terminal diagnosis
options.D: The annual number of deaths directly caused by malignant neoplasms

explanation: Incidence tracks newly diagnosed cases, which helps researchers understand changing risk factor exposures over time. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h3)

question: A public health nurse analyzing long-term disability and ongoing care requirements in a community should primarily examine which metric?

options.A: Mortality rate
options.B: Incidence
options.C: Prevalence
options.D: Case fatality ratio

explanation: Prevalence counts all existing cases at a given time, providing a clear picture of total community healthcare utilization and ongoing support needs. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following is classified as a modifiable cancer risk factor?

options.A: Advanced chronological age
options.B: Inherited BRCA1 mutation
options.C: Tobacco smoking
options.D: Biological sex

explanation: Lifestyle behaviors like smoking can be altered through public health interventions, making them modifiable risk factors unlike age or genetics. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h4)

question: A community health nurse designing a local educational campaign to reduce biological carcinogen exposure should focus heavily on which intervention?

options.A: Encouraging daily endurance running to alter genetic predispositions
options.B: Advocating for legislation that raises the legal age of retirement
options.C: Promoting hepatitis B vaccination and safe screening practices
options.D: Screening all newborn infants for rare chromosomal translocations

explanation: Hepatitis B is a well-known biological carcinogen; vaccination and infection screening directly target this preventable driver of liver cancer. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary function of tumor suppressor genes in normal cellular physiology?

options.A: Stimulating rapid angiogenesis to nourish newly forming embryonic tissue
options.B: Repairing broken bones and damaged muscular fascia following trauma
options.C: Accelerating the conversion of healthy cells into invasive metastatic clones
options.D: Regulating the cell cycle and preventing uncontrolled cellular proliferation

explanation: Tumor suppressor genes act as molecular brakes, halting the cell cycle or inducing apoptosis when DNA damage is detected. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why do most human cancers develop through acquired somatic mutations rather than inherited germline mutations?

options.A: Germline mutations are immediately lethal before an individual is born
options.B: Inherited genes completely protect individuals from all external carcinogens
options.C: Environmental exposures and lifestyle factors accumulate DNA damage over decades
options.D: Somatic cells possess no internal mechanisms to repair damaged nucleic acids

explanation: A lifetime of cumulative exposure to dietary, environmental, and chemical mutagens gradually damages somatic cell DNA, triggering carcinogenesis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of implementing a population-based cancer screening program?

options.A: Providing definitive surgical chemotherapy regimens for end-stage patients
options.B: Identifying pre-malignant lesions or early-stage disease in asymptomatic people
options.C: Replacing the need for routine physical examinations in clinical settings
options.D: Diagnosing acute infectious diseases during community outbreak events

explanation: Screening targets healthy, asymptomatic individuals to catch disease early before symptoms prompt a clinical visit. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h6)

question: Which of the following scenarios describes a diagnostic evaluation rather than a screening test?

options.A: Offering a prostate-specific antigen blood test to a healthy older adult male
options.B: Performing a biopsy on a palpable breast lump found by a patient
options.C: Administering a routine Pap smear to a healthy twenty-five-year-old woman
options.D: Checking stool samples for occult blood during a community health fair

explanation: A biopsy performed on an already symptomatic or abnormal physical finding is diagnostic, whereas checking healthy people without symptoms is screening. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h6)

question: How do clinical nurses directly contribute to cancer epidemiology research?

options.A: By manufacturing advanced linear accelerators for radiation therapy departments
options.B: By meticulously recording patient demographics and tumor data for registries
options.C: By writing national legislation regarding industrial waste disposal standards
options.D: By funding international pharmaceutical trials through private donations

explanation: Accurate nursing documentation in clinical records provides the baseline data epidemiologists use to track disease incidence and outcomes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: A community health nurse in a rural Nigerian clinic notices an unusual cluster of liver cancers over several months. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Immediately shut down all local markets selling grains and groundnuts
options.B: Advise the community that dietary habits cannot alter cancer risk
options.C: Prescribe experimental chemotherapy agents to all residents in the village
options.D: Document findings accurately and report them to public health surveillance systems

explanation: Accurate reporting and documentation help public health authorities investigate potential environmental or infectious clusters and plan appropriate interventions. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary objective of a debulking surgical procedure in cancer management?

options.A: To replace damaged lymph nodes entirely
options.B: To reduce tumor mass to ease symptoms
options.C: To completely cure the client of the disease
options.D: To deliver systemic localized radiation

explanation: Debulking surgery does not remove the entire tumor, but reducing its size helps alleviate pressure on surrounding organs and makes subsequent treatments more effective. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why does chemotherapy frequently cause side effects in healthy, rapidly dividing tissues like hair follicles and the gastrointestinal tract?

options.A: Systemic drugs accumulate preferentially in the superficial layers of the skin.
options.B: Chemotherapy agents selectively target only benign metabolic pathways.
options.C: Chemotherapy stimulates the immune system to attack normal mucosal cells.
options.D: Normal tissues share the rapid cellular division characteristic of cancer cells.

explanation: Cytotoxic drugs are designed to target cells undergoing frequent division, which inadvertently damages healthy rapidly proliferating cells in the bone marrow, gut, and hair follicles. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h1)

question: What is a primary reason for enforcing early ambulation in a client recovering from major oncological surgery?

options.A: To eliminate the need for postoperative analgesic medications
options.B: To prevent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
options.C: To stimulate immediate resumption of normal bowel motility
options.D: To accelerate the complete closure of surgical incision sites

explanation: Early ambulation promotes venous return in the lower extremities, significantly reducing the risk of blood stasis and subsequent clot formation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h2)

question: A client returns to the surgical ward following a radical neck dissection for laryngeal cancer. Which immediate nursing action is most critical?

options.A: Administering a prescribed high-protein oral diet
options.B: Encouraging the client to perform vigorous neck range of motion
options.C: Removing the primary surgical drains to check for bleeding
options.D: Assessing airway patency and monitoring for neck swelling

explanation: Surgeries around the neck area carry a high risk of airway compromise due to localized edema, hematoma formation, or tracheal displacement, making airway surveillance the top priority. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h2)

question: What term describes a chemotherapy medication capable of causing severe tissue destruction and necrosis if it leaks into subcutaneous tissue?

options.A: A vesicant
options.B: A radiolabel
options.C: A pyrogen
options.D: Anantagonist

explanation: Vesicants are highly irritating cytotoxic agents that cause blistering and deep tissue damage upon accidental extravasation into peripheral tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h3)

question: What is the appropriate initial nursing action if a client receiving a peripheral intravenous infusion of a vesicant chemotherapy agent reports a burning sensation at the needle site?

options.A: Immediately stop the infusion and disconnect the intravenous tubing
options.B: Administer a topical analgesic cream over the injection site
options.C: Flush the peripheral line rapidly with normal saline to clear the drug
options.D: Slow the infusion rate down and apply a warm compress

explanation: Stopping the infusion immediately limits the amount of drug entering the interstitial tissue, preventing further localized damage before institutional extravasation protocols are initiated. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h3)

question: Which instruction should a nurse give to a client undergoing external beam radiation therapy regarding skin markings?

options.A: Apply petroleum jelly directly over the markings every morning
options.B: Scrub the markings daily with alcohol to prevent skin infection
options.C: Cover the markings completely with adhesive waterproof bandages
options.D: Avoid washing off or altering the temporary ink markings

explanation: Radiation ink tattoos or markings are essential for ensuring the precise alignment of the radiation beam during every treatment session and must be preserved. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h4)

question: What is a recommended practice for skin hygiene within a radiation treatment field?

options.A: Applying heating pads to soothe localized radiation erythema
options.B: Wearing tight synthetic garments to protect the skin from air
options.C: Using scented commercial soaps and vigorous washcloth friction
options.D: Washing gently with lukewarm water and patting the skin dry

explanation: Gentle cleansing with mild water and patting dry prevents mechanical irritation to fragile, radiation-damaged epidermal layers. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h4)

question: Which nursing intervention is most appropriate for a client experiencing chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia?

options.A: Instructing the client to shave facial hair using an electric razor
options.B: Administering intramuscular injections for routine pain relief
options.C: Encouraging the use of hard-bristled toothbrushes for plaque removal
options.D: Applying firm pressure dressings over all venipuncture sites for an hour

explanation: Electric razors minimize the risk of accidental skin nicks and bleeding in clients with low platelet counts, whereas straight razors and intramuscular injections should be avoided. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is the single most reliable early indicator of infection in a client experiencing severe neutropenia?

options.A: An elevated core body temperature or fever
options.B: Severe localized pain in the lower abdomen
options.C: A sudden drop in systemic blood pressure
options.D: Purulent drainage visible at a surgical site

explanation: Because neutropenic clients lack sufficient neutrophils to mount a standard inflammatory response, even a mild fever can be the only sign of a potentially fatal systemic infection. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h5)

question: What clinical manifestation is most characteristic of Superior Vena Cava Syndrome?

options.A: Facial edema, periorbital swelling, and jugular vein distention
options.B: Bilateral paralysis of the lower extremities
options.C: Severe lower extremity pitting edema and calf pain
options.D: Acute left upper quadrant abdominal tenderness

explanation: Obstruction of blood flow through the superior vena cava causes venous congestion in the upper body, resulting in characteristic facial and neck swelling. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which metabolic abnormalities are classically associated with Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: Hypokalemia, hypouricemia, and hypercalcemia
options.B: Hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, and hyperphosphatemia
options.C: Hyperkalemia, hypouricemia, and hypophosphatemia
options.D: Hyponatremia, hypophosphatemia, and hypercalcemia

explanation: The massive lysis of cancer cells releases large amounts of potassium, nucleic acids that metabolize into uric acid, and phosphorus directly into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h6)

question: What is cancer cachexia primarily characterized by?

options.A: Rapid accumulation of subcutaneous adipose tissue
options.B: Excessive appetite and elevated serum albumin levels
options.C: Progressive involuntary weight loss and muscle wasting
options.D: Severe fluid retention and generalized anasarca

explanation: Cancer cachexia is a wasting syndrome driven by metabolic alterations and systemic inflammation that causes severe loss of skeletal muscle and fat mass that cannot be reversed by conventional nutrition alone. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h7)

question: Which dietary modification is most effective for a client experiencing severe cancer-related anorexia and early satiety?

options.A: Serving three large, highly spiced meals daily at standard times
options.B: Offering low-calorie liquid clear broths to stimulate digestion
options.C: Restricting fluid intake entirely during all waking hours
options.D: Encouraging small, frequent meals high in calories and protein

explanation: Small, nutrient-dense portions prevent the client from feeling overwhelmed by large quantities of food while maximizing caloric and protein intake. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h7)

question: At what point in the disease trajectory should palliative care ideally be introduced for a client with advanced cancer?

options.A: Only when all curative medical treatments have failed
options.B: Simultaneously alongside active disease-directed treatments
options.C: After the client is discharged to hospice care at home
options.D: Strictly during the final forty-eight hours of life

explanation: Modern palliative care is designed to be integrated early in the disease course alongside curative therapies to manage symptoms and improve overall quality of life. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the primary focus of nursing interventions when providing psychosocial support to a newly diagnosed cancer client?

options.A: Discouraging discussion about terminal outcomes or death
options.B: Encouraging active listening and validating emotional responses
options.C: Redirecting conversation away from personal fears toward diet
options.D: Offering immediate guarantees of complete remission

explanation: Creating a safe space for clients to express their fears through active listening helps process complex emotions and reduces feelings of isolation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of cancer rehabilitation?

options.A: To eliminate the need for routine pharmacological pain management
options.B: To restore or maintain functional independence and quality of life
options.C: To accelerate the physiological elimination of chemotherapy agents
options.D: To provide curative medical therapy for primary malignancies

explanation: Cancer rehabilitation focuses on maximizing physical, social, and psychological functioning rather than directly treating the underlying tumor. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h1)

question: Which professional is primarily responsible for helping patients relearn skills needed for daily living activities?

options.A: Occupational therapist
options.B: Oncology social worker
options.C: Diagnostic radiographer
options.D: Clinical research coordinator

explanation: Occupational therapists focus on adapting environments and retraining patients in activities of daily living like dressing, bathing, and eating. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h2)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team essential in cancer rehabilitation?

options.A: Hospital accreditation standards require a minimum of six distinct specialties per patient
options.B: Physicians lack the legal authority to prescribe physical exercise regimens
options.C: Cancer and its treatments affect multiple physical and psychosocial body systems simultaneously
options.D: Multidisciplinary models completely eliminate the risk of chronic treatment side effects

explanation: The complex multisystem impact of malignancy requires diverse professional expertise to provide holistic, effective care. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of utilizing standardized performance scales like ECOG in oncology?

options.A: To measure the exact histological grade of a tumor
options.B: To determine the financial cost of prolonged hospitalization
options.C: To quantify a patient's functional ability and independence
options.D: To calculate the precise metabolic clearance of chemotherapy

explanation: Performance scales provide objective measurements of how cancer affects daily functioning and systemic well-being. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h3)

question: A comprehensive patient assessment in cancer rehabilitation MUST include evaluation of which of the following areas? (Select the best overall answer)

options.A: Physical, psychological, and environmental factors
options.B: Prior occupational history without current functional status
options.C: Exclusively laboratory and hematological parameters
options.D: Only the direct cost of surgical interventions

explanation: Holistic assessment requires evaluating bodily systems, mental health, and home or social contexts to design an effective care plan. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h3)

question: How does cancer-related fatigue primarily differ from ordinary fatigue?

options.A: It is caused strictly by underlying electrolyte imbalances
options.B: It responds immediately to high-carbohydrate dietary intake
options.C: It exclusively occurs during the late evening hours
options.D: It is not relieved by restorative sleep or rest

explanation: Cancer-related fatigue is persistent, subjective, and disproportionate to recent activity levels, failing to improve with standard rest. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h4)

question: What is a recommended non-pharmacological intervention to help manage cancer-related fatigue?

options.A: Complete strict bedrest until treatment ends
options.B: Elimination of all daytime fluid intake
options.C: High-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy
options.D: Regular, moderate-intensity physical exercise

explanation: Structured aerobic activity has been clinically proven to reduce the severity of cancer-related fatigue and improve overall energy levels. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h4)

question: Which clinical parameter must be carefully reviewed prior to initiating high-impact physical therapy in patients with bone metastases?

options.A: Baseline renal glomerular filtration rate
options.B: Fasting serum blood glucose concentrations
options.C: Structural bone integrity and fracture risk
options.D: Patient blood type and Rh factor status

explanation: Bone metastases weaken skeletal structures, requiring modified, low-impact exercise prescriptions to prevent pathological fractures. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is a primary benefit of resistance training in cancer rehabilitation programs?

options.A: Preventing the cellular mutation of benign tumors
options.B: Reversing cancer-induced skeletal muscle wasting and weakness
options.C: Accelerating the renal excretion of radiation contrast
options.D: Completely curing localized peripheral nerve damage

explanation: Resistance exercises stimulate muscle protein synthesis, combating cachexia and generalized physical deconditioning. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h5)

question: What term describes the complex wasting syndrome associated with advanced cancer characterized by severe muscle and weight loss?

options.A: Metabolic alkalosis
options.B: Hyperosmolar dehydration
options.C: Cancer cachexia
options.D: Sarcopenic obesity

explanation: Cachexia is a multifactorial wasting syndrome driven by systemic inflammation and altered metabolism that does not respond fully to standard nutritional repletion. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h6)

question: Why is early nutritional intervention critical during active oncological treatment?

options.A: It guarantees complete tumor regression without adjuvant medical therapy
options.B: It prevents the development of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy
options.C: It preserves lean body mass and improves tolerance to chemotherapy or radiation
options.D: It eliminates the need for intravenous access lines during surgery

explanation: Maintaining optimal nutritional status helps patients withstand high-dose therapies and reduces treatment interruptions caused by severe debility. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is a primary component of a comprehensive survivorship care plan?

options.A: A structured schedule for recurrence monitoring and late-effect surveillance
options.B: An official prescription waiver for outpatient analgesic drugs
options.C: A legal document transferring medical decision-making to family members
options.D: A binding employment contract for workplace readjustment

explanation: Survivorship care plans outline follow-up imaging, clinical evaluations, and guidance on managing potential long-term treatment side effects. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h7)

question: Which psychological concern is most commonly experienced by individuals transitioning into long-term cancer survivorship?

options.A: Severe acute delirium mimicking acute intoxication
options.B: Persistent anxiety regarding cancer recurrence
options.C: Complete denial of ever having received a diagnosis
options.D: Total indifference toward routine health monitoring

explanation: The fear of cancer returning is a widespread and enduring challenge for survivors long after active treatment concludes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the primary characteristic that distinguishes malignant neoplasms from benign neoplasms?

options.A: The ability to invade surrounding tissues and metastasize
options.B: The tendency to spontaneously resolve without medical treatment
options.C: Slow and localized growth patterns within a single organ
options.D: A complete absence of blood vessel supply within the mass

explanation: Malignant neoplasms are defined by their capacity to break through basement membranes, invade adjacent structures, and spread to distant sites, whereas benign tumors remain localized. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why is early prevention emphasized so strongly in resource-limited healthcare settings like Nigeria?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs are always less effective than lifestyle modifications
options.B: Advanced-stage presentation is very common and harder to treat successfully
options.C: Preventive measures completely eliminate the genetic risk of all cancers
options.D: Surgical interventions are entirely unavailable for treating localized tumors

explanation: When patients present late in the disease course, treatment options become more complex, expensive, and less likely to result in a cure, making prevention paramount. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which nursing intervention represents a primary prevention strategy against cervical cancer?

options.A: Performing a routine Papanicolaou (Pap) smear screening
options.B: Administering the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine
options.C: Providing postoperative care following a radical hysterectomy
options.D: Instructing a patient on managing chemotherapy-induced nausea

explanation: Vaccines prevent the initial viral infection that leads to cellular changes, classifying immunization as primary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h2)

question: A community health nurse is designing a seminar to reduce cancer risk factors. Which topic should be included as a primary prevention measure?

options.A: Techniques for performing monthly self-examinations of the breast
options.B: Strategies for quitting cigarette smoking and avoiding tobacco
options.C: Managing chronic fatigue during systemic cancer chemotherapy
options.D: Interpreting the results of a routine prostate-specific antigen test

explanation: Avoiding known carcinogens like tobacco prevents cellular damage and mutation from occurring in the first place, fulfilling primary prevention goals. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h2)

question: What is the primary objective of secondary prevention activities in oncology?

options.A: Rehabilitation and palliation of end-stage metastatic illness
options.B: Complete prevention of initial cellular mutation events
options.C: Early detection and prompt treatment of asymptomatic disease
options.D: Elimination of environmental radiation and chemical hazards

explanation: Secondary prevention aims to catch neoplastic changes early when intervention can halt disease progression before symptoms appear. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h3)

question: A 45-year-old female patient visits a primary health clinic asking how to check for breast cancer before she feels any lumps. Which nursing response describes a secondary prevention action?

options.A: Providing comfort measures and emotional support for a patient undergoing radiation therapy
options.B: Discussing the recommended schedule for screening mammograms and clinical breast exams
options.C: Explaining how avoiding alcohol consumption decreases long-term breast cancer risk
options.D: Administering prophylactic antibiotics to prevent opportunistic infections during treatment

explanation: Mammograms and clinical breast examinations are standard screening tools used to detect tumors early, defining secondary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h3)

question: Which activity is classified as a tertiary prevention intervention in cancer care?

options.A: Administering routine HPV vaccinations to teenage school children
options.B: Managing lymphedema and physical therapy following a mastectomy
options.C: Conducting community outreach lectures on the dangers of smoking
options.D: Performing a routine screening colonoscopy on an asymptomatic adult

explanation: Tertiary prevention deals with rehabilitation and minimizing disability after the disease and its primary treatments have occurred. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why is long-term follow-up care considered a crucial aspect of tertiary prevention for cancer survivors?

options.A: It guarantees that the patient will never experience lifestyle alterations again
options.B: It allows early identification of disease recurrence or secondary malignancies
options.C: It eliminates all financial and social burdens associated with the illness
options.D: It replaces the need for primary prevention education within the community

explanation: Survivors remain at risk for relapse or new primary cancers, making ongoing surveillance a key tertiary prevention strategy to catch issues early. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: What is the primary role of the nurse when a family history suggests a strong hereditary cancer syndrome?

options.A: Performing genetic laboratory sequencing directly at the bedside
options.B: Ordering prophylactic surgical removal of organs without consultation
options.C: Telling the family that inherited gene mutations cannot be tested
options.D: Recognizing patterns and facilitating a referral for genetic counseling

explanation: Nurses identify at-risk families during health history assessments and connect them with specialized genetic counselors for comprehensive risk evaluation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h5)

question: Which action demonstrates effective patient education by a nurse caring for an individual undergoing cancer treatment?

options.A: Limiting educational conversations to written pamphlets without verbal discussion
options.B: Providing a highly technical research journal article for the patient to read independently
options.C: Assessing the patient's literacy level and tailoring explanations about side effect management
options.D: Assuming the patient understands all discharge instructions if they nod politely

explanation: Effective education requires evaluating the learner's needs and communication barriers to ensure comprehension of self-care and warning signs. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h5)

question: Why must nurses engage in community advocacy and public health policy regarding cancer prevention?

options.A: Advocacy is solely the responsibility of hospital administrators and physicians
options.B: Government agencies prohibit individual nurses from educating patients directly
options.C: Bedside nursing care has been proven to completely replace the need for public health laws
options.D: Systemic factors like environmental hazards and policy gaps significantly impact population health

explanation: Policy and environmental conditions dictate exposure risks and healthcare access, making broader advocacy essential for sustainable disease prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h6)

question: A public health nurse in a rural Nigerian community notices that many women refuse breast screening due to cultural stigma and fear. Which advocacy action is most appropriate?

options.A: Ignoring the cultural beliefs since they do not affect clinical screening outcomes
options.B: Focusing entirely on acute inpatient chemotherapy administration in urban hospitals
options.C: Passing strict municipal laws that fine individuals who fail to attend annual health clinics
options.D: Partnering with local community leaders and religious heads to conduct culturally sensitive awareness campaigns

explanation: Working with respected community figures helps address stigma and fatalism, improving health literacy and screening acceptance in local populations. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h6)

question: What is the primary underlying cause of oncologic emergencies?

options.A: Acute or chronic complications directly or indirectly related to malignancy or therapy
options.B: Acquired immunodeficiency unrelated to the primary tumor or treatment
options.C: Long-term side effects occurring years after successful cancer remission
options.D: Primary psychiatric disorders triggered by a terminal cancer diagnosis

explanation: These emergencies stem directly from tumor growth, metabolic changes caused by cancer cells, or toxicities from aggressive treatment regimens. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h1)

question: Why do many patients in resource-limited settings frequently present with advanced oncologic emergencies?

options.A: Strict adherence to prophylactic metabolic suppression medications
options.B: Delays in initial presentation resulting in bulky, untreated disease masses
options.C: Over-prescription of outpatient chemotherapy by community pharmacists
options.D: Excessive availability of routine screening programs in rural areas

explanation: Late presentation with large tumor volumes significantly increases the likelihood of structural compression and metabolic crises. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h1)

question: Which electrolyte abnormality is a defining hallmark of Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: Hypokalemia
options.B: Hyperkalemia
options.C: Hypomagnesemia
options.D: Hyponatremia

explanation: The massive destruction of cancer cells releases large amounts of intracellular potassium directly into the systemic circulation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h2)

question: What is the primary mechanism behind Hypercalcemia of Malignancy?

options.A: Excessive dietary calcium intake by patients undergoing palliative cancer care
options.B: Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein leading to increased bone resorption
options.C: Kidney failure causing immediate retention of dietary calcium ions
options.D: Complete failure of the parathyroid glands due to metastatic infiltration

explanation: Certain tumors secrete PTHrP or cause direct osteolytic destruction, driving excessive calcium out of the bones and into the blood. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h2)

question: What is typically the earliest clinical symptom of Malignant Spinal Cord Compression?

options.A: Inability to feel temperature
options.B: Progressive back pain
options.C: Sudden complete paralysis
options.D: Loss of bowel control

explanation: Back pain often precedes neurological deficits by weeks and should be investigated urgently in any patient with a cancer history. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h3)

question: Which physical finding is most characteristic of Superior Vena Cava Syndrome?

options.A: Tracheal deviation to the left side
options.B: Marked lower extremity pitting edema
options.C: Asymmetrical peripheral pulses in the arms
options.D: Facial edema and distended neck veins

explanation: Obstruction of blood return from the upper body causes engorgement of jugular veins and swelling of the face, neck, and arms. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h3)

question: What defines Febrile Neutropenia in an oncology patient?

options.A: Normal temperature accompanied by elevated white blood cell counts
options.B: Low-grade fever occurring only during the administration of chemotherapy
options.C: An elevated neutrophil count alongside chronic systemic hypertension
options.D: Fever combined with a severely depressed absolute neutrophil count

explanation: The condition requires both documented fever and a low ANC, signaling an inability to fight off invading pathogens. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why is fever often the only warning sign of infection in a neutropenic patient?

options.A: Bacterial pathogens mutate to evade detection by standard blood culture bottles
options.B: The body lacks enough neutrophils to mount a standard inflammatory exudate or pus formation
options.C: Chemotherapy drugs completely numb the patient's sensory nerve endings
options.D: The liver fails to release acute-phase reactants during active systemic illness

explanation: Without sufficient neutrophils, traditional signs of localized infection like swelling, redness, and purulent exudate cannot form. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h4)

question: What is the primary rationale for conducting frequent neurological checks in patients at risk for spinal cord compression?

options.A: Detecting subtle motor or sensory changes before permanent paralysis develops
options.B: Measuring intracranial pressure changes secondary to cerebral metastasis
options.C: Assessing the baseline cognitive side effects of oral anti-nausea medications
options.D: Evaluating peripheral neuropathy caused by neurotoxic chemotherapy drugs

explanation: Early identification of nerve impairment allows for immediate corticosteroid and radiation or surgical intervention, preserving mobility. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h5)

question: A patient undergoing induction chemotherapy for leukemia has a temperature of 38.5°C and an absolute neutrophil count of 300 cells/mm³. What is the most appropriate immediate nursing action?

options.A: Wait for blood culture results to return before starting any medication
options.B: Initiate prescribed broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately
options.C: Discharge the patient with instructions to return if a rash develops
options.D: Administer oral paracetamol and advise the patient to rest in bed

explanation: Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency requiring rapid empiric antibiotic therapy without waiting for culture results. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h5)

question: Which medication is commonly used to rapidly lower serum uric acid levels in Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: Sodium bicarbonate
options.B: Rasburicase
options.C: Dexamethasone
options.D: Morphine sulfate

explanation: Rasburicase acts as an enzyme that metabolizes uric acid into allantoin, which is easily excreted by the kidneys. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary role of high-dose corticosteroids in managing structural oncologic emergencies?

options.A: Reducing peritumoral edema to relieve pressure on adjacent vital structures
options.B: Permanently eradicating the primary malignant tumor mass without surgery
options.C: Stimulating the bone marrow to produce red blood cells rapidly
options.D: Lowering systemic blood pressure to prevent hemorrhagic stroke

explanation: Corticosteroids decrease inflammation and swelling around the tumor, providing rapid relief in spinal cord and vena caval compression. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h6)

question: Which discharge instruction is most critical for a patient who has completed treatment for acute leukemia?

options.A: Report any fever or chills immediately, even if mild
options.B: Stop taking prescribed prophylactic antibiotics once home
options.C: Restrict fluid intake to prevent peripheral edema
options.D: Avoid all forms of physical movement to protect bones

explanation: Immunocompromised patients can deteriorate rapidly from hidden infections, making prompt reporting of fever essential for survival. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h7)

question: What is NOT a recommended component of discharge education for a patient at risk for oncologic emergencies?

options.A: Maintaining adequate oral hydration as permitted by the medical team
options.B: Knowing the direct emergency contact numbers for the oncology unit
options.C: Recognizing signs of facial swelling and upper body venous congestion
options.D: Waiting a full week at home to see if new neurological symptoms resolve on their own

explanation: Delaying medical evaluation for structural symptoms like numbness or weakness can lead to permanent, irreversible disability. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h7)

question: What is the term for programmed cell death that maintains normal tissue homeostasis?

options.A: Hypertrophy
options.B: Necrosis
options.C: Apoptosis
options.D: Metaplasia

explanation: Apoptosis is the regulated, programmed mechanism by which the body removes damaged or unnecessary cells without triggering inflammation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h1)

question: How do normal cells differ from neoplastic cells regarding growth signals?

options.A: Normal cells completely ignore systemic inhibitory signals
options.B: Neoplastic cells maintain precise cell cycle checkpoint control
options.C: Normal cells divide only when stimulated by specific growth factors
options.D: Neoplastic cells rely strictly on external replacement cues

explanation: Normal cellular proliferation is tightly governed by external cues and growth factors, whereas cancer cells multiply autonomously. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which characteristic is exclusively associated with malignant neoplasms rather than benign ones?

options.A: Metastasis
options.B: Fibrous capsule formation
options.C: Slow growth rate
options.D: High cellular differentiation

explanation: The ability to invade distant organs and form secondary tumors is a definitive hallmark of malignancy. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h2)

question: What does the term anaplasia mean in the context of tumor pathology?

options.A: Rapid encapsulation of a growing tissue mass
options.B: Excessive production of normal structural proteins
options.C: Complete cessation of cellular division
options.D: Loss of cellular differentiation and tissue organization

explanation: Anaplasia describes cells that have reverted to a primitive, unspecialized state, which is a key indicator of aggressive malignancy. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the normal physiological function of proto-oncogenes?

options.A: Forming a protective fibrous capsule around tissues
options.B: Inducing immediate apoptosis in healthy cells
options.C: Promoting normal cellular growth and division
options.D: Repairing double-stranded DNA breaks exclusively

explanation: Proto-oncogenes are standard regulatory genes that encourage necessary cell proliferation until they undergo mutation into oncogenes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h3)

question: What happens to cellular regulation when a tumor suppressor gene experiences a loss-of-function mutation?

options.A: Proto-oncogenes are automatically deactivated by the cytoplasm
options.B: The cell loses its inhibitory brakes and multiplies unchecked
options.C: Cellular division stops permanently across all body tissues
options.D: The cell immediately transforms into a benign, encapsulated mass

explanation: Tumor suppressor genes normally restrict cell division; their inactivation removes crucial checkpoints, allowing abnormal cells to proliferate. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which stage of carcinogenesis involves an irreversible genetic mutation caused by exposure to a carcinogen?

options.A: Promotion
options.B: Metastasis
options.C: Progression
options.D: Initiation

explanation: Initiation is the initial genetic alteration caused by a carcinogen interacting directly with cellular DNA. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h4)

question: How does the promotion stage differ from initiation during the development of a malignant neoplasm?

options.A: Promotion always results in immediate distant organ metastasis
options.B: Promotion relies entirely on the destruction of tumor suppressor genes
options.C: Promotion causes the initial permanent alteration in the DNA sequence
options.D: Promotion actively stimulates the proliferation of previously initiated cells

explanation: Promotion is a protracted phase where surviving initiated cells are repeatedly stimulated to multiply, expanding the abnormal cell population. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h4)

question: Which signaling protein is primarily responsible for stimulating tumor angiogenesis?

options.A: Vascular endothelial growth factor
options.B: Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor
options.C: Epithelial growth suppressor
options.D: Tumor necrosis factor alpha

explanation: VEGF is the key angiogenic factor released by hypoxic tumor cells to stimulate new blood vessel growth. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why is neoangiogenesis critical for the survival and expansion of a malignant neoplasm?

options.A: It converts malignant cells back into well-differentiated benign tissue
options.B: It halts the production of vascular endothelial growth factor
options.C: It supplies essential oxygen and nutrients to sustain rapid cellular division
options.D: It forms a thick protective capsule that prevents host immune destruction

explanation: Without new blood vessels, a tumor quickly outgrows its nutrient supply and undergoes necrosis or ceases to expand. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h5)

question: What type of enzymes do malignant cells secrete to degrade the basement membrane during invasion?

options.A: Matrix metalloproteinases
options.B: Vascular endothelial enzymes
options.C: Insulin-like growth factors
options.D: Cyclin-dependent kinases

explanation: Matrix metalloproteinases break down extracellular matrix components, allowing cancer cells to tunnel through physical barriers. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary role of cadherins in the context of tumor invasion?

options.A: They normally maintain tight cell-to-cell adhesion within tissues
options.B: They stimulate the growth of new capillaries into the tumor core
options.C: They induce rapid apoptosis in circulating cancer cells
options.D: They repair damaged DNA strands at cell cycle checkpoints

explanation: Cadherins hold cells together; their downregulation or loss is a crucial step that allows malignant cells to break away and migrate. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which surface protein do many tumor cells express to deactivate attacking T lymphocytes?

options.A: PD-L1
options.B: VEGF
options.C: Cadherin

explanation: Tumor cells often express programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), which binds to receptors on T cells and shuts down their immune response. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common mechanism by which tumors evade the host immune system?

options.A: Secreting immunosuppressive cytokines that dampen local immune cell activity
options.B: Downregulating major histocompatibility complex class I molecules to hide from cytotoxic T cells
options.C: Upregulating robust major histocompatibility complex expression to attract heavy immune destruction
options.D: Expressing immune checkpoint proteins that exhaust responding lymphocytes

explanation: Tumors avoid destruction by hiding from the immune system, typically through reducing or altering MHC expression rather than increasing it to invite attacks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is the initial phase of carcinogenesis where a permanent genetic alteration occurs in the cellular DNA?

options.A: Initiation
options.B: Promotion
options.C: Metastasis
options.D: Progression

explanation: Initiation is the first step in carcinogenesis where a carcinogen causes a permanent, irreversible change in the cellular DNA. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h1)

question: How do malignant cells typically spread from the primary tumor site to distant organs during the progression phase?

options.A: By direct cellular diffusion across skin layers
options.B: Via rapid absorption into the digestive tract
options.C: Through the lymphatic or circulatory systems
options.D: Through passive movement in interstitial fluid

explanation: Malignant cells gain the capacity to invade surrounding vessels, allowing them to travel through lymph and blood channels to establish secondary tumors elsewhere in the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which of the following is an example of primary cancer prevention?

options.A: Performing a routine screening mammogram
options.B: Staging a newly diagnosed lung tumor
options.C: Administering the Hepatitis B vaccine
options.D: Providing palliative care for advanced illness

explanation: Primary prevention aims to prevent the disease from ever occurring, which includes vaccination against cancer-causing viruses like Hepatitis B. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h2)

question: Why are dietary modifications emphasizing high fiber and plant-based foods considered effective risk reduction strategies?

options.A: They decrease exposure to potential chemical carcinogens and support healthy gastrointestinal motility
options.B: They completely reverse established DNA mutations in initiated cancer cells
options.C: They permanently neutralize the effects of oncogenic viral infections
options.D: They destroy circulating malignant cells before they can form a primary tumor

explanation: Dietary fiber reduces bowel transit time and limits mucosal contact with ingested toxins, lowering the risk of colorectal malignancies. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the primary goal of secondary cancer prevention?

options.A: Managing symptoms during terminal disease stages
options.B: Eliminating environmental exposure to chemical toxins
options.C: Detecting malignancies at an early, treatable stage
options.D: Preventing the initial genetic mutation from occurring

explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on screening and early detection to catch cancer before it advances or spreads. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h3)

question: What characteristic of a screening test ensures that individuals without the disease are correctly identified as negative?

options.A: Reliability
options.B: Sensitivity
options.C: Specificity
options.D: Portability

explanation: Specificity refers to the ability of a test to correctly identify those without the condition, thus avoiding false-positive results. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h3)

question: Which low-cost screening method is widely utilized in primary healthcare settings in Nigeria for early detection of cervical lesions?

options.A: Routine magnetic resonance imaging
options.B: Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound
options.C: Computed tomography scan
options.D: Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid

explanation: VIA is an affordable and accessible screening method used in resource-limited settings to inspect the cervix for precancerous changes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h4)

question: A 45-year-old market woman in a rural Nigerian community visits a primary health clinic asking about breast cancer checks. Given local resource constraints, what is the most practical initial screening action?

options.A: Perform a clinical breast examination and teach her self-breast examination
options.B: Refer her immediately to an urban center for a routine mammogram
options.C: Order a comprehensive serum tumor marker panel
options.D: Advise her to wait until she turns sixty years old

explanation: Where routine mammography is unavailable, clinical breast examination and self-examination are critical and accessible first-line screening tools. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h4)

question: What does the letter 'U' stand for in the CAUTION mnemonic used to identify cancer warning signs?

options.A: Urinary frequency and urgency
options.B: Ureteral blockage from a tumor
options.C: Unexplained upper abdominal pain
options.D: Unusual bleeding or discharge

explanation: In the CAUTION acronym, the letter U represents unusual bleeding or discharge from any body orifice. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which term describes the profound, unexplained weight loss and muscle wasting commonly seen in patients with advanced cancer?

options.A: Anasarca
options.B: Alkalosis
options.C: Azotemia
options.D: Cachexia

explanation: Cancer cachexia is a complex metabolic syndrome characterized by severe muscle wasting, fatigue, and fat loss that cannot be reversed nutritionally. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h5)

question: What does the letter 'M' represent in the TNM cancer staging system?

options.A: Lymph node involvement
options.B: Primary tumor size
options.C: Distant metastasis
options.D: Mitotic cell rate
